artigo.texto: Data centers viram alvo político nos EUA e ameaçam planos da big tech Resultados das eleições legislativas nos EUA revelam onda antidata center que já obriga empresas como OpenAI a rever políticas de transparência. As eleições legislativas americanas de 2025 entregaram mais do que uma virada política. Entregaram um recado direto para a indústria de tecnologia: a expansão desenfreada de data centers encontrou um limite concreto na resistência popular. Em dezenas de votações locais espalhadas pelo país, eleitores rejeitaram medidas que facilitariam a construção de novos centros de dados. E onde o tema não estava diretamente na cédula, os candidatos eleitos fizeram campanha prometendo restringir essas instalações. O caso mais emblemático é o do Texas, onde a governadora eleita Gina Hinojosa derrotou Greg Abbott com uma plataforma que incluía limitar a expansão de data centers no estado. O movimento não é trivial. O Texas é hoje um dos principais polos de infraestrutura digital dos Estados Unidos e abriga operações centrais de várias empresas de Elon Musk, que agora se vê em uma posição desconfortável. Meio bilhão de dólares e nenhum retorno político Musk doou cerca de meio bilhão de dólares para o Partido Republicano neste ciclo eleitoral. O resultado prático foi próximo de zero. Seus candidatos perderam em disputas-chave, e o Texas, estado onde concentrou suas operações empresariais, virou democrata pela primeira vez em décadas. É um cenário inédito. O maior doador republicano e um dos maiores construtores de infraestrutura de data centers do mundo opera agora sob um governo estadual que promete dificultar exatamente esse tipo de projeto. A ironia não escapou aos analistas do setor. Mas o problema de Musk é apenas a ponta mais visível de uma tendência mais ampla. A rejeição a data centers virou um fenômeno bipartidário, como já abordamos ao analisar os impactos da inteligência artificial na infraestrutura global. Republicanos, democratas e independentes em diversas regiões se uniram contra projetos que consideravam opacos e prejudiciais ao meio ambiente. Por que eleitores estão contra os data centers A resposta passa por três fatores que se acumularam nos últimos anos. Primeiro, o sigilo excessivo. Grandes empresas de tecnologia, as chamadas hyperscalers, frequentemente exigiam acordos de confidencialidade até de autoridades eleitas antes de compartilhar detalhes de seus projetos. Em muitos casos, a escala real das instalações só ficava clara após a aprovação. Segundo, o impacto ambiental. Data centers consomem volumes enormes de água para resfriamento. No sudoeste americano, onde a escassez hídrica já é uma crise, isso se tornou um ponto de atrito real. Uma única instalação de grande porte pode consumir milhões de litros de água por dia, competindo diretamente com o abastecimento residencial e agrícola. Terceiro, o consumo energético. Em um momento em que a demanda por energia dispara por conta da expansão acelerada da inteligência artificial, comunidades locais começaram a perceber que data centers pressionam as redes elétricas e, em alguns casos, elevam o custo da energia para os moradores. Essa combinação transformou o tema em uma questão genuinamente popular. Não foi uma pauta imposta de cima para baixo, mas algo que emergiu de comunidades que sentiram os efeitos no dia a dia. OpenAI já mudou de postura O mais revelador dos desdobramentos veio rápido. A OpenAI, uma das empresas que mais investem em infraestrutura de computação no mundo, publicou o que chamou de “política de campus de computação”. O documento traz mudanças relevantes: fim da exigência de NDAs para autoridades locais, compromisso de compartilhar planos com as comunidades e promessa de operar com mais transparência. O rebranding também chama atenção. A OpenAI evita deliberadamente o termo “data center” e adota “campus de computação”, uma tentativa clara de se distanciar de uma expressão que se tornou tóxica no debate público americano. É difícil imaginar que a troca de nomenclatura, por si só, mude a percepção popular. Mas as mudanças operacionais que a acompanham são concretas. O episódio ilustra uma dinâmica que investidores e analistas de mercado deveriam observar com atenção: quando o ambiente regulatório sinaliza restrições, as empresas se adaptam. Quando não há pressão, elas operam no limite do que é permitido. O que isso significa para o setor de tecnologia Os próximos dois anos serão mais difíceis para a expansão de infraestrutura digital nos Estados Unidos. E o problema pode se estender para 2028 e além, dependendo de como o sentimento popular evoluir. Para as big techs, o impacto é direto. A corrida pela inteligência artificial depende fundamentalmente de capacidade computacional, e capacidade computacional depende de data centers. Se a construção dessas instalações desacelerar, o ritmo de desenvolvimento de modelos de IA também pode ser afetado. Isso não significa que a expansão vai parar. Significa que vai custar mais, demorar mais e exigir negociações mais complexas com comunidades e governos locais. Empresas que anteciparam essa mudança e construíram relações transparentes com as comunidades terão vantagem. As que operaram no sigilo vão pagar o preço político. Para o mercado como um todo, o recado das urnas americanas é um lembrete de que infraestrutura tecnológica não existe no vácuo. Ela ocupa espaço físico, consome recursos naturais e afeta pessoas reais. Ignorar isso deixou de ser apenas uma falha ética. Agora é um risco de negócio mensurável. A questão que fica para os próximos trimestres é se esse movimento americano vai inspirar restrições semelhantes em outros países. Na Europa, onde a regulação de tecnologia já é mais rígida, a tendência pode se acelerar. No Brasil, onde a discussão sobre data centers ainda é incipiente, a experiência americana serve como antecipação do debate que inevitavelmente chegará. artigo.texto: Você sabe qual é o real impacto da Inteligência Artificial (IA)? Para processar todos os dados necessários, a inteligência artificial precisa de mega data centers: estruturas computacionais gigantes que ocupam áreas equivalentes a dezenas de campos de futebol e consomem tanta energia quanto países inteiros, causando impactos sociais, ambientais e climáticos em escala industrial. Essas imensas infraestruturas dependem de muitos minérios, territórios e milhões de litros d’água para funcionar sem pausa, além de encarecer as contas de luz, gerar ruído constante, agravar a escassez hídrica e aumentar as emissões de gases de efeito estufa. O Brasil é um dos alvos da expansão desses centros de dados de hiperescala, que estão chegando sem considerar os danos às pessoas, à natureza e ao controle de dados no nosso país. Alguns lugares nos Estados Unidos e na Europa já começaram a dizer não para suas instalações até que exista uma regulamentação rígida. É isso que queremos aqui também! Antes de trazer mega data centers pra cá, precisamos avaliar seus riscos e garantir que sirvam ao bem comum e à nossa soberania. Não podemos deixar que o lucro de bilionários das Big Techs passem na frente dos interesses do povo brasileiro. Parem os mega data centers! O que estamos pedindo? Queremos a paralisação imediata dos projetos de centro de dados de hiperescala no país, até que exista uma legislação capaz de garantir: - Consentimento e Transparência: As comunidades impactadas precisam ter participação social ativa e as comunidades tradicionais têm direito à consulta livre, prévia e informada. - Licenciamento Ambiental: Exigimos o Estudo e Relatório de Impacto Ambiental (EIA/RIMA), assegurando transição energética justa e excluindo zonas de alta sensibilidade ecológica e oferta de água limitada. - Fim da isenção de impostos: quem lucra com infraestrutura digital em larga escala deve devolver valor à sociedade, com investimento em pesquisa, projetos e autonomia tecnológica.

artigo.texto: Is this the only U.S. town to vote 'yes' on data centers? On Election Day, voters approved more than 40 measures to slow or ban data center growth. But not all Americans decided against data centers. The majority of voters in Harwood, North Dakota, said "no" to a ballot measure calling for additional steps when the town evaluates, approves, and administers developments like that of data centers, Tech Insider reported. In a town of 845 people, 430 voted, and around 75 percent voted against added restrictions. (As Tech Insider notes, however, that documentation on small towns could be varied — The Washington Post reports that Harwood's population is 845, while other outlets report 940.) The big project in question is a $3 billion, 1.8-million-square-foot data center right outside Harwood, the Washington Post reports. Data center developer Applied Digital is behind the project. You May Also Like The vote caused the Post to claim that Harwood is "the only town in the U.S. that said yes to data centers." artigo.texto: How We Found Eight Data Center Community Benefit Agreements and Why It Matters These days, data centers are the hot-button topic in policy circles everywhere. Between the explosion of AI and the sheer scale of some of these facilities, it seems like people cannot go a single day without hearing them come up in some capacity. Communities weighing a data center project are considering real opportunities: construction jobs, new tax revenue, and the promise of economic development that comes with a major capital investment landing in town. But they are also considering real costs. Data centers bring elevated noise, especially for homes sitting close to a facility; they also can consume significant amounts of water and energy, affecting rates and the energy grid. And the tax breaks that some of the data centers receive could outweigh any financial benefits the community gets in return. Local governments face a surmounting number of questions, with best practices not readily available. The policy decisions we make today will affect much of the work that comes tomorrow and the decades after that. Beginning in early 2026, FAS began interviewing experts in the field, as well as searching for executed agreements on data center developments that were difficult to find. This included tracking local government ordinances as well as finding Community Benefit Agreements (CBAs). Many times, the negotiations between data center developers and officials from the municipality or county are conducted behind closed doors, protected by non-disclosure agreements (NDAs). As a result, community members have significantly fewer opportunities to influence the terms by which the data center should abide by as a fixture in the community. In the spirit of increased transparency, FAS wants to share our experience of “flipping over rocks” and discovering the hard-to-find contract. This is how we discovered eight community benefit agreements and why it matters. Local Policy Levers: The Ordinance and The Contract Generally, local governments have two enforceable levers to create policies around data centers. First, an ordinance considers issues such as zoning, land use requirements, and other permitting features – ultimately providing a pathway to allowable activities (and specific limitations). The ordinance process includes a public comment period, and it applies to all projects that qualify under the definition of a “data center.” A CBA involves the power of contract law, crafting and entering into binding bilateral (or sometimes multilateral) agreements that dictate the expectations of each party. CBAs are helpful in cases where existing zoning and permitting do not specifically identify “data centers” as a specific type of property to regulate (this is most frequent as the proliferation of data centers is so new). However, CBAs can be negotiated with fewer public comment opportunities, and they are required on a case-by-case basis. CBAs are not a new legal concept, and they have been used for large scale projects before on major development projects, like airports or energy generation infrastructure. They very recently started to be used in the context of data centers, after the explosion in usage of AI. Thus, FAS went searching for every agreement that fit the CBA model. As of the time of this writing, only one fully executed and publicly posted CBA exists that pertains to data centers: The Lancaster AI Hub agreement entered into by the City of Lancaster, Pennsylvania and the developers of two large data center campuses in the city. Lancaster’s CBA contains many terms and conditions that are beneficial to a data center agreement with the host community. It covers community transparency, water use, energy, noise restrictions, funding for public works, decommissioning, and many more. However, this agreement appears to leave much of the substance to be decided later on. Oftentimes, it requires the parties to submit separate plans to the city which detail the specifics of how the developers will conduct themselves. Finding Agreements: Discovering CBAs Finding executed CBAs took expertise, a concentrated effort, and follow-up. To expand beyond the Lancaster CBA, FAS first turned to blog posts that mentioned CBAs from sources like the Brookings Institution and Columbia University to see if there were any stories about localities that are negotiating terms with data center developers, or that have already done so. Initially, that is how FAS found Cedar Rapids, IA, St. Louis, MO, and El Paso, TX. Then, we looked for news articles referencing data center construction in these cities to see if they mentioned anything about an agreement between the city and the developers. If the terms of the agreement, or even discussion about its existence, were covered in these articles, that was where we knew we had to dig deeper. While the majority of agreements found were publicly available, the only way to obtain some of them was through a public records request. Thankfully, most states did not have such broad prohibitions on what can be public record, allowing FAS to uncover more contracts to serve as references. Over the summer of 2026, seven other agreements were uncovered besides the one in Lancaster between cities, counties, and data center developers that mention community benefits: During the search for more agreements, FAS was making note of the trends in each one, and comparing trends among the different agreements. Many of these agreements contain a heavy focus on money and taxes. Tax abatements, exemptions, and Payment in Lieu of Taxes (PILOT) schemes served as incentives for the data centers to be built in various communities. artigo.texto: Riot Platforms Inc (Riot), a digital infrastructure and Bitcoin mining company has signed a 15 year lease with an unnamed Frontier AI Lab for its entire Corsicana data center campus in Texas, covering 910 MW of critical IT capacity and representing approximately US$ 28 billion in contracted revenue with AI safety and research company Antropic as the first tenant. According to a press release, the triple net powered land lease covers a contiguous 332 acre site and is expected to generate approximately US$ 1.8 billion in average annual rent over the initial term. Riot estimates a net operating income (NOI) margin of approximately 99 percent. The contract value could reach US$ 54 billion if the tenant exercises both five year extension options. The project will be delivered in three phases, 400 MW in September 2027, 200 MW in January 2028 and the remaining 310 MW in July 2028. Rent for each phase will begin no later than 60 days after delivery of its powered pads and will be payable on the full contracted capacity regardless of utilization. “Today, we are excited to announce the largest lease in Riot’s history: a 15-year triple-net powered land lease with a leading Frontier AI Lab for the entirety of our Corsicana campus, representing 910 megawatts of critical IT capacity and approximately $28 billion of contracted revenue over the initial term,” said Jason Les, CEO, Riot Platforms. “Together with our AMD contract and the lease signed with the same Frontier AI Lab at Rockdale earlier this year, Riot has contracted 1,151 megawatts and approximately US$ 38 billion of data center revenue, which we expect will generate more than US$ 2 billion of average annual net operating income at full deployment, firmly establishing Riot as a leading developer of large-scale digital infrastructure.” Riot estimates total capital costs of US$ 5.5 billion, or approximately US$ 6 million per IT MW, the company will contribute US$ 2 million per MW toward site work and electrical infrastructure. While the remaining US$ 4 million per MW will be reimbursed by the tenant in stages after each phase is delivered and begins generating rent. The reimbursements are expected to be financed through non-recourse project debt backed by contracted rental income. If financing on comparable market terms is unavailable, the tenant will fund the reimbursements directly and recover the amounts through credits against rent over the remaining lease term. Riot expects to fund its share from existing liquidity and does not currently anticipate issuing equity for the project.

artigo.texto: The United States Department of Energy (DOE) has launched the Battery Manufacturing Accelerator (BattMan), a national initiative to help bring new battery technologies into commercial production, strengthen domestic manufacturing, and reduce reliance on foreign sourcing. The BattMan Initiative BattMan’s aim is to bring together national labs, universities, and manufacturers to address difficulties in producing new battery technologies on a commercial scale. The initiative plans to use AI, digital models of manufacturing processes, and real-time monitoring to identify production problems earlier, improve manufacturing methods, and reduce costs. The program is led by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, with participation from Argonne National Laboratory, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and the National Laboratory of the Rockies. University partners include Arizona State University, Binghamton University, the University of Alabama, the University of Michigan–Dearborn, and the University of Washington. US Battery Supply Chain Although the DOE has recently invested heavily in domestic battery cell and pack manufacturing, production of the materials and components needed to make them has not increased at the same rate. As a result, the US still relies heavily on imported battery materials and components, particularly from China. US battery demand for transportation and electricity grid applications is projected to rise from 179 gigawatt-hours in 2025 to 707 gigawatt-hours by 2035. The DOE aims to establish a domestic battery supply chain covering everything from raw materials to finished products by 2030. BattMan will also focus on battery technologies that require fewer critical minerals and cost less to manufacture. Image credit: IM Imagery/Shutterstock

artigo.texto: Fortunes are diverging lately for Korean and Chinese companies competing in the global battery market. Expectations are rising that domestic manufacturers including LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI will keep improving results on stronger demand in the U.S. energy storage system (ESS) market. Chinese companies, by contrast, face a red light as oversupply worries and U.S. restrictions on Chinese-made products cloud growth. ◇ China's CATL grows in size, but profitability flashes warning signs According to the battery industry on the 9th, China's CATL, the world's largest battery maker, posted third-quarter revenue of 165.221 billion yuan (about 33.3 trillion won), up 58.9% from a year earlier. Net profit rose 14.5% to 21.246 billion yuan (about 4.3 trillion won). Despite double-digit increases in both revenue and net profit from a year earlier, the results fell well short of market expectations. London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) had projected CATL's third-quarter revenue growth rate at 60.2% and net profit growth rate at 41.2%, respectively. The underwhelming results were immediately reflected in the share price. On the 20th of last month, when the third-quarter results were released, CATL's stock on the Hong Kong market fell 6.6% from the previous day. Global investment bank JPMorgan also cut its rating on CATL shares listed in Hong Kong to Neutral from Overweight. Chinese battery makers including CATL continue to expand in scale. In particular, Chinese products have increased their share of the electric-vehicle market this year. Market researcher SNE Research said that from January through September, Chinese companies—seven suppliers including CATL—accounted for a 73% share of batteries installed in electric vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) and hybrids (HEVs) worldwide, up 3.5 percentage points from a year earlier. Korea's big three—LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On—had a 12.6% share, down 4.1 percentage points. The problem is profitability is slipping relative to topline growth. With domestic competition saturated, China has been pushing large volumes overseas at low prices. Automakers struggling amid cutthroat competition are also diversifying supply chains to smaller battery vendors that sell cheaply to cut costs, a trend seen as squeezing margins at major manufacturers including CATL. According to the South China Morning Post (SCMP), Chinese EV makers Xiaomi and Li Auto said they will team up with battery manufacturers such as CALB and EVE Energy to reduce battery procurement costs. CALB and EVE Energy are classified one tier below giants like CATL and BYD in China. ◇ Korean battery makers spread their wings on rising U.S. ESS demand Korean battery makers, by contrast, are beating market forecasts with improving results. They have struggled in EV batteries against a flood of cheap Chinese products, but demand for ESS batteries has surged in the United States, benefiting domestic suppliers. Samsung SDI posted third-quarter revenue of 4.6856 trillion won and operating profit of 407.8 billion won. Revenue rose 52.6% from a year earlier, and operating profit swung to a surplus from a 591.3 billion won loss. Operating profit, in particular, was twice the previous quarter's 203.8 billion won and the highest in 12 quarters since the third quarter of 2023. Samsung SDI's operating profit far beat the market consensus—an average forecast—of 235.4 billion won, an earnings surprise that stood in contrast to CATL. LG Energy Solution also saw revenue jump 59% in the same period to 9.6434 trillion won, while operating profit rose 25.7% to 756 billion won. Both were record highs on a quarterly basis. Its third-quarter operating profit was more than double the 320 billion won market consensus. Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution said soaring demand for ESS used in U.S. artificial intelligence (AI) data centers drove the improvement. A gradual recovery in Europe's EV market, which lifted EV battery sales, was also a tailwind. ◇ U.S. midterms: Democrats win by a landslide; ESS demand seen rising, China curbs to continue Industry officials expect the U.S. ESS market to grow quickly, likely extending domestic makers' run of stronger results. Many also see the Democrats' landslide in the U.S. midterms held on the 3rd—on a platform of expanding energy infrastructure including ESS—as a boon for Korean companies. Voice of America (VOA) reported on the 9th that although counting was not yet complete, the Democrats had already secured 252 of the 435 House seats, far more than a majority and beating the Republicans' 161. They also won 52 Senate seats to the Republicans' 44. In gubernatorial races, Democrats won in 28 states, ahead of Republicans who won in 20. The Democrats announced in May an energy agenda that included plans to expand investment in the national power grid and energy storage systems (ESS). While they take a dim view of regulating AI data center construction, they intend to keep growing the ESS market as part of grid expansion. Hyundai Motor Securities said in a pre-midterm report, "If Democrats control both chambers, they will push to restore renewable energy tax credits and expand ESS investment," adding, "Both parties have previously toughened tariff policy on Chinese batteries, so the post-election direction will likely remain to block China's supply chain." Some, however, see a chance for a rebound by Chinese battery makers. China is also ramping up ESS investment, and once plants under construction in Europe start up, they could further encroach on Europe's EV battery market. The European Union (EU) is currently imposing high tariffs on Chinese EVs. It is also finalizing details of the Industrial Acceleration Act (IAA), pursued to counter China and protect domestic industry, ahead of its entry into force. artigo.texto: - Australian Vanadium awarded $15 million from Investment Attraction Fund (IAF) to establish vanadium electrolyte manufacturing facility - IAF supporting a diversified economy and unlocking private sector investment - Funds will support large-scale battery installations as well as increasing local content in the vanadium flow battery supply chain The Cook Labor Government has awarded $15 million through the Investment Attraction Fund (IAF) New Energies Industries Round 2 to Australian Vanadium Limited (AVL) to establish a high-capacity, relocatable vanadium electrolyte manufacturing facility in Western Australia. The project will expand AVL's capacity to produce vanadium electrolyte to support large-scale battery installations as well as increasing local content in the vanadium flow battery supply chain. Vanadium flow batteries use liquid vanadium electrolyte solutions in separate tanks to both store and release electricity. Skilled employment and training opportunities in advanced manufacturing, chemical processing, engineering, construction, commissioning, and plant operations will be created, while its modular and relocatable design enables deployment across regional and industrial centres throughout the State. The project presents an opportunity for the State to further invest in energy transition initiatives by supporting grid-scale energy storage, strengthening critical minerals supply chains, and help to build local industries required for a low-carbon future. The IAF funding will also support the development of grid-scale vanadium flow batteries and long-duration energy storage infrastructure in the State. The IAF has supported 47 projects since first launching in 2022 with over $215.2 million in funding awarded, generating 290 direct jobs and 1,479 contractors engaged. To date, more than $4 in spending is generated from every $1 distributed through the fund. For more information on the IAF, see: Investment Attraction Fund As stated by State Development and Economic Diversification Minister David Michael: "The Investment Attraction Fund continues to play a critical role in attracting projects that strengthen Western Australia's industrial capabilities and support our energy transition. "By supporting AVL's electrolyte manufacturing capability, we're creating new opportunities in advanced manufacturing while helping position WA at the forefront of long-duration energy storage technologies. "The development of a high-capacity vanadium electrolyte facility will support local jobs, strengthen our manufacturing capability, and provide the foundations for future grid-scale battery projects across the State." As stated by Energy and Decarbonisation and Manufacturing Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson: "The Cook Labor Government wants to see more things made right here in WA. "Our Made in WA plan is working, with new data showing manufacturing jobs have risen 13 per cent over the past year. "This is another great example of the Cook Labor Government backing innovative Western Australian manufacturing projects."

artigo.texto: Diferentemente dos sistemas de alimentação ininterrupta (UPS) convencionais, o BESS (Sistema de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias) é um sistema de armazenamento de energia em larga escala conectado diretamente à rede elétrica. O sistema pode carregar e armazenar eletricidade em momentos apropriados e devolvê-la à rede quando necessário. O BESS pode ser concebido como uma "instalação de armazenamento de energia" capaz de operar em duas direções: quando o sistema está em estado de flutuação, o BESS recebe eletricidade para armazenamento; quando há necessidade de suporte, o sistema gera eletricidade de volta para a rede. Dessa forma, o BESS pode contribuir para suavizar a curva de demanda, reduzir a pressão durante os horários de pico e aumentar a flexibilidade da operação do sistema elétrico. Com a crescente demanda por eletricidade e as significativas flutuações de carga dependendo do clima e da hora do dia, a melhoria da capacidade operacional do sistema elétrico de Hanói exige não apenas investimentos em fontes de energia e redes, mas também em novas soluções tecnológicas. Antecipando a tendência da tecnologia de armazenamento de energia, a EVNHANOI concluiu a instalação, energização e operação piloto de cinco sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) nas subestações de 110 kV de Bac Thang Long, Quang Minh, Sai Dong 2, Phung Xa e Thanh Oai. Cada sistema possui capacidade de armazenamento de 10 MW/20 MWh, elevando a capacidade total de armazenamento para 50 MW/100 MWh. Esta é a primeira vez que a tecnologia de armazenamento de energia em larga escala é aplicada à rede elétrica de Hanói, representando um novo passo na modernização da infraestrutura de energia e no desenvolvimento de uma rede inteligente. A seleção das subestações para o projeto piloto baseou-se nas características de carga e nos requisitos operacionais da rede elétrica de Hanói. O sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) é uma tecnologia completamente nova na rede elétrica da capital. Desde a instalação, testes e energização até a operação oficial, as unidades da EVNHANOI trabalharam em estreita coordenação para garantir que o sistema atendesse plenamente aos requisitos técnicos e operasse de forma estável e segura. Durante a operação, a equipe técnica monitora continuamente o status das baterias, a capacidade de carga e descarga, a temperatura, os sistemas de proteção e os alertas técnicos. Cada turno de inspeção é realizado de acordo com procedimentos rigorosos, com coordenação entre a equipe de despacho, a unidade de gestão técnica e a equipe diretamente na subestação para garantir que todos os parâmetros permaneçam dentro dos limites de segurança. O processo de operação prática também proporciona à EVNHANOI a oportunidade de acumular dados, aprimorar os procedimentos técnicos, avaliar a confiabilidade dos equipamentos e adquirir experiência em gestão para uma tecnologia ainda muito recente no Vietnã. Segundo o Sr. Pham Huu Manh, Diretor Adjunto do Conselho de Gestão do Projeto de Desenvolvimento de Energia de Hanói, a implementação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) não visa substituir as fontes de energia existentes, mas sim adicionar uma ferramenta técnica que ajude o sistema elétrico a ser mais proativo na resposta às flutuações de carga, além de criar uma base para a pesquisa de modelos modernos de operação da rede no futuro. Quando combinado com sistemas de coleta de dados, monitoramento, controle e gestão de energia, automação da rede e tecnologias digitais , o BESS deixa de ser apenas um sistema de armazenamento de energia e se torna um elo na estrutura de uma rede inteligente. No próximo período, a EVNHANOI continuará monitorando e avaliando a eficiência operacional, aprimorando os procedimentos técnicos e pesquisando soluções de aplicação adequadas. Isso servirá de base para a construção gradual de uma rede elétrica mais inteligente, flexível, segura e moderna na capital, atendendo às necessidades do desenvolvimento socioeconômico e melhorando a qualidade do fornecimento de energia elétrica para a população de Hanói.

artigo.texto: When using electric vehicles or smartphones, users often experience inconvenience from long charging times and gradually shortening battery life. To increase charging speed and extend usage time, next-generation batteries with high energy density are essential. However, fast charging has had limitations because deposits can accumulate inside batteries, degrading performance and even increasing the risk of fire. A Korean research team has developed a new foundational technology to address this problem by creating a "highway" through which lithium ions can move rapidly inside a battery. KAIST (President Choongsik Bae) announced on November 9 that a joint research team led by Professors Dong Ki Yoon and Hye Ryung Byon from the Department of Chemistry developed a next-generation battery separator technology that precisely controls lithium-ion transport pathways by regulating the molecular alignment of liquid-crystalline polymers. Lithium metal batteries can store more energy than conventional batteries. However, during charging, lithium can accumulate in sharp, branch-like structures known as "dendrites." This phenomenon has been a major cause of reduced battery life and can damage the internal separator, potentially leading to explosions. The research team sought to solve this problem using liquid crystal materials, which combine the ordered characteristics of solids with the fluidity of liquids. Because the orientation of liquid crystal molecules can be altered through surface treatment and other methods, the researchers used this property to regularly align the pathways through which lithium ions travel. Based on this liquid-crystal alignment control technology, the team also created a porous liquid-crystalline polymer separator containing nanoscale pores. Polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains, which facilitate lithium-ion transport, were incorporated into the separator. In particular, the researchers freely controlled the alignment direction of the liquid-crystal molecules either vertically or horizontally and compared the resulting lithium-ion transport characteristics. The results showed that the liquid-crystalline polymer separator with vertically aligned molecules formed a kind of "highway" that allowed lithium ions to move directly toward the electrodes. Compared with a horizontally aligned separator, it reduced the tortuosity of the ion transport pathway by approximately 2.5-fold, enabling lithium ions to move much faster and more uniformly. This effectively suppressed dendrite formation and significantly improved stability. The research team applied the newly developed separator to an actual lithium metal battery and verified its fast-charging performance. Even under demanding fast-charging conditions at a high charging rate of 4 C*, the battery retained 94% of its initial capacity after 100 charge-discharge cycles. This demonstrates that controlling the molecular alignment of liquid-crystalline polymers can be a highly effective strategy for improving both the charging speed and lifespan of next-generation batteries. *4C charging rate: A rate at which a battery can theoretically be fully charged in approximately 15 minutes based on its rated capacity. C is a unit indicating the charging and discharging rate of a battery: 1C corresponds to 1 hour, 2C to 30 minutes, and 4C to 15 minutes. Professor Dong Ki Yoon said, "This study demonstrates that controlling the molecular alignment of liquid-crystalline polymers can be used to efficiently design lithium-ion transport pathways and thereby improve battery performance and stability," adding, "We expect this approach to contribute to the development of high-energy-density next-generation battery technologies, for which long driving ranges and rapid charging are essential." Geunjung Lee, a Ph.D. student at KAIST, and Dr. Rak Hyeon Choi participated in the study as co-first authors, while Professors Hye Ryung Byon and Dong Ki Yoon participated as co-corresponding authors. The research was published in the international journal ACS Nano in September 2026. Paper title: Directional Li+ Flux Control via Liquid-Crystalline Polymer Separators for Fast-Charging Lithium Metal Batteries, DOI: https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.6c09591 Author information: Geunjung Lee†, Rak Hyeon Choi†, Geonhyeong Park, Juri Kim, Younwoo Kim, Hye Ryung Byon*, Dong Ki Yoon*; † co-first authors, * corresponding authors. This research was supported by the Mid-Career Researcher Program of the Ministry of Science and ICT and the National Research Foundation of Korea, as well as the GIST InnoCORE Program.

TNP Solution, a specialist in next-generation secondary batteries, has successfully completed a field demonstration of an energy storage system (ESS) linked to solar power in a multi-housing complex using aqueous zinc-ion batteries, and is accelerating its push toward commercialization. The company announced that it completed the "Demonstration of High-Safety Energy Storage System Based on Aqueous Zinc Batteries Linked to Solar Power" as the lead organization for the "2025 Climate Change Response Innovative Technology Demonstration Project," which is being promoted by Seoul City and managed by the Seoul Research Institute. Professor Kim Chan-hoon's research team at Hanyang University participated as a technology cooperation partner, while the Seoul Housing and Communities Corporation (SH) served as the demonstration site operator. This demonstration is significant because it involved operating an aqueous zinc-ion battery-based ESS linked to solar power generation equipment in an actual multi-housing complex where residents live, rather than in a laboratory setting. The company explained that through the process of storing generated solar power in batteries and supplying it when needed, it verified the feasibility of charge/discharge control, integration with power conversion devices, and system operation. For batteries to be installed in living spaces inside and outside buildings, verification is required not only for cell-level performance but also for safety, system control, and operational reliability. TNP Solution plans to utilize the operational experience gained from this demonstration in the product development of future urban-type ESS and building energy storage systems. Kang Seong-gu, CEO of TNP Solution Co., Ltd., stated confidently during a phone interview with this outlet, "The safety of batteries is a value that cannot be compromised in spaces where actual citizens carry out their daily lives." He added, "This demonstration marks a turning point proving that aqueous zinc batteries are high-safety energy solutions immediately applicable in real-life environments, going beyond the laboratory level. We will actively pioneer the urban power market, which absolutely requires safety and reliability, differentiating ourselves from markets focused on high density." Meanwhile, the "aqueous zinc-ion battery" is a secondary battery that has recently attracted attention. As the adoption of solar power and distributed power sources expands, total costs—including energy density, fire safety, installation costs, and maintenance fees—are becoming increasingly important in domestic and international ESS markets. In particular, in spaces where people reside or essential facilities are located, such as multi-housing complexes, hospitals, data centers, and telecommunications facilities, battery safety is a core condition for adoption. An aqueous zinc-ion battery is a secondary battery that utilizes a water-based electrolyte and a zinc metal anode. By using a non-flammable aqueous electrolyte, it can minimize the risk of ignition from the electrolyte itself. Additionally, by utilizing relatively abundant zinc, it possesses competitiveness in terms of raw material and manufacturing costs. Although it may have lower energy density than lithium-ion batteries, it is gaining attention as an alternative or complementary technology for stationary ESS, UPS, emergency power for telecommunications facilities, and industrial applications where safety and economic efficiency are prioritized. *This content was translated by AI.View Original

artigo.texto: Voters just told pollsters, loudly, that they do not want a data center down the road. An NBC News exit poll reported that 76% of voters opposed building a new data center in their community, and the Associated Press reported the same roughly three-quarters share. Yet the AI industry still needs the buildings, the chips and the power that those facilities concentrate in one place. That tension is the political story of November 2026, and it sits at the center of where AI model development goes next. The ballot results backed up the polling. According to The Detroit News, voters in at least 29 jurisdictions passed data-center bans or restrictions on November 3, 2026. The New York Times counted 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives going against the industry. We tracked the early returns in our report on 41 data center votes putting the AI boom on notice, and this piece takes the next step: what the backlash means for the people who build and fund AI models. A caution on the framing first. Headlines this week say voters “hate” data centers, and that phrase is not what the polling shows. The numbers confirm opposition to proposed facilities in voters’ own communities. They do not confirm a blanket rejection of every data center, and they do not confirm that voters understand how much of the AI stack depends on them. The gap between those two readings is where the next two years of policy will be fought. For wider context on the models themselves, see our AI and machine learning coverage. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What the NBC Exit Poll Actually Measured The headline number from NBC News is the 76% share of voters who opposed building a new data center in their community. That is a question about a specific, local, physical thing. It asks whether a respondent wants a building, its noise, its traffic and its power draw near their home. Voters answer that kind of question differently from an abstract one about whether AI is good for the country. The same poll then asked how much data centers mattered to the congressional vote. NBC reported that 23% of voters called them “crucial” to their choice, and 33% called them a “major” factor. Add those two groups together and you reach 56%, which matches a separate report summarizing the NBC findings as showing that 56% of voters viewed AI and data centers as a crucial or major factor in their vote. The Associated Press framed the same finding more narrowly, reporting that about one-quarter of voters called AI data centers crucial to their vote for Congress. Those figures deserve a careful read. A voter who ranks an issue as “major” has not necessarily switched parties over it. Nothing in the reported results tells us how many votes actually moved, or in which direction. What the numbers do establish is salience. A topic that barely registered in national polling a few years ago now shows up as a top-tier concern for more than half the electorate, according to the NBC exit poll as summarized in that separate report. We covered the salience angle in more detail in our piece on how midterms put AI on trial. The short version is that the industry can no longer treat local siting fights as isolated zoning disputes. They now function as a national referendum, fought one county at a time. 29 Jurisdictions and 40 of 41 Local Measures Two outlets counted the local results in slightly different ways, and both counts point the same direction. The Detroit News reported that voters in at least 29 jurisdictions passed data-center bans or restrictions on November 3. The New York Times reported that in 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives, voters chose to limit or prevent data-center development. The two figures measure different universes, so they should not be added together or treated as a contradiction. A 40-to-1 split is rare in American politics. Most ballot measures on contested land use come out closer, because developers can usually point to jobs and tax revenue. That the industry lost nearly every contest suggests the usual promises of local economic benefit failed to persuade. The reported results do not tell us why in each case, and we have no verified breakdown of turnout or margins for individual measures, so we will not guess at them. It is also worth separating what a ban or restriction does from what it prevents. A local measure can block a new facility without touching existing ones. It can also set conditions, such as approval requirements, that slow construction without stopping it. The reporting we have confirms that voters chose to limit or prevent development. It does not give a uniform definition of the rules that now apply across those jurisdictions, and readers should treat each measure as its own legal text. Ohio Sits at the Center of the Backlash The New York Times reported that more than half of those 40 successful initiatives were in Ohio. That concentration matters. It means the national count owes a large share of its weight to a single state where organized opposition, local politics and a heavy pipeline of proposed facilities collided at once. The statewide race pointed the same way. According to The Detroit News, Amy Acton was reported as winning election as Ohio’s next governor, and the report said she favored a moratorium and tougher regulations on the industry. We should be precise here. The report describes her policy preference. It does not tell us what legislation she will propose, whether the legislature will go along, or how a state-level moratorium would interact with the local measures already passed. For AI companies planning capacity, Ohio is a warning about concentration risk. A region can look like an ideal site on paper, with land, fiber and power access, and still turn hostile once several projects arrive close together. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no COP31 começa nesta segunda (9) na Turquia com Brasil no centro do debate climático e data centers na agenda Publicado 08/11/2026 • 19:44 | Atualizado há 11 horas KEY POINTS A 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31) começa nesta segunda-feira (9), em Antalya, na Turquia, com o Brasil no centro das discussões sobre a continuidade dos compromissos assumidos na COP30, em Belém, e uma nova frente de debates sobre o impacto ambiental dos data centers. Até 20 de novembro, representantes de governos, empresas e organizações internacionais discutirão como ampliar o financiamento climático, acelerar a transição energética e abastecer a expansão da inteligência artificial com eletricidade de fontes renováveis. A COP é o principal fórum multilateral de decisões climáticas vinculado à Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima. As negociações buscam transformar os objetivos do Acordo de Paris em medidas de redução de emissões, adaptação aos eventos extremos e apoio financeiro e tecnológico aos países mais vulneráveis. A conferência será presidida pela Turquia, com o ministro Murat Kurum indicado para comandar a COP31. O australiano Chris Bowen terá a função de presidente das negociações, em um arranjo que divide as responsabilidades políticas e diplomáticas do encontro. Leia também: COP30 termina com aprovação do Pacote de Belém e foco em implementação climática Entre os temas centrais estão a passagem dos compromissos climáticos para a execução, a ampliação dos investimentos em energia limpa e a redução da dependência de combustíveis fósseis. Os governos também discutirão medidas de adaptação, como proteção contra secas, enchentes e ondas de calor. O financiamento climático será outro ponto decisivo: países em desenvolvimento cobram recursos mais acessíveis para reduzir emissões e enfrentar perdas e danos associados a eventos extremos. Também entram no debate mercados de carbono, proteção de florestas e infraestrutura resiliente. A COP31 marca ainda o início do segundo balanço global do Acordo de Paris, processo destinado a avaliar coletivamente o avanço dos países e identificar onde é necessário acelerar a ação climática. Leia também: Presidência da COP30 propõe cronograma global para abandonar combustíveis fósseis até 2033 A expansão dos data centers, instalações que sustentam serviços digitais e sistemas de inteligência artificial, terá espaço específico na programação paralela da conferência. Na terça-feira (10), o Pavilhão da Itália receberá um encontro sobre soluções para abastecer essas estruturas com energia limpa e avaliar seus benefícios climáticos. O evento reunirá especialistas em planejamento energético e infraestrutura digital. Na segunda-feira (16), a Agência Internacional de Energias Renováveis (Irena) e a Global Renewables Alliance organizarão uma discussão sobre data centers verdes, consumo de eletricidade e integração com as redes elétricas. Entre os pontos previstos estão o uso de energia renovável, a transparência das informações de consumo e formas de evitar que a demanda da inteligência artificial amplie a geração baseada em combustíveis fósseis. A programação de Ação Digital Verde também inclui o Compromisso de Antalya sobre Inteligência Artificial, iniciativa da presidência da COP31 para incentivar práticas digitais alinhadas às metas climáticas. No mesmo dia 16, o Pavilhão Brasil receberá o lançamento do AI Climate Institute. Esses eventos integram a agenda de debates e iniciativas da conferência, sem representar, por si só, um acordo obrigatório entre os países. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC A Cúpula de Líderes ocorrerá na quarta-feira (11) e na quinta-feira (12). O presidente turco Recep Tayyip Erdoğan e o secretário-geral da ONU, António Guterres, estão previstos na abertura. O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva também participará, conforme confirmação do governo brasileiro. Entre os nomes esperados estão ainda o primeiro-ministro britânico Andy Burnham e outras autoridades nacionais. A programação de alto nível prevê discursos, encontros bilaterais e mesas sobre eletrificação, indústria verde, financiamento, adaptação urbana e proteção das florestas. Além dos chefes de Estado, terão papéis importantes Murat Kurum, na presidência da conferência, Chris Bowen, na condução das negociações, e representantes de organizações internacionais, do setor privado e de comunidades afetadas pela mudança do clima. Leia também: Lula participará da COP31 na Turquia O Brasil chega à COP31 depois de sediar a COP30, em Belém, e pretende manter protagonismo nas negociações. Lula participará da cúpula de 11 e 12 de novembro e deverá defender medidas concretas de transição energética, combate ao desmatamento e financiamento da proteção florestal. A presidência brasileira da COP30 levará à conferência propostas de mapas do caminho para o afastamento dos combustíveis fósseis e para a reversão do desmatamento. O governo também pretende ampliar o apoio ao Fundo Florestas Tropicais para Sempre (TFFF) e apresentar resultados de políticas ambientais brasileiras. O Pavilhão Brasil será o principal espaço nacional na Zona Azul, área reservada às negociações oficiais. Organizado pelo Ministério do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima, pela presidência da COP30 e pela ApexBrasil, reunirá governos, povos indígenas, comunidades tradicionais, empresas, universidades e organizações sociais. A programação inclui debates sobre energia eólica, combustíveis sustentáveis, financiamento verde, mercados de carbono, agroecologia, cidades resilientes, proteção indígena e uso de tecnologia na política climática. A inauguração do pavilhão está prevista para segunda-feira (9). Leia também: Governo aprova 18 diretrizes para reduzir dependência de combustíveis fósseis O resultado da COP31 dependerá de acordos entre países com interesses e capacidades econômicas

artigo.texto: NVIDIA has just come through a sharp pullback, with the stock down over the past month and year after a very large multiyear rise. This leaves a straightforward question for you as an investor: Are today's cash flows, and the ones buyers expect over time, enough to support the current share price after this reset? - Over the past 5 years, NVIDIA has returned roughly 5x. This means a lot of future cash generation is already embedded in expectations and needs to be weighed carefully against the recent slump. - Fresh scrutiny over AI data center regulation, export controls and the CEO misconduct probe can influence how quickly data center demand translates into cash inflows and how much capital NVIDIA may need to commit to maintain its position. - What if you looked at NVIDIA through its earnings instead? See what NVIDIA's 23.4x P/E says about the price. For investors, the debate is whether NVIDIA's recent price, after the sell off and rebound attempts, is adequately supported by the cash it produces and is expected to produce in the years ahead. If you want to test the same cash flow question you are asking of NVIDIA across a wider set of AI infrastructure plays, take a look at 53 AI infrastructure stocks. Is NVIDIA Still Cheap on Cash Flow? The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model here focuses on the cash Nvidia can return to shareholders over time. On the latest twelve month view, Nvidia generated roughly $126.7b of free cash flow, and the model assumes those cash flows keep growing rather than shrinking from that base. Projected free cash flows step up materially into the early 2030s, then slow into a more measured second stage as the business matures in the model. That path helps explain why the DCF outcome sits substantially above the current share price of $186.64, even after the recent pullback. The Democratic midterm sweep, and the renewed focus on AI data center regulation it triggered, helps explain why the market price can still sit below what these cash flow projections support. Find out what NVIDIA could be worth using our Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) estimate. The NVIDIA Narrative: What Would Justify Today's Price? NVIDIA's valuation puzzle only really comes into focus once you spell out the futures that might justify it. Simply Wall St Narratives on the Community page do that explicitly by linking different views of NVIDIA's potential on growth, profitability and earnings to what the stock could be worth under each path, and each one anchors its number to a clear view of where expansion, margins and key risks might go next so you can revisit the logic as fresh information turns up.

artigo.texto: BYD Yangwang Altior Debuts as Ultra-Luxury Flagship Sedan – 1,000 km Range, 5.6-Metre Length and Limited Production BYD's premium Yangwang brand has unveiled the Altior in Abu Dhabi, challenging established luxury carmakers with an imposing executive sedan featuring coach doors, a lavish four-seat cabin and next-generation battery technology. Chinese automotive giant BYD has taken another significant step into the global ultra-luxury automobile market with the unveiling of the Yangwang Altior, a flagship executive sedan designed to compete with some of the world's most prestigious luxury cars. Unveiled in Abu Dhabi on November 7, 2026, the Altior represents Yangwang's latest attempt to establish itself as an alternative to established European luxury manufacturers, particularly Mercedes-Maybach, Bentley and Rolls-Royce. Measuring an imposing 5.6 metres in length, the new sedan combines an executive-focused interior, distinctive coach doors and BYD's latest battery technology. The manufacturer is initially accepting pre-orders for an exclusive four-seat limited edition, with production restricted to just 399 examples worldwide. The limited-edition model is expected to cost approximately 2.08 million yuan (around ₹2.8 crore, indicative), although the final selling price has not been confirmed. Yangwang Altior – Key Highlights Exterior Design – A 5.6-Metre Luxury Limousine The Altior's styling reflects Yangwang's ambition to move beyond conventional premium vehicles and compete in the chauffeur-driven luxury segment. Its imposing front fascia incorporates a gemstone-inspired grille, drawing design inspiration from traditional Chinese ceremonial vessels. The sedan also features an elaborate two-tone exterior finish, enclosed alloy-wheel styling and floating wheel-centre emblems. One of the most distinctive elements is its rear-hinged coach doors. Opening to almost 90 degrees, these doors are designed to provide more convenient access to the rear passenger compartment. Integrated umbrella storage adds another traditional luxury-car touch. The Altior's 3,500 mm wheelbase is particularly noteworthy. Rather than prioritising compact exterior dimensions, Yangwang has designed the vehicle around maximising passenger space and creating a commanding road presence. Its substantial width of 2,030 mm further reinforces its positioning as a full-size executive limousine. Interior – Four-Seat Executive Lounge Inside, the Altior takes a passenger-first approach, with its initial four-seat configuration emphasising rear-seat luxury rather than maximum seating capacity. Two individual rear seats are separated by an elaborate centre console, creating a private executive environment. The seats incorporate leg rests, while champagne-glass holders, rear-seat controls and electrically operated privacy sunshades further enhance the chauffeur-driven experience. The interior combines quilted upholstery with decorative wood and metallic trim. Yangwang has also incorporated Chinese design influences to differentiate the Altior from its European competitors. The first special edition, named Shanhe Dingyun, features an exclusive brown-and-white colour scheme with details including jade-decorated air vents, gold-finished speaker grilles and unique commemorative badges. A conventional five-seat configuration is planned for a later stage, potentially broadening the car's appeal beyond customers seeking a dedicated executive limousine. Battery Technology – Over 1,000 km Claimed Range Despite its emphasis on luxury, the Altior also serves as a showcase for BYD's battery development. The sedan incorporates the company's second-generation Blade Battery technology alongside its latest Flash Charging system. Yangwang has quoted a driving range exceeding 1,000 km under China's CLTC testing cycle. However, it is important to distinguish the claimed test-cycle figure from real-world driving performance. Actual range will depend on driving conditions, speed, climate control usage and other factors. Yangwang has not yet fully clarified the model's production powertrain configuration. Detailed specifications covering battery capacity, motor output and charging duration also remain to be officially established. Limited Edition – Just 399 Units Worldwide Yangwang has opened pre-orders in China for the four-seat Shanhe Dingyun limited edition, with customers required to pay a deposit of 300,000 yuan. Only 399 examples of this edition will be offered globally, giving it an exclusivity-driven positioning from the outset. The anticipated price of 2.08 million yuan would place the Altior considerably above mainstream luxury sedans, signalling that BYD intends to compete on exclusivity, technology and craftsmanship rather than affordability. Yangwang is also offering exclusive customer experiences, including private previews, dedicated purchase consultants and priority test drives. The company has not confirmed the Altior's broader international delivery schedule or an India launch. Auto Punditz Analysis – Can BYD Challenge Europe's Ultra-Luxury Dominance? The Yangwang Altior marks an important shift in BYD's global ambitions. While the Chinese manufacturer has established a strong presence in mass-market electric vehicles, its latest flagship demonstrates an effort to compete at the highest end of the automotive industry. Three developments stand out. - First, BYD is moving beyond volume-driven growth. The Altior is unlikely to generate substantial sales volumes, particularly with its limited-edition positioning. Instead, the vehicle could strengthen BYD's brand image and demonstrate its technological and manufacturing capabilities to affluent customers. - Second, Chinese manufacturers are increasingly challenging established luxury brands. Traditionally, the ultra-luxury segment has been dominated by European manufacturers whose reputations have been built over decades. artigo.texto: Safety risks, noise and location are top concerns as Douglas County gathers input for battery energy storage rules photo by: Josie Heimsoth/Journal-World As Douglas County weighs rules for battery energy storage facilities, residents raised questions about fire hazards, toxic gases and risks to nearby communities. The county held the drop-in event on Friday afternoon to gather feedback from the community about battery energy storage systems, or BESS, to figure out where they should be allowed in unincorporated Douglas County and at what point should it require a permit. While BESSes can be installed in homes occupying residential solar systems, the county is interested in implementing regulations of the larger-scale facilities – whether they consist of rows of large, weatherproof shipping containers or metal enclosures packed with interconnected battery models. A BESS is not currently defined in the county’s zoning regulations, but it is addressed only as an accessory to a solar development. photo by: Josie Heimsoth/Journal-World When it came to some of the biggest concerns about BESS, community members pointed to fire safety. If a large facility caught on fire, people wondered about the methods firefighters would use to extinguish it. One attendee also questioned whether water could safely be used to fight a battery fire, adding that some fires could burn for days and potentially release harmful gases. County planner Karl Bauer said as the department continues research, they will explore requirements such as defensible perimeters, containment systems, adequate setbacks and plume analysis studies that could help determine whether evacuations would be necessary in certain situations. Where the facilities should be allowed in unincorporated Douglas County and how their presence could affect the surrounding land also prompted questions. While some preferred BESS installations to only be allowed with industrial developments, some said they could be allowed in areas with agricultural or residential zoning. photo by: Josie Heimsoth/Journal-World Bauer said the county will also be exploring decommissioning requirements, requiring the developers to restore the property and address its future use. There was no draft language presented to attendees at Friday’s event, as the purpose was to answer questions and hear concerns. Among the topics discussed were what size BESS installation should require a permit and how large the notification area should be for a proposed installation. With the technology rapidly evolving, county commissioners initiated a text amendment in July 2024 so staff could begin drafting potential regulations for battery energy storage systems, data centers and cryptocurrency mining operations. “These technologies are advancing rapidly,” Bauer said. ” … They’re constantly changing … It might be a different landscape a few years from now, and that is one of the challenges with regulations. You’re always playing catch up with those.” Former County Commissioner Nancy Thellman said oftentimes, data centers and BESS are discussed together. Thellman also said that it was making it difficult to discuss regulations for one without the other. photo by: Josie Heimsoth/Journal-World Thellman suggested that the county should take a more holistic approach to planning for the two uses so their regulations are consistent and account for how they could operate together. However, after county commissioners received an update on the regulation process in May, as the Journal-World reported, it decided for staff to begin working on regulations for BESS first. The county commissioners wanted to save more detailed conversations about data centers and digital asset retrieval until after the county’s zoning diagnostic review was completed. Bauer said Douglas County has not received any applications for a BESS installation. “The whole reason this is being done is to get ahead of any kind of development that may come forward,” Bauer said. A draft of BESS regulations is currently scheduled to be shared with Lawrence-Douglas County Planning commissioners during their meeting on Dec. 16. The proposed regulations would then require final approval from the Douglas County commissioners, which is anticipated for early 2027. People who did not attend the community drop-in session can still provide input on BESS by contacting Zoning and Codes staff on the county’s website at https://www.dgcoks.gov/zoning-and-codes/contact. photo by: Josie Heimsoth/Journal-World photo by: Josie Heimsoth/Journal-World photo by: Josie Heimsoth/Journal-World

artigo.texto: Google compra data center da Crusoe no Wyoming por US$ 17 bi Crusoe vendeu projeto problemático no Wyoming ao Google após falhas de custo e prazo. O caso expõe os limites das startups de data centers na era da IA. A Crusoe, desenvolvedora de data centers sediada em Denver e avaliada em US$ 30,9 bilhões, confirmou a venda de um projeto inacabado no sudeste do Wyoming para o Google. A gigante de Mountain View, que ironicamente havia sido cortejada pela Crusoe como cliente para essa mesma instalação sem sucesso, agora assume o desenvolvimento com planos de investir US$ 17 bilhões no campus. O valor exato pago pela aquisição não foi divulgado. Mas o contexto da negociação diz muito sobre o momento do mercado de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial: mesmo empresas bilionárias estão esbarrando nos limites físicos e logísticos de construir na velocidade que a demanda por computação exige. O que deu errado no projeto da Crusoe no Wyoming A Crusoe havia anunciado o projeto no ano passado em parceria com a Tallgrass, empresa de infraestrutura apoiada pela Blackstone. O plano original era ambicioso: escalar a instalação até 10 gigawatts de capacidade energética. Para dimensionar esse número, a maioria dos grandes data centers em operação hoje trabalha com capacidades muito inferiores. O Google, segundo relatos, levantou preocupações sobre o custo e o cronograma de construção sob a gestão da Crusoe. Garantir equipamentos, assegurar fornecimento de energia e lidar com a crescente oposição de comunidades locais tornaram a entrega dentro do prazo e do orçamento uma tarefa que a startup não conseguiu cumprir sozinha. É um padrão que se repete no setor. Desenvolvedoras independentes de data centers enfrentam gargalos que vão da cadeia de suprimentos de transformadores e geradores até disputas regulatórias com prefeituras e concessionárias de energia. O caso da Crusoe no Wyoming é emblemático, mas está longe de ser isolado. Por que o Google decidiu assumir em vez de abandonar A decisão do Google de comprar o projeto, em vez de simplesmente buscar alternativas, revela uma dinâmica central do mercado de infraestrutura de IA: terrenos com acesso a energia em escala são ativos escassos. Encontrar um novo local, negociar conexões com a rede elétrica e obter licenças ambientais pode levar anos. Assumir um projeto já em andamento, mesmo que problemático, encurta esse caminho. Os US$ 17 bilhões que o Google pretende investir no campus do Wyoming se somam a uma ofensiva global da empresa em infraestrutura. A corrida por capacidade computacional para treinar e rodar modelos de IA transformou data centers no ativo mais disputado do setor de tecnologia. Apesar do revés no Wyoming, a relação entre Google e Crusoe não foi encerrada. A startup continua desenvolvendo um outro data center para o Google próximo a Amarillo, no Texas. Isso sugere que a questão não era de confiança na empresa como um todo, mas de capacidade de execução naquele projeto específico. Crusoe: da mineração de Bitcoin aos maiores contratos de IA A trajetória da Crusoe é, por si só, um retrato das transformações do setor de tecnologia nos últimos anos. Fundada por Chase Lochmiller e Cully Cavness, a empresa começou como um negócio de mineração de criptomoedas alimentado por gás natural que seria queimado e desperdiçado. O modelo de aproveitar energia residual para minerar Bitcoin era engenhoso, mas o verdadeiro salto veio com a migração para infraestrutura de IA. Hoje, a Crusoe opera em uma escala completamente diferente. Seu campus em Abilene, no Texas, está sendo construído em fases para Oracle e OpenAI. Um segundo campus de 900 megawatts na mesma região atende a Microsoft, com o primeiro prédio previsto para entrar em operação em meados de 2027. A Meta também é cliente. E, segundo informações de mercado, a firma de trading Jane Street assinou um contrato de US$ 13 bilhões por cinco anos para serviços de nuvem com a Crusoe. Em setembro, a empresa levantou uma rodada de US$ 3,9 bilhões, mesmo com o problema do Wyoming já público. Entre os novos membros do conselho está JB Straubel, cofundador da Tesla e fundador da Redwood Materials, que havia investido na Crusoe em 2021. A Crusoe se tornou, inclusive, a primeira cliente do negócio de armazenamento de energia de Straubel. O que isso significa para o mercado de data centers O episódio Crusoe-Google ilustra uma tensão estrutural. A demanda por computação para IA cresce em ritmo exponencial, mas a construção de infraestrutura física segue presa a limitações do mundo real: tempo de construção, disponibilidade de energia, capacidade de fabricação de equipamentos e aceitação comunitária. Grandes empresas como Google, Microsoft e Amazon têm balanço para absorver atrasos e estouros de orçamento. Startups, mesmo aquelas avaliadas em dezenas de bilhões, operam com margens de erro muito menores. O modelo de negócio da Crusoe, que gera receita alugando espaço em data centers, cedendo suas próprias GPUs e vendendo poder computacional para inferência de modelos de IA, é sólido em tese. Mas a execução de projetos na escala de 10 gigawatts exige um nível de maturidade operacional que poucos players independentes possuem. Para o investidor que acompanha o setor de tecnologia, o recado é claro. A infraestrutura de IA é o novo petróleo em termos de demanda, mas os custos e riscos de construção são reais e frequentemente subestimados. Empresas que conseguem entregar projetos no prazo e no orçamento terão vantagem competitiva duradoura. As que não conseguem acabam vendendo ativos para quem pode. O Wyoming da Crusoe agora é o Wyoming do Google. E os US$ 17 bilhões que vêm a seguir mostram que, nessa corrida, capital não é o problema. Execução é. Este conteúdo é informativo e educacional e não constitui recomendação de investimento. Rentabilidade passada não é garantia de resultados futuros.

artigo.texto: A expansão de grandes centros de processamento de dados nos Estados Unidos enfrenta uma crescente resistência popular. Nas eleições de meio de mandato realizadas na terça-feira (3), eleitores de diferentes estados se posicionaram contra projetos de instalação de data centers, estruturas essenciais para o funcionamento de sistemas de inteligência artificial (IA). Segundo o levantamento apresentado pela organização Ballotpedia, 40 dos 41 plebiscitos locais realizados em dez estados terminaram com resultados contrários à expansão dessas instalações ou favoráveis à imposição de restrições. O resultado coloca em evidência uma preocupação que vai além dos debates sobre os benefícios da tecnologia: os impactos econômicos e ambientais provocados pela infraestrutura necessária para sustentar o crescimento da inteligência artificial. Entre os principais pontos levantados pelas comunidades estão o consumo elevado de eletricidade, a utilização de água para resfriamento dos equipamentos e o possível aumento das despesas domésticas. Data centers entram no centro do debate eleitoral A oposição à construção de grandes centros de processamento de dados ganhou espaço durante a campanha eleitoral americana. Pesquisa de boca de urna da NBC News, citada no levantamento, apontou que 57% dos entrevistados acreditavam que a inteligência artificial poderia provocar mais prejuízos do que benefícios à sociedade. O mesmo levantamento indicou que 76% se posicionavam contra a instalação de data centers em suas próprias comunidades. Os números refletem a preocupação de parte da população com a velocidade dos investimentos no setor e a ausência de garantias de que os benefícios econômicos serão compartilhados com os moradores das regiões afetadas. O debate também passou a influenciar disputas políticas locais e nacionais, com candidatos defendendo regras mais rígidas para a instalação de grandes empreendimentos tecnológicos. Consumo de energia e água preocupa comunidades Os data centers concentram servidores e equipamentos utilizados para armazenar, processar e distribuir grandes volumes de informações. Com o crescimento da inteligência artificial generativa, a demanda por capacidade computacional aumentou, impulsionando investimentos em instalações cada vez maiores. Essas estruturas podem exigir quantidades expressivas de eletricidade para alimentar servidores e sistemas de refrigeração. Dependendo da tecnologia empregada, também podem utilizar volumes significativos de água para controlar a temperatura dos equipamentos. A instalação de grandes empreendimentos pode exigir investimentos adicionais em redes elétricas, sistemas de abastecimento e outras estruturas locais. O economista André Roncaglia, professor da Universidade de Brasília (UnB) e diretor-executivo do Fundo Monetário Internacional (FMI), segundo a identificação apresentada no material, avaliou que os impactos sobre os preços da energia e da água ajudaram a estimular a mobilização popular. Na avaliação do especialista, regiões que ofereciam menos restrições à construção de data centers atraíram investimentos, mas também passaram a enfrentar questionamentos sobre seus custos ambientais e sociais. Plebiscitos mostram rejeição a grandes instalações Boa parte das consultas populares foi organizada a partir de iniciativas de moradores, que reuniram assinaturas para submeter propostas de restrição ao voto. Ao longo de 2026, foram programados 50 plebiscitos relacionados ao tema nos Estados Unidos, segundo os dados apresentados no levantamento. Desse total, 41 ocorreram nas eleições de terça-feira (3), enquanto outras consultas haviam sido realizadas anteriormente. As propostas envolvem principalmente limitações ou proibições à instalação de data centers de hiperescala, categoria que reúne estruturas de grande capacidade de processamento. Um dos critérios utilizados nas consultas é o consumo de energia igual ou superior a 25 megawatts. Em Ottawa, no Kansas, uma proposta para proibir a construção de centros com demanda acima desse limite recebeu 72% dos votos, conforme os resultados citados pela Ballotpedia. O caso exemplifica a força da oposição local a projetos que podem alterar significativamente a demanda por recursos e infraestrutura. Resultado eleitoral amplia pressão por regulamentação O desempenho dos democratas nas eleições de meio de mandato também aumentou as expectativas de mudanças na política americana para o setor tecnológico. O presidente Donald Trump vinha defendendo uma abordagem de menor intervenção governamental, com incentivo aos investimentos privados e mecanismos de autorregulação da inteligência artificial. Já integrantes do Partido Democrata passaram a defender regras mais rigorosas para o desenvolvimento de sistemas avançados e para a expansão da infraestrutura digital. Segundo André Roncaglia, a possibilidade de mudanças regulatórias altera as expectativas dos investidores e pode provocar ajustes no mercado financeiro. O economista relacionou parte da reação das bolsas à perspectiva de que empresas de tecnologia passem a enfrentar maiores exigências regulatórias. O material original também registra queda de 5,5% no índice Nasdaq Composite nesta sexta-feira (6), informação que exige confirmação do período de referência e do fechamento do mercado. Debate ultrapassa divisões partidárias Para Paulo Abraão, diretor-executivo da Brazil Office Alliance, a oposição aos grandes data centers não pode ser interpretada apenas como uma rejeição à inovação tecnológica. O especialista considera que a mobilização representa uma cobrança por maior participação da sociedade nas decisões sobre a expansão da inteligência artificial. Segundo ele, 56% dos eleitores consideraram a IA e os data centers fatores importantes ou decisivos para suas escolhas eleitorais. Abraão também destacou que a resistência aos empreendimentos ultrapassa as divisões tradicionais entre democratas e republicanos.
