artigo.texto: A Moura prevê investir cerca de R$ 200 milhões para fornecer sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, conhecidos como BESS, às empresas que participarão do primeiro Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência (LRCAP). A disputa nacional para projetos de armazenamento está marcada para 2 de dezembro e prevê requisitos de conteúdo local. A companhia atuará em parceria com a chinesa CATL, líder global em tecnologias de armazenamento. O histórico da Moura com equipamentos credenciados para financiamento do BNDES antecede o leilão: seu BESS para os mercados comercial e industrial tem credenciamento no FINAME desde 2024. O instrumento do banco financia máquinas e equipamentos e exige comprovação de fabricação nacional. A empresa já está na relação do BNDES como fabricante de sistemas de armazenamento para o certame. Os contratos previstos terão duração de 15 anos, com fornecimento a partir de agosto de 2028. Além do conteúdo local, o modelo estabelece requisitos para o desenvolvimento nacional de componentes estratégicos. Para a Moura, a produção local envolve atividades industriais efetivas, como engenharia, integração, montagem, testes e prestação de serviços no Brasil, e não somente a importação de sistemas prontos. A companhia afirma que essas atividades podem fortalecer fornecedores, gerar oportunidades de trabalho e ampliar a capacidade técnica próxima aos projetos. Em contratos de longo prazo, a presença local também pode diminuir a exposição a riscos logísticos e facilitar a manutenção e o suporte. Para os participantes do leilão, equipamentos elegíveis ao FINAME podem ampliar as opções de crédito, conforme as condições de cada operação. Na parceria, a CATL fornecerá sua tecnologia de armazenamento, enquanto a Moura ficará responsável pela industrialização e integração dos sistemas no país. A capacidade anunciada para atender às empresas participantes supera 8 GWh e está ligada à expansão de uma estrutura produtiva e técnica já existente. A fabricação do Moura BESS ocorre em Belo Jardim (PE), e a unidade de Itapetininga (SP) concentra o suporte técnico e o pós-venda de soluções em lítio. Com quase 70 anos de atuação em tecnologias de acumulação de energia, a Moura começou a desenvolver BESS em meados da década de 2010 e apresentou o Moura BESS em 2019. A empresa relata ter experiência em mais de 40 projetos instalados no Brasil, com aplicações em setores como indústria, agronegócio, saúde, saneamento e entretenimento, além da geração, transmissão e distribuição de energia. O investimento anunciado inclui uma expansão recente e um novo ciclo de ampliação e modernização da fábrica de Belo Jardim para atender projetos de grande porte. A empresa também considera importante o anúncio feito pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia no fim de setembro sobre leilões adicionais nos próximos anos. O cronograma divulgado para 2027 a 2029 prevê três certames abertos a soluções de armazenamento em baterias. Para a Moura, a previsibilidade da demanda favorece novos investimentos, o aumento gradual da produção nacional de componentes e a formação de profissionais especializados. Em projetos de armazenamento, a operação confiável por muitos anos depende de manutenção, acompanhamento técnico e capacidade de resposta. A Moura avalia que, nos contratos de longo prazo previstos para o mercado de reserva de capacidade, os participantes devem considerar não apenas o custo inicial dos equipamentos, mas também a tecnologia, a continuidade dos serviços e os riscos operacionais. A experiência e a estrutura de atendimento no Brasil, afirma a companhia, são aspectos relevantes para as empresas que disputarão o leilão.

artigo.texto: 1 in 4 data centers sits in a water-stressed area — here’s what that means for nearby communities When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission. AI has become integrated into our lives whether we like it or not. Despite big tech forcing schools to choose and lawsuits highlighting its dangers, the controversial technology is here to stay. New research published in Environmental Science & Technology puts specific AI concerns on a global map, highlighting 9,347 identified data centers, with roughly a quarter located in areas where water demand would exceed available supply for at least one month a year. The water has to come from somewhere Data centers use water to remove heat from their equipment. In evaporative cooling systems, some of that water evaporates rather than returning to the local water system. Electricity generation and hardware manufacturing add an indirect water footprint, too, according to the Pacific Institute. Where and when that consumption happens matters. The institute warns that data center water demand peaks during hot, dry periods, when supplies may be constrained, and other users also need more. Meeting those peaks can require additional utility infrastructure and spending. "They are landing on top of the water supply of cities and farms," study lead author Lorenzo Rosa said in an American Chemical Society release. That makes data center construction relevant to people who may never pay for an AI subscription. Before approving a facility, a community needs to understand whether its water system can accommodate a large new customer during a dry summer. Cities and municipalities are the largest water users, accounting for nearly 41% of the facilities studied, while agriculture is the primary user, accounting for another 28%, according to the American Chemical Society. A yearly average can miss the pressure The Potomac River basin offers a useful example. An analysis by the Interstate Commission on the Potomac River Basin describes current average data center water consumption in the Washington metropolitan area as relatively small. Its estimated 2025 average was about 4 million gallons a day, with peak-day consumption of approximately 15 million gallons. Cooling choices help explain the variation. Around 40% of facilities in the analysis rely exclusively on air cooling, while many others take advantage of cooler winter weather to reduce cooling demands. The commission cautions that approaches using less water often require more energy. For residents, an annual consumption figure only answers part of the question. They also need to know how much water a facility could require during the hottest days, when local supplies may already be under pressure. What communities deserve to know The same global study also examined existing data center locations under a scenario of 3°C of global warming relative to around 1900. The share exposed to water shortages rose to roughly a third. That projection applies future climate conditions to the facilities identified in the study; it doesn't account for where additional data centers might be built. Better disclosure would make proposed projects easier to assess. The Pacific Institute identifies a lack of standardized reporting on data center size, location and water use as an obstacle for communities and water managers. Residents deserve clear answers about a proposed facility's water source, expected summer demand and plans for drought. They also deserve to know who would pay for any necessary infrastructure upgrades. What communities can do now If a data center is proposed near your home, get answers now. Start with your local planning board or water utility and ask where its cooling water would come from, how much it could use on the hottest days, and what would happen during a drought. Be direct and ask who would pay for any water-system upgrades, too, and whether the operator would be required to make its water use public. Those details can help residents assess a project before approval. To learn more about the infrastructure behind AI, start with Google's data center water reporting or Microsoft's local environmental fact sheets. These disclosures can help you understand water use where facilities operate, though they won't tell you the footprint of your individual chats.

artigo.texto: De bateria de alta potência a suspensão inteligente: conheça por dentro o Yangwang U9, supercarro elétrico da BYD Modelo terá apenas 30 unidades produzidas, combina quatro motores elétricos de 30 mil rpm, bateria de 1.200 volts e suspensão ativa capaz de ajustar individualmente cada roda Quatro motores elétricos, 3.019 cv de potência e capacidade para atingir 30 mil rotações por minuto. O Yangwang U9 Xtreme, hipercarro da marca de luxo da chinesa BYD, reúne tecnologias desenvolvidas para levar o desempenho dos veículos elétricos a outro patamar. Com apenas 30 unidades previstas, o modelo chegou a 503,17 km/h em uma rodovia de Abu Dhabi, nos Emirados Árabes Unidos, em 1º de novembro. A velocidade superou os 496,22 km/h registrados pelo mesmo piloto, o alemão Marc Basseng, na Alemanha, em setembro de 2025. A conquista rendeu dois reconhecimentos do Guinness World Records, nas categorias de maior velocidade alcançada por um carro de produção em uma única direção e por um elétrico de produção nas mesmas condições. O desempenho é resultado de um conjunto mecânico diferente do encontrado no U9 convencional, que entrega 1.287 cv. Na versão Xtreme, são quatro motores elétricos, um em cada roda, capazes de desenvolver aproximadamente 755 cv cada. A potência combinada chega a 3.019 cv, com relação de 1.217 cv por tonelada. Yangwang U9 Xtreme, hipercarro elétrico da BYD, supera os 500 km/h A configuração permite distribuir o torque individualmente entre as rodas, com ajustes mais de cem vezes por segundo, segundo a fabricante. O objetivo é melhorar a tração e o controle do veículo, especialmente em situações de aceleração e curvas. Para suportar as rotações elevadas, os motores utilizam materiais específicos, como lâminas de aço-silício de apenas 0,1 milímetro no estator e alumínio de grau aeroespacial na carcaça. As soluções buscam aumentar a resistência mecânica e controlar a temperatura do conjunto. Bateria e arquitetura elétrica Outro destaque é a arquitetura elétrica de 1.200 volts, superior à de 800 volts do U9 convencional. Uma tensão mais elevada permite reduzir a corrente necessária para fornecer a mesma potência, diminuindo as perdas associadas ao aquecimento dos componentes. O hipercarro utiliza a bateria Blade, desenvolvida pela BYD com química de lítio-ferro-fosfato (LFP). Segundo a Yangwang, o conjunto tem capacidade de descarga de 30C e consegue fornecer 1.800 kW de potência mesmo quando está com apenas 20% de carga. Na desaceleração, a recuperação de energia pode superar 700 kW. O sistema devolve eletricidade à bateria e auxilia o funcionamento dos freios convencionais, especialmente em situações de maior exigência. A potência elevada também exige mecanismos capazes de manter o veículo estável. Para isso, o U9 Xtreme utiliza a suspensão ativa DiSus-X, que ajusta cada roda de maneira independente para controlar os movimentos da carroceria e favorecer o contato dos pneus com o asfalto. Nas curvas, a tecnologia permite reduzir a inclinação lateral e até fazer a carroceria pender para o lado interno da trajetória, em um movimento semelhante ao de uma motocicleta. A fabricante informa que o sistema pode alcançar inclinação de até 2,43 graus sob aceleração lateral de 0,3 g. Os pneus, desenvolvidos em parceria com a fabricante Giti, também receberam soluções específicas para suportar as exigências de aceleração, frenagem e curvas em velocidades elevadas. O desempenho não se limita às tentativas de velocidade máxima em retas. O modelo registrou 6min59s157 no circuito de Nürburgring Nordschleife, na Alemanha. Segundo a Yangwang, o resultado foi alcançado com a mesma configuração utilizada na tentativa de recorde em Abu Dhabi. Apenas 30 exemplares do U9 Xtreme serão produzidos para compradores de diferentes mercados. A fabricante afirma que parte dos clientes já aprovou as configurações individuais dos veículos e avançou nas etapas de contratação e programação da produção. O primeiro exemplar apresentado pela marca recebeu o nome Dawn Moment e foi exibido no Salão de Pequim. O acabamento incorporava pó de ouro ultrafino sob várias camadas de verniz, em uma pintura concebida para mudar de aparência conforme a incidência da luz.

artigo.texto: Chinese battery giant CATL is reportedly exploring a new type of air-breathing battery known as a lithium-air battery, which could, in theory, deliver over 1,243 miles (2,000 km) of range for electric vehicles (EVs). What’s more, these so-called lithium-air batteries could deliver at least five times the energy density of solid-state batteries. All this without adding extra weight to the technology and, critically, the EV. However, it is not all gravy. It turns out that lithium-air batteries are exceptionally good at storing energy (at least on paper). But, it turns out, they are very difficult to make rechargeable, durable, and practical. For the uninitiated, the simplest way to understand it is to think of a lithium-air battery as a rechargeable battery that works a little like a combustion engine. It draws oxygen from the atmosphere to help release energy, rather than carrying all its reactive materials internally. Batteries that breathe By contrast, a conventional lithium-ion battery has two electrodes containing materials that store and release energy. Everything it needs is essentially contained within the battery. A lithium-air battery, on the other hand, does something very different. They essentially use oxygen from the surrounding atmosphere as one of its reactants. During discharge, lithium metal reacts electrochemically with oxygen in the air to produce lithium peroxide (Li₂O₂) and release electrical energy. More from Energy See All This provides the free electrons to power the EV’s motors and systems during operation. When charging, electrical energy forces the reaction to reverse, breaking down the lithium peroxide, releasing oxygen and restoring the lithium metal. The big advantage of this is that you don’t have to carry the oxygen reactant around inside the battery from the start. And that’s where the technology’s enormous energy density of 3,505 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg) figure comes from. Critically, that’s a theoretical figure based on its chemistry and oxygen mass. It doesn’t necessarily translate into the battery’s actual performance. To put that into context, a typical conventional lithium-ion cell has an energy density of around 200–300 Wh/kg. Advanced solid-state batteries come in at 350–500 Wh/kg. Still experimental, CATL explains So, quite an improvement, at least in theory. One major problem with it is that the technology has a tendency to “clog itself up.” The produced lithium peroxide is a solid substance that accumulates within the battery’s porous electrode. You can liken it to a sponge that gradually fills with a solid deposit. Eventually, oxygen struggles to penetrate the electrode, reactions become more difficult, and usable capacity falls. This is supposed to be reversed during charging, but the process isn’t 100 percent effective. Another issue is that air isn’t just pure oxygen; it contains other gases like water and carbon dioxide. Both of these can interfere with the battery chemistry, producing “contaminant” products that are hard to remove. So, to work at peak efficiency over time, such a battery would likely need some form of air filtration system built in too. CATL isn’t claiming the new technology will revolutionize the industry just yet. It remains, at present, a long-term exploratory research project. In other words, CATL is interested enough to research it, but it hasn’t established that the technology can be commercialized. At least, not yet.

artigo.texto: As opposition to building artificial intelligence (AI) data centers spreads across the United States, struggling small towns are betting their survival on luring those facilities. Major U.S. cities are tightening rules on data centers over heavy power consumption, noise, and environmental concerns. By contrast, rural towns where manufacturing has collapsed and populations are shrinking—unlike affluent suburbs—see data centers as the only tax base left to keep schools and roads running. The Washington Post (WP) reported on the 8th (local time) that the midterm elections held on the 3rd featured 41 local ballot measures across 10 states that could restrict data center development. Of those, 40 measures, or 97.6%, produced outcomes favorable to limiting data center construction. In network exit polls, 76% among respondents said they opposed building a new data center where they live. Fifty-seven percent said AI will do more harm than good to society. In Piqua, Ohio, residents banned a large data center that Meta planned to build for $1 billion (about 1.3566 trillion won) and recalled officials who had backed the project. In Texas, where data centers have clustered, Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned on a moratorium on new construction, was elected governor. Even amid nationwide pushback, the tiny city of Harwood, North Dakota, with a population of 845, chose the opposite path. On the 3rd, Harwood residents voted down a ballot measure that would have required independent reviews and public hearings for large industrial projects, with 105 votes in favor and 325 against. It is seen as 75.6% of voters rejecting additional rules that could slow data center development. Residents backed the project on the calculation that once the data center is completed, the city's property tax revenue would grow to six times the 2024 level. Harwood's population is 845—about one-twenty-fourth the size of a Korean eup (20,000 people). The town has little industrial base beyond a few bars and grain elevators. Most residents commute to Fargo, North Dakota's largest city nearby. On Harwood's outskirts, Texas-based developer Applied Digital is building a data center of about 167,000 square meters with a $3 billion (about 4.09 trillion won) investment. Harwood Mayor Blake Henke has sparred with neighboring Fargo over annexing the data center site since the project began. He concluded that even if Harwood refused, the center could go up on land under Fargo's jurisdiction right next door. In that case, Harwood would bear the noise and traffic while Fargo collected the taxes. "If the data center is going to end up in essentially the same spot anyway, we'd rather receive the tax breaks and the revenue," Henke told WP. The city estimated annual property taxes from the completed facility at $1.65 million (about 2.2 billion won), roughly six times Harwood's 2024 property tax take. Applied Digital has also pledged more than 200 full-time jobs. It has already contributed funds to the city fire department and a park warming shelter. Across U.S. small towns hollowed out by industrial decline, data centers are seen as relief pitchers that can stave off extinction. Ellendale, a rural town of about 1,100 in the same state of North Dakota, embraced Applied Digital before Harwood did. The company is now expanding a data center campus there with a $5 billion (about 6.82 trillion won) investment. Mayor Don Flaherty said that if the campus grows to three buildings with up to 530 megawatts (MW), the number of full-time jobs will rise to 300 to 350—close to one-third of the current population. Ellendale's assessed value stood at $3.5 million (about 4.7 billion won) at the end of 2025, and the city projected that figure would more than double within a few years. "By 2028–2029, Applied Digital will pay more than $25 million (about 3.39 billion won) a year in property taxes and become North Dakota's largest property taxpayer," Flaherty said. There are also cases where attracting data centers has transformed public infrastructure. Quincy, an agricultural city about 240 kilometers east of Seattle in the northwest, used to grow potatoes. But over the past 20 years, more than 30 tech firms followed Microsoft in seeking cheap land and abundant power, completely changing the city's finances. An analysis by local outlet the Spokesman-Review of the city's audit reports found that Quincy's annual total revenue jumped from $6 million (about 810 million won) in 2006 to $47 million (about 6.4 billion won) in 2024. The population also grew from about 5,300 two decades ago to about 8,200. Data centers now account for 57% of Quincy's total local government tax revenue. With the expanded funds, the city built a new hospital, high school, fire station, and library. In rural Mecklenburg County, Virginia, a former correctional site that once produced no tax revenue became the highest-taxed property after Microsoft arrived in 2010. Data centers now support about 45% of the county's general fund. In Richland Parish, a rural area in northeastern Louisiana considered one of the poorest parts of the United States, data centers are shaking up the local economy. According to the New York Times (NYT), Meta announced in 2024 that it would build the $10 billion Hyperion data center there. In July this year, it raised the investment to more than $50 billion (about 67.83 trillion won). As construction ramped up, Richland collected $38.7 million (about 5.25 billion won) in sales taxes just in the first quarter this year from materials and equipment purchases. With tax revenue surging, annual bonuses for teachers in Richland jumped more than fivefold from about $10,000 last year to more than $50,000 (about 68 million won) this year. Still, attracting data centers does not yield only rosy outcomes. Communities face internal rifts, and rising incomes bring side effects. artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Canary Live Bay Area By Canary Media This analysis and news roundup come from the Canary Media Weekly newsletter. Sign up to get it every Friday. Americans aren’t happy about the data center boom, and they made their displeasure pretty clear this Election Day. Voters not only selected a slate of Democratic candidates who campaigned against data centers; they also approved more than 30 ballot measures aimed at reining in the power-hungry facilities. You could argue that the “data center elections” really started a year ago, when Virginians selected Democrat Abigail Spanberger as their next governor. Virginia has more than earned its status as the data center capital of the world, with the latest estimates counting more than 700 facilities around the state, and Spanberger ran on a promise to keep their intense power demand in check. In the months that followed, it became clear that data center developers were circling in on Great Lakes states and their abundant water resources — and that fighting the facilities was a winning campaign strategy. Take Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who made data center regulation a prominent piece of his candidacy, and William Lawrence, a Democrat who won his U.S. House race after showing up at a local council meeting to fight a proposed data center. Meanwhile in Ohio, Sherrod Brown, a three-term Democratic senator who was ousted in 2024, will return to the chamber. Brown’s campaign painted his Republican opponent as “the face of data centers,” even though it cost Brown the support of some union labor allies who’ve backed him for decades but see data centers as creators of construction jobs. Data centers’ threat is even more palpable in Georgia and Texas, which have more projects in the pipeline than any other state except Virginia. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) was easily reelected after criticizing data centers as part of his campaign and investigating their impact on power bills in the Senate. Georgia’s Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms has meanwhile pledged a “pause” on new data center construction once she takes office in January. And Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa scored historic wins in Texas for U.S. Senate and governor, respectively, after promising to pursue a slate of data center regulations. Anti–data center sentiment this election cycle was so strong that even some Republicans promised restrictions — Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers called for a one-year moratorium in the state, for example. But some still sided with data centers, like Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina, who benefited from an industry-funded ad campaign before losing a seat she had been expected to retain. And when the data center debate showed up in ballot measures across dozens of counties and municipalities, voters gave a resounding response: Rein them in. How energy prices showed up on the ballot Data centers weren’t the only energy issue motivating voters this week. With gasoline prices at their highest level of any Election Day in U.S. history, and falling temperatures getting Americans thinking about heating bills, it’s no wonder that voters were looking for a change. While President Donald Trump has been promising to curb energy costs since his 2024 campaign, his decisions have driven prices in the opposite direction. Experts say that perhaps his most drastic mistake was starting a war with Iran, spiking oil prices that have yet to return to anything resembling the pre-conflict normal. That impact has been especially obvious in Maine, where half the residents rely on heating oil — and where voters ousted longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins on Tuesday. Utility bills were literally on the ballot in nine states this week, as voters selected new members to regulatory boards that oversee utility rate hikes and other energy-related decisions. While most of the states preserved the status quo and elected Republicans, Georgia voters gave Democrats the majority on their Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years. What do Democrats’ wins mean for permitting? As the U.S. Senate prepares for its drastically new makeup come January, it’s also got a major vote to tackle in the next few days. The chamber is planning to vote Nov. 9 on long-awaited energy permitting reform legislation — that is, if newly emboldened Democrats don’t try to reshape the bill. While the package was crafted by two Democrats and two Republicans, some Congress members on the left have demanded edits to minimize its benefits for fossil fuels and prioritize clean energy development. They’ve renewed that call in the blue wave’s wake, with Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), who is likely to chair the House Natural Resources Committee in a Democrat-led Congress, saying that voters showed “they don’t want this dirty, fossil-fuel-expanding bill.” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D) also called for revisions to the bill to protect tribal sovereignty and blunt impacts to the National Environmental Policy Act. Bill co-sponsor Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) contended that the election results revealed the opposite: Americans are focused on “affordability,” he wrote on X, and achieving that requires building more clean energy projects by passing the permitting bill. More election results: Democrats are poised to take full control of six more state governments, giving them leverage to enact more ambitious clean-energy policies. Voters also approved a handful of clean energy–boosting ballot measures, and rejected some that would prop up fossil fuels and weaken environmental regulations. Last week, those outside of that select community finally had their say. Voters of all stripes chose to pull hard on the only lever available to them. Building data centers in the U.S. just became even more difficult, but perhaps as important, voters issued a challenge to the AI billionaires behind them. Victorious Democrats must now contend with the outcome while ensuring U.S. AI labs remain competitive on the global stage. In China, the bottleneck is in finding enough cutting-edge chips to fill its AI factories. In the U.S., the challenge is building enough factories to hold all of its chips. Which scarcity proves the greater handicap in the AI race remains to be seen.

artigo.texto: If you had asked Dr. Lukas Swan five years ago what he would be working on today, he never would have said sodium-ion batteries or Nova Scotia’s offshore wind future. Yet here he is, leading a groundbreaking project that could redefine how the province harnesses and stores renewable energy. A long-time electrification expert, Dr. Swan has spent decades championing a system where wind and solar power homes, buildings, and charge electric vehicles, with the excess energy being stored in batteries for later use. “I remember people laughing at me 15 and 20 years ago, saying, ‘Natural gas is cheap, or oil will become cheaper, or let's burn wood instead because we have lots of trees,’” he says. “And now people are buying electric vehicles like hotcakes, and virtually all new communities are being built with heat pumps.” Things are changing again. Dr. Swan, a professor in the Faculty of Engineering, is now turning his expertise toward sodium-ion batteries, a chemistry he has never worked with before. And he’s exploring how it could complement or even surpass in some ways lithium-ion for stationary energy storage. Powering the future Funded through the Canada First Research Excellence Fund (CFREF), the seven-year, $123-million Voltage (VOLT-AGE) grant unites universities, government agencies, industry, and indigenous partners to explore electrification, including batteries. Unlike lithium-ion, sodium-ion batteries use abundant, lower-cost materials and are ideal for stationary applications like grid storage, where size and weight matter less than in mobile application like cars or phones. Starting with a seed grant just over a year ago, Dr. Swan dove headfirst into sodium-ion. “We’re learning as we go,” he says. “We’re running into problems, finding solutions, trying different techniques.” The research quickly expanded, bringing on PhD and undergraduate students and giving them hands-on experience with partners ranging from Canadian and U.S. companies to defence organizations, Indigenous groups, and public agencies. Dr. Lukas Swan is leading research into sodium-ion batteries, an emerging technology that could help store renewable energy and support Nova Scotia's growing wind-energy sector. To kick things off, the lab invested about $30,000 in cells, from thumb-sized cylinders to shoebox-sized prismatic modules and began cycling them through rigorous tests of temperature range, voltage range, and real-world load simulations. Their goal: to design modules and packs for stationary storage, powering everything from homes to commercial buildings and the wider electricity grid. Dr. Swan isn’t working alone. He’s also teaming up with experts at other universities, including Concordia, Calgary, ETS Montreal, and Carleton. For students, it’s a front-row seat to the future of energy. Over the next four years, about 23 PhD students will dive into the project, tackling new technologies and collaborating with partners across North America. “It's allowing them to go off and do their individual PhD research tasks, but recognizing this web of interlinks between sciences and engineering and social science, and drawing them back together to share and collaborate” explains Dr. Swan. Perfect timing The timing couldn’t be better. With Nova Scotia ramping up onshore wind and solar, and making major commitments to offshore wind, current electrical grids may not be ready for all that extra power. “We do battery research because we need to store energy,” says Dr. Swan. “These sodium-ion batteries are exclusive for stationary. That’s our focus. We need to store wind and solar energy when there’s excess, and release it at later points when the sun goes down, when the wind stops blowing, or when the temperature drops and the heat pumps come on.” He adds that while Asia leads in sodium-ion production, and Europe and China dominate offshore wind, Nova Scotia offers unique advantages: abundant land, strong winds, and a chance to develop domestic battery supply. We’re pivoting fast, filling research gaps, and doing work that’s critical for the province of Nova Scotia and the region as a whole. “Five years ago, I wouldn’t have imagined working on offshore wind and sodium-ion batteries. But that’s where I am. We’re pivoting fast, filling research gaps, and doing work that’s critical for the province of Nova Scotia and the region as a whole,” he says. With this work, Dalhousie Engineering is emerging as a hub for renewable energy research. While the rest of the world has valuable expertise, Dr. Swan says their technologies may not be suited for the province’s unique conditions. “Although the Europeans have done a phenomenal job and the Chinese now lead at this point in offshore wind energy, they have not seen a resource like we have here in Nova Scotia,” he says. “Our winds are just substantially stronger, and you really need boots on the ground and local research. That’s where the fun is for us in our research work.”

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Eleitor americano barra data centers e o Redata tenta atrair as obras para o Brasil, e a COP31 vai falar muito sobre isso Publicado 08/11/2026 • 19:44 | Atualizado há 11 horas Nano Banana 3 Placas contra data centers em rua residencial dos Estados Unidos, onde eleitores rejeitaram projetos em consultas locais na terça-feira (3) Duas fileiras de fardos de feno, a de cima soletrando "no data" e a de baixo "centers", com três deles pintados com a bandeira americana, ilustram a reportagem da agência Stateline sobre a terça-feira (3), dia em que eleitores de dez estados rejeitaram, em quase todas as consultas locais, a instalação de data centers perto de casa. O recado de beira de estrada interessa ao Brasil porque o Redata, regime de isenção de impostos para esses prédios de servidores sancionado em setembro, é a oferta nacional a quem ficou sem endereço, e interessa ainda mais na semana em que a COP31, a conferência do clima da ONU, abre em Antalya, na Turquia, na segunda-feira (9). O rastreador Data Centers on the Ballot contou 38 consultas em que prevaleceram restrições e uma única derrota, em Harwood, na Dakota do Norte. Na boca de urna da NBC, 56% dos eleitores disseram que a inteligência artificial e os data centers pesaram muito ou bastante no voto para o Congresso. O mercado entendeu o recado: as ações de Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet e Meta subiram na quarta-feira (4), mas o ganho foi em boa parte desfeito na quinta-feira (5), quando a Nvidia caiu 9,3% e a Dell, 15%. Na quarta-feira (4), no evento WSJ Tech, a presidente da Meta, Dina Powell McCormick, afirmou que será muito difícil construir novos data centers nos Estados Unidos e que todo hyperscaler, como se chamam as gigantes de nuvem, se pergunta se precisa construir fora do país. A consultoria STL Partners, citada pela CNBC, soma US$ 77 bilhões (R$ 413 bilhões, pelo câmbio de 29/10) em projetos americanos adiados ou cancelados por oposição local e US$ 42 bilhões na Europa. Carlos Barrera, presidente da Atlas Renewable Energy, disse à Fortune que a América Latina pode ser uma válvula de escape para a falta de capacidade nos Estados Unidos, o que dá ao Redata uma freguesia em potencial antes mesmo de ele funcionar. A presidência turca da COP31, com a Austrália à frente das negociações, publicou o Compromisso de Inteligência Artificial de Antalya, de adesão voluntária, que pede energia de baixa emissão nos data centers e relatórios sobre o impacto ambiental da IA, e que reconhece que o consumo de eletricidade dessas instalações subiu 50% em 2025. O Google já se mexeu: anunciou na quinta-feira (5) um data center em Wyoming que pagará por 100% da energia que consumir e será refrigerado a ar, para poupar a água local, segundo a Barron’s. Evan Tachovsky, do World Resources Institute, avaliou que o texto aponta a direção certa, mas não prevê responsabilização de empresas e governos. O Brasil chega a essa mesa com uma matriz de quase 87% de fontes renováveis e eletricidade que custa menos da metade da americana, com 60% dos dados do país processados no exterior, segundo o Ministério do Desenvolvimento. A lei 15.504 suspende por cinco anos tributos federais como PIS/Cofins e IPI sobre equipamentos, exige que 10% da capacidade atenda o mercado interno e que 2% do valor dos bens volte em pesquisa e desenvolvimento, mas o regime ainda não opera porque depende de decreto. A Fazenda resiste a incluir o gás natural entre as fontes aceitas, nove frentes parlamentares e 32 entidades pediram a Lula, em carta de outubro, que publique o texto com gás e deixe os pontos técnicos para depois, e o presidente já disse que quem vier terá de investir na construção de energia renovável. O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, disse em outubro que o governo trabalha para concluir a regulamentação até o fim do ano. Quem espera o decreto já sentiu o custo, pois, segundo a Elea Data Centers, os investimentos em novos data centers caíram para cerca de R$ 2 bilhões em 2025, menos de um décimo da média anual de R$ 25 bilhões entre 2020 e 2024, e a empresa atribui a queda à demora do Redata. O diretor-geral do ONS, Marcio Rea, disse em setembro que os pedidos de conexão somam quase 20 gigawatts, cerca de 30% da energia do país, enquanto a projeção do próprio órgão para a carga dos data centers em 2030 é de 3,5 gigawatts, o que sugere que boa parte da fila é intenção e não obra. A obra mais adiantada, o Data Center Pecém, do TikTok, no Ceará, com 300 megawatts e R$ 50 bilhões na primeira etapa de um plano que chega a R$ 200 bilhões até 2036, mostra o obstáculo da licença. Em setembro, na quinta-feira (10), o Ministério Público Federal e a Defensoria Pública da União foram à Justiça para impedir que ele opere antes de uma consulta ao povo indígena Anacé e de um estudo de impacto ambiental, porque, segundo a ação, foi enquadrado como empreendimento de baixo ou médio impacto numa região que depende de poços e tem histórico de escassez de água. A Omnia, responsável pelo projeto, afirma que o licenciamento segue o rito regular conduzido pela Semace, órgão ambiental do Ceará. A mesma ação cita 120 geradores a diesel, detalhe que entraria no relatório de impactos previsto no compromisso de Antalya, se o Brasil aderir. Leia todas as colunas de AI-451. artigo.texto: Editor's note; With opinion polls registering widespread distrust by local residents in data centers, the foundation asked an expert to review best practices to both avoid the pitfalls and realize the opportunities. These comments were delivered at a recent colloquy in Roanoke. I want to start in New Carlisle, a town of about 1,800 people in St. Joseph County, which recently found itself negotiating with the largest company on earth — and doing so, at first, in secret. When Amazon's $11-billion data center campus came to New Carlisle, members of the Town Council signed nondisclosure agreements. The agreements barred them from disclosing what they called "nonpublic information relating to Amazon." The town's residents, in other words, were not permitted to know the terms of a deal that would reshape their water system, their roads, and their tax base for a generation — until the deal was essentially done. The reported terms, when they emerged, were these: a 10-year, 50-percent abatement on real property taxes, and an 85 percent exemption on enterprise technology equipment for 35 years. Thirty-five years. There are children in New Carlisle today who will be grandparents before that exemption expires. Alongside it, a $114 million water and sewer agreement and a $7 million contribution to roads and an interchange. Now, I am not here to tell you that New Carlisle got a bad deal. I am here to tell you something more unsettling: For a long time, nobody in a position to judge was allowed to know whether it was a good deal or a bad one. And that is the subject of my talk: the complete contract. I come at this as a Public Choice economist in the tradition of James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock. Public Choice begins with a simple, almost rude assumption: People in politics behave like people everywhere else. They pursue their own interests. A mayor wants to announce a jobs triumph before the next election. A company wants the lowest cost and the least scrutiny. A bureaucrat wants a bigger budget and a quieter life. None of them is paid, day to day, to maximize something called "the public interest." That sounds cynical. It is actually optimistic, because it tells us what to do. If you cannot rely on goodwill, you must rely on rules. And a contract between a municipality and a data center is the most important rule a town will write in a generation. A complete contract is one that answers, in advance, four questions: who pays for what, who bears the risk when things go wrong, how do we measure compliance and what happens at the end. An incomplete contract is not a neutral document. It is an invitation. Tullock taught us about rent-seeking: the art of getting rich not by producing something, but by persuading government to give you something. Every gap in a contract is a future rent-seeking opportunity, and the party with the lawyers will find it. So let us walk through the four places where these contracts are most often left incomplete — power, water, noise and land — and see what completeness looks like. First, power. A data center is, electrically speaking, a small city that never sleeps. A single large campus can draw several hundred megawatts — the equivalent of a few hundred thousand homes — and it wants that power on Day One. The question is who pays for the wires, the substations and the generation to serve it. Left vague, the answer defaults to: everybody else, through their electric bills. Ohio gave us the cautionary version of the good answer. Under a tariff approved by the state's utility commission, large data centers must commit to paying for at least 85% of their contracted load, for eight years, with a three-year exit fee and full reimbursement if they cancel a project after the utility has built for them. Think about what that does. It means a company cannot reserve a gigawatt of capacity, watch the utility build a substation, and then walk away leaving ratepayers holding the bill. The risk sits with the party that created it. Indiana produced a structurally elegant variant: in the AWS–NIPSCO arrangement, the data center load is served through a separate generation company, ring-fenced from the ordinary rate base, with roughly a billion dollars in bill credits over 15 years flowing back. The principle is what matters: the load that causes the cost is the load that pays for it. And Virginia gave us the warning about what happens when nobody writes the number down at all. The state's data center sales-tax exemption was projected, back in 2008, to cost about $1.5 million a year. By fiscal year 2025 it cost $1.9 billion. That is not a rounding error; that is fiscal illusion — a benefit that grows in the dark because no one put a cap, a sunset, or a review date in the original deal. A complete contract has an expiration date. An incomplete one has a surprise. Second, water. A data center that cools with water can drink like a town. And water contracts are where good intentions go to evaporate. Goodyear, Arizona, is my favorite story, because it is a story of a second chance. Microsoft originally promised to pretreat its cooling water on site and return roughly 5 million gallons a day to the city's surface-water plant, where it would become drinking water. It was a beautiful promise. It failed, almost immediately, over regulatory trouble. The city renegotiated: Microsoft would pay $36 million toward a $90 million expansion of the 157th Avenue treatment plant, post a $5 million assurance for the sewer line, fund a city coordinator, and — critically — air-cool its later buildings instead of evaporating water. Goodyear got real concessions. But notice the arithmetic: $36 million of a $90 million plant. The residents still carry the majority of a facility sized partly for Microsoft. Renegotiation after construction has begun is negotiation with one hand tied. artigo.texto: Startup turns 112 discarded e-scooter batteries into solar energy storage with surprising results A startup based in Germany is turning 112 used e-scooter batteries into a system that stores solar energy for businesses. Testing found the batteries had lost only about 10% of their strength on average. Here's what to know EDENenergy has sold its first commercially available unit, a 70-kilowatt-hour energy-storage system aimed at businesses that already generate their own solar power but have no way to bank it for later. A solar inverter is built into the unit as well, according to InsideEVs. EDENenergy operates with just three founders and three additional staffers who work part time. The founders, who previously worked as researchers at Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems, had expected the secondhand batteries to keep only about 80% of their former power. "In mid-October, we delivered the first storage system to a customer, which was an important milestone for our young company," said Florian Bierwirth, one of the EDENenergy co-founders. "With this storage size, we initially aim to target medium-sized companies in the region that have a photovoltaic system but do not yet have a storage solution." More background Each year, millions of batteries from e-bikes and e-scooters are discarded despite still having usable capacity, according to InsideEVs. Inside the storage unit, the batteries don't face the shaking and temperature swings they dealt with on the road. That absence gives them an easier environment to work in. What's being done? EDENenergy can swap out individual battery modules without shutting down the rest of the unit. The company said it keeps track of every module remotely and can make a swap without turning the whole unit off. For a business facing substantial losses if its power goes out, keeping the system running during a replacement is particularly useful. By swapping in new modules whenever old ones wear out, the company can hold the system's total capacity at 70 kilowatt-hours for years to come, according to InsideEVs. EDENenergy's next goal is getting its system to handle battery types from several different companies. "To do this, the connector interfaces, battery management system, and communication protocols must be adapted for each new battery," Bierwirth explained to InsideEVs. "There's a particularly wide range of options when it comes to e-bikes." Where can I learn more? EDENenergy's system joins other efforts to reuse old batteries and develop new ways to store electricity. • Across the U.S., Canada, and Australia, old EV batteries could store solar energy. • Texas adds 28 MWh of storage using repurposed EV batteries to support its grid. • A DIY solar owner considered $150 batteries on Facebook as commenters questioned their condition. • In Germany, a homeowner went fully off-grid with sodium-ion batteries after rejecting indoor lithium. • Jackery unveiled a 100 kWh home battery in Berlin, expanding beyond portable power. artigo.texto: CATL is exploring lithium-air battery research that carries a theoretical range of up to 2,000 km (1,243 miles) on one charge, and Yahoo Autos reported the story under a headline that calls CATL the world’s biggest EV battery maker. The figure comes from a theoretical specific energy of roughly 3,500 Wh/kg. That is a lab-side projection, not a measurement from a finished battery pack. The distinction matters because the number travels faster than its caveats. Reporting describes the CATL lithium-air battery as exploratory, experimental research. No tested 1,243-mile vehicle exists. No announced production battery exists either, and the available coverage identifies no confirmed CATL quote, no price, no vehicle partner and no production schedule. This piece looks at the story from the hardware side. We already published an earlier breakdown of the CATL lithium-air cell, so here we focus on how the 3,500 Wh/kg figure turns into a range claim, which engineering steps stand between theory and a car, and what buyers, suppliers and investors can reasonably do with the news today, November 09, 2026. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The CATL Lithium-Air Battery Claim in Plain Terms Strip away the headlines and the story has four moving parts. First, CATL is the battery maker at the center of it. Second, the chemistry is lithium-air, sometimes called air-breathing, which uses oxygen from the surrounding air as a reactant. Third, the theoretical specific energy sits at about 3,500 to 3,505 Wh/kg. Fourth, that figure converts into a theoretical range of up to 2,000 km, or 1,243 miles. What the story does not contain is just as important. Nobody has shown a car driving 1,243 miles on this chemistry. Nobody has published a complete automotive pack specification. CATL has not named a product, and the phrase lithium-air battery describes a chemistry family, not an officially announced CATL product line. Readers who skim only the number could walk away believing a showroom model is coming. Readers who read the verbs get a different picture. Outlets use words like explores and theoretical, and they frame the work as research. That is the honest reading, and it is the one this article follows. The takeaway for anyone tracking battery hardware: treat the 2,000 km figure as a ceiling that physics might allow under ideal conditions. It is not a forecast of what drivers will see. What 3,500 Wh/kg Means and Where It Stops Specific energy measures how much energy a battery stores per kilogram of mass. A higher number means a lighter battery for the same range, or a longer range for the same weight. The 3,500 Wh/kg figure attached to the CATL lithium-air battery means one kilogram of the theoretical active material could, in principle, deliver 3.5 kWh. That is simple arithmetic from the reported figure. The word theoretical carries most of the weight in that sentence. Theoretical specific energy usually describes the chemistry on paper, before engineers add the housing, the electrolyte, the current collectors, the cooling, the safety systems and the air-handling hardware a real pack requires. Every one of those parts adds mass, and every gram added lowers the number a driver actually benefits from. The table below separates what the reporting states from what it leaves open. The range depends on battery mass, usable energy, vehicle efficiency, durability and recharge performance. Change any one of those inputs and the 1,243-mile figure moves. A heavier car, a colder day or a faster highway speed would all cut it, and none of those variables appears in the reporting. How a Lithium-Air Cell Differs From Lithium-Ion A conventional lithium-ion cell stores everything it needs inside a sealed package. The lithium-bearing anode and cathode materials both live in the cell, and the cell carries the mass of both. Charging and discharging shuttles lithium ions between them. That design has powered phones, laptops and nearly every electric car on sale. A lithium-air cell swaps the heavy cathode for an air electrode. Instead of hauling all of its reactants, the cell draws oxygen from the surrounding air. Dropping the stored cathode material is where the large theoretical gain comes from. The cost is complexity, because the cell now depends on an air electrode and an oxygen-management system rather than a sealed block of solid materials. Reports say the theoretical energy density would sit several times above the figures commonly associated with emerging solid-state batteries. Those reports also warn against treating it as a verified cell specification. For context on where solid-state work stands in the lab, see our coverage of a solid-state coating that kept 82.3% capacity after 300 cycles. That result shows how slowly even the more mature next-generation chemistry moves from a paper to a product. Think of it as two different engineering problems. Lithium-ion is a packaging and materials-refinement problem. Lithium-air is a systems problem, because the battery must breathe, filter and protect itself while the car keeps moving. Why Outlets Framed the Same Story Four Different Ways Coverage of the CATL lithium-air battery split along a clear line. Some outlets led with the big number. Others led with the caveat. Reading them side by side shows how much a headline can change what a reader believes happened. Yahoo Autos framed the story as an exploration of a theoretical 1,243-mile range, which matches the fact pattern. EVXL went further in the cautious direction, with a headline arguing that CATL’s lithium-air research is not a 1,243-mile EV battery. ShiftDelete used a similar tone, describing the 2,000 km figure as one that remains theoretical. Interesting Engineering ran a more aggressive headline. artigo.texto: Anthropic compra equipamentos para geração de energia para data centers de IA em negócio de US$ 3,4 bi, diz jornal Segundo o Financial Times, trata-se da maior aquisição individual conhecida de equipamentos de geração de energia já realizada por um laboratório de inteligência artificial A Anthropic concordou em pagar US$ 3,4 bilhões por geradores movidos a gás natural destinados a data centers, informou o Financial Times. Segundo o jornal, trata-se da maior aquisição individual conhecida de equipamentos de geração de energia já realizada por um laboratório de inteligência artificial. De acordo com a publicação, no fim de setembro a empresa adquiriu compromissos de fornecimento de 1,7 gigawatt em geradores de alta potência da OnePWR Solutions, fornecedora de equipamentos sediada em San Antonio, no Texas, sem, contudo, comprar a própria companhia. Inicialmente, a Anthropic planejava comprar energia da OnePWR, mas posteriormente decidiu assumir os pedidos de geradores da Caterpillar feitos pela fornecedora, acrescentou o jornal. A aquisição é o mais recente sinal de que os laboratórios de IA estão avançando cada vez mais sobre o setor de energia e eliminando intermediários na corrida para garantir equipamentos de geração de eletricidade, cuja oferta é escassa. - Em meio a dúvidas sobre IA: Vendedor misterioso coloca US$ 500 milhões em dívidas de data centers à venda O negócio também reflete o esforço da Anthropic para obter maior controle sobre a infraestrutura que sustenta suas operações de inteligência artificial, depois de depender fortemente de parceiros para garantir energia, chips, centros de dados e terrenos. Na segunda-feira, a empresa afirmou que pretende gastar mais de US$ 895 bilhões nos próximos anos, sendo a maior parte desse montante destinada a custos de capacidade computacional e infraestrutura. A OnePWR e a Anthropic se recusaram a comentar o assunto ao Financial Times e não responderam imediatamente aos pedidos de manifestação da Bloomberg.

artigo.texto: O olhar único que há 50 anos acompanha o que é notícia no Brasil e no mundo Crise no Paraguai não deve afetar investimento americano em data center, mas pode frear ímpeto de empresas brasileiras Os investimentos americanos para a construção de um data center no Paraguai, abastecido pela energia da usina hidrelétrica de Itaipu, não devem sofrer revés com a crise dos sistemas financeiro e político, provocada pela quebra do Ueno Bank, dizem especialistas. Anunciado pelo Departamento de Estado dos Estados Unidos em outubro, o projeto deverá atender clientes de serviços de computação em nuvem norte-americanos e da América Latina. Na avaliação de Welber Barral, ex-secretário de Comércio Exterior e doutor em Direito Internacional pela USP, o maior impacto da derrocada do Ueno Bank é sobre as pessoas físicas. Apesar disso, ele acredita que pode haver um freio no interesse das empresas brasileiras por investimentos no país vizinho. Já o investimento americano não deve ser alterado, diz Barral, que conversou com o blog diretamente de Genebra, onde participa de um painel da Organização Mundial do Comércio (OMC). — O caso do Paraguai é tão chocante justamente pelo número de pessoas físicas que foram atingidas. Mas pode afetar eventualmente alguns investimentos menores, empresas brasileiras que estavam planejando investir lá, achando que o Paraguai é uma maravilha, por temor e até pelo desconhecimento, porque, na realidade, o grande efeito foi sobre pessoas físicas. Agora, os investimentos americanos fundamentalmente não dependem de nenhum financiamento nem de grande relação com bancos paraguaios. O grande investimento em data center vai passar muito mais por bancos americanos e grandes fundos. Por isso, não vejo um efeito imediato. - Como a crise de um banco digital derrubou o presidente do Paraguai em apenas dois dias? Veja a cronologia Carlos Frederico de Souza Coelho, professor de Relações Internacionais da PUC-Rio e da Escola de Comando e Estado-Maior do Exército (Eceme), ressalta ainda que, apesar de o anúncio ter vindo do Departamento de Estado dos EUA, o negócio foi firmado entre empresas: a americana Crusoe, que desenvolve infraestrutura para inteligência artificial, e a Araico, desenvolvedora paraguaia de projetos de energia e infraestrutura. Nesse sentido, explica Carlos Frederico, qualquer mudança significaria romper um contrato de longo prazo com o investidor estrangeiro. — Tem um segundo elemento, que é até mais importante: mudar o presidente não muda o alinhamento com os Estados Unidos. A não ser que houvesse um colapso econômico e social no Paraguai que levasse à remoção do Partido Colorado do poder. Algum atraso ou efeito sobre o acordo de investimento dependeria do grau de contágio econômico, o que ainda não pode ser entendido por completo — diz o professor. Especialista em comércio exterior, Karina Turbay Schnaid, assim como Barral, acredita que pode haver uma desaceleração temporária nas decisões de investimento das empresas brasileiras no Paraguai, principalmente entre empresas que ainda estão avaliando sua instalação. Ela pontua, no entanto, que as vantagens competitivas do país não são extintas com a crise. — O interesse de empresas brasileiras pelo Paraguai vinha crescendo, impulsionado pela busca de competitividade, redução de custos e integração das cadeias produtivas. Setores como autopeças, confecções, plásticos e alimentos estão entre os segmentos que encontram oportunidades de industrialização no país. A crise pode provocar uma desaceleração, entretanto, os fatores econômicos que motivaram esse movimento não desapareceram com a instabilidade política. O Paraguai mantém vantagens competitivas relevantes, especialmente nos custos de produção, energia e incentivos à industrialização. A competitividade não pode ser medida exclusivamente pela carga tributária. Segurança jurídica, estabilidade financeira, infraestrutura e eficiência logística são igualmente importantes. Para muitas empresas, a estratégia pode não ser transferir integralmente suas operações, mas desenvolver uma estrutura produtiva complementar entre Brasil e Paraguai, aproveitando as vantagens de cada mercado — afirma Karina. Carlos Fernando ressalta que no ranking de exportações brasileiras o Paraguai aparece como o 24º destino e na 19ª posição na lista de origem das nossas importações. A corrente de comércio entre os dois países, de US$ 5,84 bilhões corresponde a cerca de 1% das transação comerciais do Brasil com o mundo. Portanto, diz o especialista, o impacto deve ser limitado.

A ministra da Casa Civil, Miriam Belchior, disse nesta sexta (6/11) que o texto está “praticamente finalizado”, mas que o governo priorizou a agenda da conferência. O Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, criado pela lei 15.504 (PL 278), sancionada em 15 de setembro, depende do decreto para que as empresas possam se habilitar aos incentivos. O atraso encurta o prazo para usar o benefício neste ano. A suspensão de PIS/Pasep, Cofins e IPI vale até 31 de dezembro de 2026, por causa da reforma tributária. Depois, fica a do Imposto de Importação, até completar cinco anos. A Fazenda chegou a prever a assinatura do decreto para 28 de setembro. Um dos pontos em disputa é o uso de gás natural. A lei exige que os data centers habilitados atendam toda a demanda de eletricidade com fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. A expressão “baixa emissão”, incorporada na tramitação no Senado, abriu espaço para o MME defender o enquadramento do gás. A Fazenda resiste à inclusão. A minuta do decreto, antecipada pelo eixos pro, cobertura exclusiva para assinantes (teste grátis), deixa a definição para um ato conjunto de Fazenda, Minas e Energia, Meio Ambiente e Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços. artigo.texto: Engine manufacturer Cummins (NYSE:CMI) fell short of the market's revenue expectations in Q3 2026, but sales rose 13.5% year on year to $9.44 billion. Its non-GAAP profit of $8.25 per share was 0.7% above analysts' consensus estimates. Is now the time to buy CMI? Find out in our full research report (it's free). Cummins (CMI) Q3 2026 highlights: - Revenue $9.44 billion vs S&P analysts' estimates of $9.96 billion (13.5% year-on-year growth, 5.2% miss) - Adjusted EPS $8.25 vs S&P analysts' estimates of $8.20 (0.7% beat) - Adjusted EBITDA $1.82 billion vs analyst estimates of $1.86 billion (19.3% margin, 2.4% miss) - Operating margin 15.3%, up from 10.2% in the same quarter last year - Market capitalization $61.75 billion StockStory's take Cummins delivered third quarter results that disappointed Wall Street's revenue expectations, triggering a negative market reaction. Management attributed the shortfall to a combination of ongoing supply chain constraints in its Power Systems segment and weaker-than-anticipated demand for North American pickup truck engines. CEO Jennifer Rumsey highlighted that robust demand for data center power solutions and heavy-duty truck engines partially offset these headwinds, stating, "order intake in the third quarter exceeded what we thought it would be," but bottlenecks limited shipments, especially in Power Systems and Distribution. Looking forward, management's guidance is built on continued strength in power generation—especially driven by data center customers in North America, China, and Asia-Pacific. The company expects to recover most delayed shipments in the next quarter and is expanding manufacturing capacity for future demand. However, CEO Jennifer Rumsey cautioned that uncertainty around EPA regulations and elevated diesel prices could moderate pickup truck engine sales, while CFO Mark Smith flagged that supply chain and regulatory factors will impact the pace of new product transitions. Key insights from management's remarks Management pointed to strong data center-related orders, supply chain challenges, and evolving regulatory dynamics as key themes shaping the quarter's performance and their updated outlook. - Data center power demand: Cummins saw exceptionally strong demand for power generation equipment from data center operators, with multi-year orders extending into 2028. This trend is global, with accelerated growth in China and the Asia-Pacific region, not just North America. - Supply chain bottlenecks: Delays from a key supplier in Power Systems constrained shipments, resulting in lower-than-anticipated revenues in that segment and Distribution. Management expects these issues to be largely resolved in the next quarter, allowing delayed deliveries to catch up. - North American truck uncertainty: Weaker-than-expected demand for pickup truck engines was attributed to elevated diesel prices and interest rates, as well as regulatory uncertainty surrounding upcoming EPA emissions rules. Customers are delaying some purchases as they await clarity on Non-Conformance Penalties (NCPs) and the phased transition to 2027-compliant products. - Product launches and feedback: Cummins completed the "Forever Rising Tour," showcasing its upcoming X15, X10, and natural gas X15N engines to customers. Feedback was positive, particularly regarding reliability and drivability, supporting confidence in the 2027 product launch schedule. - Investment in capacity and new technologies: The company opened a new manufacturing facility for cooling systems and is expanding production to meet rising demand, especially for smaller generator sets. This includes investment in battery energy storage systems (BESS) for data centers, marking Cummins' largest deployment to date.

artigo.texto: MEMPHIS, TN — Elon Musk says two additional data centers tied to SpaceXAI’s expanding artificial intelligence operation in the Memphis area are expected to begin operating before the end of the year. The announcement comes as the rapid growth of the facilities faces increasing scrutiny from residents and city officials concerned about the effects of large-scale data center development. The two sites, known as Gun Range and Spam, are part of the company’s Colossus 2 computing complex. Musk said Gun Range is expected to become operational by the end of November, with Spam scheduled to follow in December. Those dates are projections from Musk and have not been independently confirmed. The names reflect the properties’ previous uses. Gun Range was formerly a police and fire training facility, while Spam was a warehouse that stored products made by Hormel Foods. Both properties are in Southaven, Mississippi, across the state line from Memphis. Together, the two facilities are expected to house approximately 420,000 Nvidia GB300 graphics processing units. Musk indicated that Gun Range would contain about 220,000 chips configured to train artificial intelligence models. Spam is expected to house approximately 200,000 chips designed to handle inference, the process of responding to requests from users and running already-trained AI systems. The new buildings will expand Colossus 2, which already includes facilities known as Macrohard, Macroharder and Minihard. Musk has said the broader Colossus 2 complex is expected to contain approximately 1.2 million Nvidia Blackwell chips by the end of 2026. The company uses the computing infrastructure to support its Grok artificial intelligence platform. The expansion follows the launch of the original Colossus supercomputer in 2024 at a former Electrolux manufacturing facility in South Memphis. The company later expanded its operations into the Whitehaven area and Southaven. Musk has also said he has been spending several days a week in Memphis overseeing construction. The projects have drawn opposition from nearby residents who have raised concerns about pollution, noise, electricity demand and water use. In April, the NAACP filed a federal lawsuit against xAI and subsidiary MZX Tech, alleging that the companies operated methane gas turbines without required permits at the Southaven site. A federal judge recently rejected the companies’ request to dismiss the lawsuit, allowing the case to proceed. Meanwhile, the Memphis City Council approved a 135-day pause on new data center permitting after rejecting a proposed yearlong moratorium. The measure is intended to give city officials time to develop land-use and siting rules addressing neighborhood protections, infrastructure and environmental concerns. It does not stop existing facilities from operating or automatically halt projects with protected approvals. The latest expansion highlights the challenge facing communities across the Mid-South as technology companies move quickly to build the infrastructure needed for artificial intelligence while residents and local governments seek greater oversight of the projects. artigo.texto: O Comitê Interministerial sobre Mudança do Clima (CIM) fixou nesta sexta-feira, 6, os limites para a venda de créditos de carbono brasileiros a outros países. A autorização de Resultados de Mitigação Transferidos Internacionalmente (ITMOs, na sigla em inglês) ficou restrita a 50 milhões de toneladas de CO2 equivalente no ciclo 2026-2030 e a 100 milhões de toneladas no período 2031-2035. As definições saíram da 6ª Reunião Ordinária do colegiado, realizada em Brasília, conforme apurou a Estadão Conteúdo. Os ITMOs são o instrumento que permite a nações compradoras abater resultados de mitigação gerados em território brasileiro no cumprimento de suas próprias metas climáticas, dentro do artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris. O país também poderá cooperar em esquemas de compensação de emissões com outros governos, inclusive nos mecanismos ligados à aviação internacional. Critérios priorizam remoção de carbono e metano O colegiado também estabeleceu os parâmetros que vão compor a lista de atividades elegíveis. A preferência será para projetos de remoção de carbono, caso da restauração florestal, e para iniciativas que cortem as emissões de metano em aterros sanitários e em resíduos orgânicos. Na mesma reunião, o comitê tratou das orientações para o funcionamento do mercado doméstico de carbono e para a participação do Brasil nos mecanismos internacionais de compensação. Mapa do Caminho e transparência climática Além dos tetos, o CIM aprovou o Mapa do Caminho que tem como meta deter e reverter o avanço do desmatamento e da degradação das florestas até 2030. O documento aposta na ampliação do financiamento e na assistência técnica para destravar a execução de metas e planos já estabelecidos. A construção do plano responde a um chamado do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva feito durante a COP30, para que os países apresentem estratégias de cumprimento do compromisso coletivo firmado no primeiro Balanço Global do Acordo de Paris. O comitê validou ainda o 2º Relatório Bienal de Transparência (BTR) e a 5ª Comunicação Nacional do Brasil, documentos que atualizam os dados sobre emissões nacionais de gases de efeito estufa e os esforços para cumprir a Contribuição Nacionalmente Determinada (NDC). Os textos serão encaminhados à Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (UNFCCC).

artigo.texto: AMD agora prioriza data centers; mas e os jogos e os PCs? Aplicações de IA aumentaram demanda por data centers que, por sua vez, agora são principal fonte de receita para a AMD. Lisa Su declarou recentemente que a AMD é uma “data center first company”, ou seja, uma empresa focada em soluções para data centers. Seria apenas mais uma declaração de uma liderança corporativa — Su é a CEO da companhia — se não fosse por uma pergunta que ficou no ar: isso significa que a AMD deixou o mercado de jogos em segundo plano? A declaração foi dada em uma entrevista de Lisa Su ao Yahoo Finance, em 5 de novembro. Note que a executiva não afirma que a AMD se transformará em uma companhia focada em data centers, mas que a companhia já trata esse setor com prioridade. Há uma boa razão para isso: considerando somente o terceiro trimestre de 2026, o segmento de data centers registrou, sozinho, receita de US$ 8,55 bilhões para a AMD. Já os segmentos de soluções para PCs (como a linha Ryzen), jogos (como os chips para o PS5) e sistemas embarcados responderam, juntos, por quase US$ 5 bilhões de receita no mesmo período. Na prática, isso significa que o setor de data centers é responsável, atualmente, por cerca de 65% da receita total da AMD. Não surpreende, afinal, a demanda por esse tipo de infraestrutura está elevada em todo o mundo devido, em grande medida, ao crescimento acelerado das aplicações de inteligência artificial. A AMD tem atendido ao setor principalmente com os processadores Epyc e os aceleradores gráficos Instinct, que não são linhas novas. Esta última existe desde 2017, por exemplo. Se esses produtos convivem há anos com as soluções para PCs, o temor sobre um eventual abandono do segmento gamer é exagerado, certo? Pode até ser exagerado, mas é compreensível. A demanda por data centers está tão elevada que muitas companhias de tecnologia migraram quase que totalmente para esse segmento, deixando o mercado consumidor em situação marginal. Um exemplo notável: no fim de 2025, a Micron abandonou a marca Crucial, focada em PCs, para se concentrar em memórias para data centers. Apesar de o temor ser justificado, a AMD não deu nenhum sinal de que abandonará os segmentos de jogos ou de PCs como um todo. Basta nos lembrarmos, como exemplo, que a companhia continua envolvida com o Project Helix, a futura geração do Xbox. Outro: em PCs de alto desempenho, a companhia segue atualizando a linha de chips Ryzen X3D. Por outro lado, não podemos descartar a possibilidade de a AMD priorizar investimentos em soluções para data centers a ponto de linhas como as GPUs Radeon serem atualizadas com uma frequência menor ou até terem menos unidades disponibilizadas no mercado. Em resumo: o momento não é para pânico, mas requer atenção. {{ excerpt | truncatewords: 35 }} {% endif %}

artigo.texto: Entering Q4, the sodium-ion battery industry chain has reached the most critical delivery verification period of the year. SMM data shows that in October, sodium-ion battery cathode material production increased 3% MoM and surged 260% YoY, while hard carbon anode production pulled back slightly by 4% MoM but surged 186% YoY—the high YoY growth rates confirm that the industry remains on a zero-to-one volume expansion trajectory, but the mediocre MoM performance reveals another reality: the pace of capacity ramp-up has generally lagged market expectations, with a clear time lag between order growth and actual delivery. On the pricing side, NFPP cathode quotes diverged, precursors hovered near cost lines, and iron phosphate supply-demand tension stayed high. The two-way squeeze of cost pressure and order losses below cost is reshaping the industry's competitive landscape. 1. Cathode Materials: Production Up 3% MoM, Capacity Release Falls Short of Expectations, Orders Accelerating Toward Top-Tier Players 1. Supply side: Ramp-up hindered, delivery capability supplemented by "outsourcing + toll processing" In October, sodium-ion battery cathode material production increased 3% MoM and surged 260% YoY. The overall market operated steadily, but capacity release falling short of expectations was the most prominent contradiction this month. Although 10 kt-class new lines gradually entered commissioning, compounded by line switchovers and equipment changes, actual output still failed to meet the original ramp-up targets. Some enterprises improved delivery capability through outsourced processing and other means; once downstream processes are fully connected after mid-November, monthly capacity is expected to reach the kt level. 2. Demand side: Clear divergence, growth concentrated in small power and energy storage The demand side showed significant divergence: in October, some enterprises shipped only in the hundreds of mt, while November orders have already increased to several hundred mt and will be delivered in batches, with growth mainly coming from small power and some energy storage orders. However, it is worth noting that if lithium carbonate prices continue to weaken, December market conditions may fall short of November—some clients' new orders have already shown losses below cost, and downstream willingness to take orders has clearly declined. From the perspective of enterprise operations, the trend of orders concentrating toward top-tier players is becoming increasingly evident: industry leaders have orders on hand exceeding 1 kt, while their in-house monthly capacity is only several hundred mt and cannot fully cover demand, requiring a dual-line approach of "in-house production + toll processing" to ensure delivery. 3. Price side: NFPP quotes diverge, with cost pressure centered on iron phosphate October NFPP quotes remained relatively stable, with mainstream transaction prices concentrated at 24,000-27,000 yuan/mt. In the short term, there is clearly no room for price increases, nor for price cuts, and prices have entered a stalemate range. Cost-side pressure remains concentrated in the iron phosphate segment. Although phosphoric acid prices have pulled back from 12,000 yuan/mt to around 9,000 yuan/mt, iron phosphate prices remain at approximately 16,000 yuan/mt due to tight supply and demand, significantly above the reasonable range of 12,000-13,000 yuan/mt. Persistently high raw material costs are pushing downstream material enterprises to accelerate self-built iron phosphate production lines or form joint ventures with phosphorus chemical companies, advancing industry chain integration. In the precursor segment, mainstream transaction prices are 19,000-20,000 yuan/mt, with large orders as low as 17,000-18,000 yuan/mt, already essentially at cost levels. Enterprises generally adopt tiered pricing to secure major clients. 4. Competitive landscape: Tier differentiation accelerates, market exit approaches From the competitive landscape perspective, tier differentiation within the industry is accelerating. Top-tier cathode enterprises with planned capacity of 10 kt-level projects are coming online successively, steadily expanding their leading edge. Small and mid-sized startups are under pressure due to tightening financing environments and delayed production line construction, with some enterprises' publicly claimed capacity still lagging behind actual production. Another noteworthy signal: NFPP precursor enterprises generally show low willingness to cross over into cathode production, mainly due to concerns about direct competition with downstream clients—this has objectively maintained the existing competitive boundaries in the cathode segment. Looking ahead: Q4 cathode shipments may show a "high-then-low" trend, with prices remaining weak under the dual squeeze of cost support and inverted order losses. Top-tier players with scale capacity, integrated costs, and quality client structures will benefit first, and industry consolidation and concentration are expected to accelerate. November sodium-ion battery cathode production is expected to increase 9% MoM and surge 162% YoY. II. Hard Carbon Anode: Production Edges Down 4% MoM, Commissioning Window Determines Year-End Output, Stockpiling Intent Rises 1. Supply Side: Orders in the Hundreds of mt, Deliveries Yet to Scale Up In October, the hard carbon anode material market remained generally stable, with production edging down 4% from September while surging 186% YoY. Although most enterprises received orders in the hundreds of mt in October, actual deliveries have yet to scale up due to capacity constraints—"orders without goods" is the current reality for this segment. 2. On the All-In podcast episode released November 7, which covered the midterm elections, the AI selloff, and what the hosts called a data center freeze, David Sacks said: "Nobody can make a $50 billion investment in conditions of uncertainty. I think by 2028 the pipeline will be closed or significantly reduced." His argument rests on permitting. Sacks said the biggest danger is breaking ground and then, halfway through, getting "enjoined" or stopped by a worker strike or a community group. According to Sacks, governors in the largest data center states are "basically indicating that they favor a moratorium" until certain conditions are met. Why a Permitting Freeze Reaches Every Supplier A data center needs land, power, and a finished building before a single chip goes in. Broadcom's chief executive made the same point on the company's September call: "Before you get the chips out there, you have to get the data center shell in place and ready for production." If the buildings stall, chip, networking, and cooling orders slow down after them.
