Over the same month, Equinix (NASDAQ:EQIX) slipped only 1.85% and Digital Realty 3.47%. One explanation is that a freeze could help companies that already own permitted, powered sites. Equinix's chief executive said, "If there are a number of projects canceled, then it only makes what is already scarce capacity much more of a scarce resource." She added that across its 3 gigawatts of planned capacity, "the land, power and permitting are largely secured." Digital Realty has 1.5 gigawatts under construction, 63% pre-leased, and a record $2.5 billion backlog that gives it visibility through 2027 and into 2028. Sacks's view is a forecast. Proposed moratoriums can be narrowed, delayed, or dropped, and nobody knows yet how state policy will land. Vertiv's chief executive called power, permitting, and labor pacing items that "are not slowing down growth." NVIDIA expects fiscal 2028 revenue growth of approximately 70% and describes that outlook as limited by supply, with customer demand running higher. NVIDIA also cited top-five hyperscaler capex of nearly $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027. What Retirement Investors Should Watch Next Many people own this trade without picking a single stock. Four signals stand out: State action: whether moratorium talk in the big data center states turns into passed rules or remains at the proposal stage. Guidance checks: NVIDIA's results against its $108.0B guide, and Broadcom's against expected Q4 AI revenue of $21.7B. Vertiv orders: customers order 12 to 18 months ahead, so a slowdown in orders would be one of the first signs that 2028 projects are being pushed back. REIT pre-leasing and pricing: rising rents at Equinix and Digital Realty would suggest that scarcity is helping the landlords even as new construction slows down. If permitting tightens, investors with heavy index exposure to AI hardware should know which parts of the chain depend on new construction and which ones collect rent on capacity that is already built. artigo.texto: Analog chipmaker Microchip Technology (NASDAQ:MCHP) beat Wall Street's revenue expectations in calendar Q3 2026 (fiscal Q2 2027), with sales up 42.2% year on year to $1.62 billion. On the other hand, next quarter's revenue guidance of $1.61 billion was less impressive, coming in 1.4% below analysts' estimates. Its non-GAAP profit of $0.97 per share was 3.4% above analysts' consensus estimates. Revenue $1.62 billion vs S&P analysts' estimates of $1.61 billion (42.2% year-on-year growth, 0.8% beat) Adjusted EPS $0.97 vs S&P analysts' estimates of $0.94 (3.4% beat) Adjusted operating income $639.9 million vs analyst estimates of $628.9 million (39.5% margin, 1.8% beat) Revenue guidance $1.61 billion at the midpoint for Q4 CY2026, below analyst estimates of $1.63 billion Adjusted EPS guidance $0.91 at the midpoint for Q4 CY2026, below analyst estimates of $0.95 Operating margin 28.6%, up from 7.8% in the same quarter last year Inventory days outstanding 184, up from 175 in the previous quarter Market capitalization $35.21 billion StockStory's take Microchip Technology's latest quarter saw sales climb on robust demand in industrial and data center end markets, with management attributing growth to new design wins and strength across key verticals. However, the market reacted negatively to the results, reflecting concerns over the sustainability of these gains. CEO Steve Sanghi noted that several non-recurring items, including licensing revenue and a distribution price adjustment, boosted reported sales. He emphasized, "Industrial and data center end markets were the two biggest drivers of our growth." The company also faced rising inventory levels as it prepared for future customer needs. Looking ahead, Microchip Technology's guidance reflects cautious optimism tempered by supply chain constraints and seasonal factors. Management highlighted that some high-margin orders in advanced products cannot be fulfilled this quarter due to extended lead times at foundries and outsourced assembly and test (OSAT) suppliers. Sanghi explained, "Our net sales guidance is lower than what we would have expected a quarter ago," citing both the absence of last quarter's one-time items and supply limitations. The company expects incremental capacity additions and a gradual improvement in fulfillment, but does not anticipate a swift normalization of gross margins given ongoing supplier price increases and operational bottlenecks. Key insights from management's remarks Management credited broad-based design win momentum, particularly in data center and industrial applications, for the quarter's growth. Non-recurring revenue items and evolving supply chain dynamics contributed to deviations from consensus expectations. Industrial and data center momentum: Management pointed to strong demand and recent design wins in industrial automation, robotics, and data center infrastructure, with the data center segment now representing nearly 17% of sales. The company is ramping next-generation PCIe Gen 6 switch and retimer products, highlighting 24 design wins that will scale revenue over the next year. Impact of non-recurring items: The quarter benefited from approximately $53 million in one-time revenue from licensing, pricing changes on channel inventory, and a customer contract. CFO Eric Bjornholt clarified these items carried 100% gross margin but are not expected to repeat, creating a less favorable comparison for the coming quarter. Supply chain bottlenecks: CEO Steve Sanghi described persistent constraints at both internal fabrication sites and external OSAT partners, with the AI sector crowding out capacity for legacy and analog products. Lead times for many core products have lengthened from 4-8 weeks to as long as 32 weeks, affecting the timing of high-margin shipments. Inventory management and production shifts: Inventory days outstanding increased as Microchip received high-value wafers in anticipation of demand and shifted some production internally to offset external bottlenecks. The company is qualifying new OSAT partners and rebalancing its internal versus external manufacturing strategy but expects these transitions to take several quarters. Acquisitions and portfolio expansion: Microchip completed the acquisitions of Hailo (AI edge computing) and VORAGO (aerospace and defense), integrating these into existing business units. While these deals will add to operating expenses in the short term, management expects them to accelerate the roadmap in AI and provide high-margin opportunities in aerospace and defense. Drivers of future performance Microchip's forward outlook is shaped by ongoing supply constraints, pricing pressures from suppliers, and the need to balance capacity with persistent demand across end markets. Supply chain and capacity expansion: Management stressed that lead times remain extended due to capacity constraints at foundries and OSAT partners, impacting fulfillment of high-margin products. While incremental internal and external capacity additions are planned for the coming quarters, the timing of improvements remains uncertain, and some backlog will spill into future periods. Supplier price increases and margin headwinds: Sanghi acknowledged that further price hikes from foundry and OSAT suppliers starting in January will pressure gross margins. While Microchip is reluctant to push another immediate price increase to customers, the company will need to assess whether these costs can be absorbed or passed on, with a long-term gross margin target of 65%. Diversified end-market demand: Despite concerns about an overheated data center market, management highlighted steady momentum in industrial, aerospace and defense, automotive, and communication segments. The company's relatively modest exposure to data center revenue, compared to peers, leaves it less vulnerable to a slowdown in that sector, while broad-based design wins are expected to support growth. artigo.texto: ARRAY Technologies, a provider of structural balance-of-system (SBOS) solutions for utility-scale solar, and Shoals Technologies Group, which supplies electrical balance-of-system (EBOS) equipment for utility-scale solar and battery energy storage, said the companies have agreed to combine in a stock-for-stock merger. The firms on Nov. 4 said the deal "creates an integrated energy infrastructure platform that brings together complementary, market-leading solutions across foundations, trackers, fixed-tilt racking, electrical infrastructure, wire management and power delivery systems."The companies in a news release said ARRAY will serve as the corporate parent of the combined company. Shoals' shareholders will receive a fixed exchange ratio of 1.6931 ARRAY shares for each Shoals' share they own. After closing, Shoals' shareholders are expected to own about 65% of the combined company's basic shares outstanding, and ARRAY shareholders will own the rest.Officials said the combined company will serve solar and battery energy storage customers through a unified design package, with coordinated purchasing and integrated warranty support across SBOS and EBOS solutions. The groups said the merger supports delivery of "increasing levels of integration over time designed to reduce installation costs, streamline project execution and lower long-term maintenance requirements.""Today marks an important milestone for Shoals, ARRAY and the customers we serve," said Brandon Moss, CEO of Shoals. "By bringing together two highly complementary businesses with experienced teams, we are creating an integrated platform with broader capabilities, deeper customer relationships and a stronger foundation for long-term growth. We believe the combined company will be positioned to better service customers, deliver more innovative and integrated solutions, realize meaningful synergies and pursue expansion opportunities across the solar value chain, data center markets and beyond."Kevin Hostetler, ARRAY's CEO, said, "This transaction represents a compelling opportunity to create meaningful value for customers of both ARRAY and Shoals by bringing together our complementary strengths. Although structural and electrical systems must operate seamlessly together in the field, they have historically been designed and sourced through separate channels. This combination changes that. Together, we expect to deliver a differentiated, technically integrated and interoperable platform that simplifies project execution, enhances project economics and accelerates innovation for customers." Strategic and Financial Rationale The companies said the merger will bring several benefits for customers, including more effective service through a unified design package, with coordinated purchasing and integrated warranty support across combined offerings. The combined company intends to offer customers enhanced flexibility and packaging choice across foundations, trackers, electrical infrastructure and wire management solutions, including the solar industry's best performing ground screw, single-axis tracker, DC wiring solution and cable management hanger.The groups said customer value will be enhanced "by streamlining project execution, reducing installation costs, and lowering long-term maintenance requirements through increased product integration. SBOS and EBOS solutions are highly symbiotic across solar and battery storage projects. By bringing these complementary product categories together, the combined company expects to deliver more integrated solutions that reduce interface complexity, enhance energy yield and reliability, simplify installation and lower customers' total cost of ownership."Officials also highlighted both companies technical expertise in their respective markets, which should support innovation. The combined company also expects to realize savings in overhead and other expenses, and noted "Year-one cost synergies are expected to deliver approximately $20 million of incremental, run-rate Adjusted EBITDA [Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization]." The combined company expects to benefit from Shoals' approximately $1.6 billion of tax amortization and $237 million of Net Operating Losses, which are anticipated to reduce taxable income and limit the cash tax obligations of the combined company for the next several years. Leadership Structure Moss will serve as CEO of the combined company. Hostetler will serve as special advisor. Brad Forth, current chairman of the board of both ARRAY and Shoals, will serve as board chairman after the merger."Having had the privilege of serving as chairman of both ARRAY and Shoals, I have seen firsthand the complementary products, talented teams and shared commitment to customers offered by both companies," said Forth. "Together, ARRAY and Shoals are well positioned to deliver enhanced value to customers, shareholders and employees. I also want to thank Kevin for his leadership and important contributions to ARRAY, as well as his valuable insights as he transitions to a Special Advisor role. I look forward to continuing to work with Brandon, who brings proven leadership, deep industry expertise and strategic vision to lead the combined company in this next phase of growth."The combined company intends to announce a new corporate name and ticker symbol in the coming months to reflect the expanded scope of its products, services and strategic opportunities.—Darrell Proctor is a senior editor for POWER.

artigo.texto: Após vitória eleitoral dos democratas complicarem novos data centers, Meta olha para fora dos EUA para construir Presidente da companhia diz que começar projetos do zero ficou mais difícil; projetos no exterior e ampliação de instalações existentes entram no cálculo de uma expansão de até US$ 145 bilhões neste ano Atualizado 06/11/2026 A Meta considera construir data centers fora dos Estados Unidos e ampliar instalações existentes para reduzir o risco de sua expansão em inteligência artificial. A mudança de estratégia foi apresentada por Dina Powell McCormick, presidente da Meta e vice-presidente do Conselho de Administração da companhia, depois que candidatos contrários a novos empreendimentos venceram eleições importantes no país. “Começar novos projetos de data centers hoje nos Estados Unidos será muito desafiador”, afirmou McCormick durante o WSJ Tech. A executiva disse que a Meta e outras gigantes da tecnologia já discutem se precisam levar uma parte maior dos investimentos para outros países. “Posso dizer que todas as empresas de grande escala em nuvem estão pensando: ‘Precisamos construir fora dos Estados Unidos?’”, afirmou. “Como são investimentos enormes, proteger esses investimentos é uma decisão sensata.” A declaração explicita uma consequência empresarial das eleições de meio de mandato. A resistência aos data centers ajudou democratas a conquistar os governos do Texas, da Geórgia e de Ohio, três estados envolvidos na expansão da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. Novos governadores defenderam interrupções condicionais, maior controle sobre licenças e proteções para impedir que moradores paguem pela energia exigida pelos projetos. Essa pressão chega quando a Meta tenta assegurar capacidade suficiente para levar seus agentes pessoais de IA a uma base de 3,6 bilhões de usuários. Mark Zuckerberg colocou o sistema Muse no centro da estratégia da empresa e elevou a previsão de investimentos em infraestrutura e equipamentos para até US$ 145 bilhões neste ano, de acordo com o WSJ. McCormick disse que dedica cerca de 80% de seu tempo a garantir capacidade computacional para a Meta. A executiva assumiu a presidência da companhia em janeiro com a missão de desenvolver parcerias com governos e investidores para financiar e instalar data centers em diferentes países. Quem já construiu ganha vantagem A mudança política cria uma diferença entre empresas que já têm instalações em funcionamento e aquelas que ainda precisam encontrar terrenos, negociar energia e obter licenças. Segundo McCormick, ampliar data centers existentes tende a ser mais fácil porque as comunidades já conhecem o projeto e seus efeitos sobre empregos, arrecadação e infraestrutura. Começar do zero exige construir também a aceitação política. A vantagem pode aumentar o valor da capacidade já instalada. “É por isso que a computação está se tornando um ativo ainda mais escasso, que não foi totalmente precificado pelo mercado”, afirmou a executiva durante o evento. A avaliação coincide com a reação dos investidores depois das eleições. Empresas que dependem da construção de novas instalações sofreram fortes quedas, enquanto Amazon, Microsoft e Alphabet chegaram a subir no primeiro pregão. Analistas interpretaram que grandes proprietárias de infraestrutura poderiam gastar menos e se beneficiar da valorização dos data centers que já controlam. A Meta chega a essa disputa com duas décadas de experiência na construção dessas instalações. McCormick afirmou que a companhia tem data centers em 23 estados americanos e planeja ao menos cinco projetos com capacidade de um gigawatt ou mais. O tamanho da aposta também aumenta o custo de um atraso. Em outubro, a Meta anunciou a criação de uma nova classe de ações sem direito a voto para futuras captações. Na semana seguinte, apresentou um plano para levantar até US$ 97,5 bilhões em sucessivas ofertas de ações, segundo o Wall Street Journal. A busca por capital ocorre depois que a companhia registrou fluxo de caixa livre negativo pela primeira vez desde 2012, ano de sua abertura de capital. O aumento dos gastos em IA já vinha inquietando investidores antes de as eleições acrescentarem o risco de licenças mais lentas, novas exigências ambientais e maior resistência local. Projeto de US$ 14 bilhões no Texas entra no radar O principal exemplo da exposição da Meta está no Texas. A companhia se associou à BlackRock para desenvolver um campus de um gigawatt em El Paso, com previsão de começar a operar em 2028. A estrutura envolve aproximadamente US$ 14 bilhões em custos de desenvolvimento dos prédios e da infraestrutura de energia, refrigeração e conectividade, segundo o anúncio oficial da Meta. A empresa afirma que seu investimento no local supera US$ 10 bilhões. Fundos administrados pela BlackRock terão 80% do empreendimento, enquanto a Meta manterá os outros 20%. A operação inclui US$ 12,5 bilhões em financiamento por dívida. A Meta será inicialmente a única ocupante e poderá permanecer no campus por até 20 anos. O contrato ainda prevê garantias da companhia sobre o valor futuro das instalações, com limite inicial próximo de US$ 13 bilhões e redução ao longo do tempo. Esse desenho procura atrair capital externo sem retirar da Meta o controle operacional e o acesso à capacidade computacional. Mais de 2,3 mil pessoas já trabalhavam na construção quando a parceria foi anunciada, em julho. A Meta projeta quatro mil empregos no pico das obras e 300 postos permanentes depois da conclusão. O futuro político do Texas mudou desde então. A governadora eleita Gina Hinojosa defendeu a suspensão de novos projetos até que o Legislativo aprove regras sobre energia, água, incentivos fiscais e participação das comunidades. O estado concentra cerca de 25% da capacidade americana de data centers planejada, segundo uma estimativa do Goldman Sachs publicada pela Reuters. artigo.texto: South Korean defense and technology giant Hanwha Ocean plans to advance the power and control system for its Floating Data Center (FDC). The company announced on Friday that it has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with ABB, a transnational corporation specializing in electrification and automation, for this purpose. Hanwha Ocean introduced the FDC at the Gastech Exhibition & Conference 2026 in September. The solution is designed to operate offshore, generating its own power and using seawater-based cooling systems to improve energy efficiency. Now, under the new deal with ABB, Hanwha Ocean will lead the basic design and power system configuration, establish design criteria for LNG engine-based power generation, and assess equipment layouts and suitability for offshore conditions. ABB, in turn, will analyze power system reliability and power quality based on Hanwha Ocean’s design and conduct technical reviews to improve efficiency amid fluctuating demand in the offshore environment. “AI data centers can experience rapid fluctuations in power demand during computing operations. Together, we will develop technologies to adjust LNG engine output in response to these changes and maintain stable operation of power equipment,” Hanwha Ocean shared on social media. Through this collaboration, Hanwha Ocean aims to extend its offshore engineering and construction capabilities into digital infrastructure and continue strengthening the core technologies behind FDCs.

artigo.texto: UK has no plans to slow down AI data center construction The country’s growth minister said the data centers will continue as “essential infrastructure” projects. As the US deals with the fallout associated with the ongoing demand for data centers, the UK is looking to capitalize on it instead, according to one of the country's ministers. Dan Tomlinson, the UK's minister for growth, told the The Financial Times that data center construction will continue as "essential infrastructure." Tomlinson told FT that AI is becoming more widely used throughout the UK's economy, meaning the country will need more data centers to support that growth. However, the minister added that data center construction in the UK will have to invest in local communities and create jobs to receive government support. Tomlinson also told FT that the UK government has taken away some lessons from the "free-for-all in parts of the US" with data center construction and that the country would take a more nuanced approach with better oversight. According to the UK Compute Roadmap, a policy paper detailing how the country can meet AI's growing power demands, the UK needs to have at least a computing capacity of 6GW from data centers by 2030. The UK previously made it easier for data centers to earn approvals, thanks to the "AI Growth Zones" initiative introduced by former prime minister Keir Starmer in 2025. However, UK residents have taken to protesting on sites of planned data center construction. Across the Atlantic, a majority of American voters said they're in favor of restricting the rapid pace of data center construction in local ballot results.

artigo.texto: A COP31 começa na segunda-feira (09/11), na Turquia, com novas regras para o Brasil negociar resultados de redução de emissões no exterior. A decisão, aprovada pelo governo federal na sexta-feira (06/11), estabelece limites para transferências internacionais de carbono e pode atrair investimentos para projetos ambientais. Entretanto, a abertura dessas oportunidades dependerá de autorizações, compradores e comprovação dos resultados. O Comitê Interministerial sobre Mudança do Clima aprovou a medida com base no Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris, que permite a cooperação internacional para o cumprimento de metas climáticas. Assim, o país passa a contar com parâmetros para autorizar operações que envolvem resultados de mitigação transferidos internacionalmente, conhecidos como ITMOs. Créditos de carbono na COP31 terão limites para negociação internacional O Brasil poderá autorizar transferências de até 50 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ equivalente entre 2026 e 2030. Para o período de 2031 a 2035, o limite previsto sobe para 100 milhões de toneladas, com possibilidade de revisão. As regras priorizam atividades capazes de remover carbono da atmosfera, como a restauração florestal, além de projetos que reduzam emissões de metano em aterros sanitários. Há, porém, uma diferença importante: os ITMOs são resultados de mitigação autorizados para transferência internacional e não se confundem automaticamente com créditos comercializados no mercado voluntário. Além disso, a regulamentação estabelece condições distintas para projetos florestais. Em regra, metade dos resultados de restauração poderá ser transferida. Já iniciativas dentro ou no entorno de unidades de conservação poderão comercializar a totalidade dos créditos, observadas as exigências aplicáveis. Como as novas regras podem atrair investimentos? Para empresas e investidores, a definição dos limites permite avaliar projetos com maior previsibilidade regulatória. Isso pode favorecer iniciativas de recuperação ambiental e aproveitamento de metano, cujas receitas dependem da capacidade de demonstrar reduções ou remoções de emissões. O interesse por esse mercado já aparece nos projetos de créditos de carbono florestal na Amazônia, que atraíram propostas de restauração ambiental. Contudo, o volume autorizado não representa créditos vendidos nem receita garantida. Cada operação dependerá de requisitos técnicos, validação dos resultados e condições comerciais negociadas com compradores internacionais, observando as regras aprovadas pelo governo federal. A decisão integra a agenda brasileira que será apresentada na COP31, em Antália, de 9 a 20 de novembro. O governo também aprovou diretrizes para o mercado regulado nacional, previsto na Lei nº 15.042/2024, mas esse sistema possui regras próprias. Para os projetos brasileiros, a próxima etapa será demonstrar viabilidade financeira. A autorização internacional amplia as possibilidades de negociação, mas o retorno dependerá do preço obtido pelos resultados ambientais e dos custos para gerá-los, comprová-los e transferi-los.

artigo.texto: Bloom Energy (NYSE:BE) turned up in two big data center announcements on Nov. 5. NTT DATA said it had agreed to deploy 900 megawatts of the fuel cell maker's onsite power across data center projects around the world. And Alphabet's Google said Bloom would build the fuel cells for a 702-megawatt plant powering its first data center in Wyoming, a $17 billion project. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » The stock had a bad day anyway. Shares ended at $167.52, off around 16%, amid worries that rising opposition to new data centers after the Nov. 3 midterms might slow the build-out of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. The growth stock is still up over 90% this year. But it now sits about 52% below the $345.85 record close it set on June 22. How much new business did Bloom win on Nov. 5? Less than the headlines may suggest, because just one of the two deals is new. I think the other still matters, though, and the stock looks much more reasonably priced than it did in October. Image source: The Motley Fool. Google's fuel cells were ordered in January Google won't buy the fuel cells itself. American Electric Power plans to invest around $4 billion in the 702-megawatt project near Cheyenne, Wyoming, the utility said on Oct. 14. It'll sell the plant's output to Google under a 20-year power purchase agreement, and it expects the plant to be fully running by late 2028. The fuel cell order came months earlier. In January, an AEP subsidiary agreed to buy solid oxide fuel cells for around $2.65 billion for a plant near Cheyenne. The purchase used most of an option for 900 extra megawatts under AEP's 2024 supply deal with Bloom. For a sense of scale, that one order is worth over half of Bloom's full-year revenue forecast of $4.4 billion to $4.6 billion for 2026. So, Google's news didn't add to Bloom's orders. The fuel cells were bought in January, and AEP had already named Google as the plant's customer in October. That still means something, I think. A fuel cell order backed by a 20-year power contract with Google looks more likely to become revenue on time than one linked to an unnamed buyer. NTT DATA is the new business NTT DATA's deal is the new business, and the companies called it Bloom's biggest international project so far. NTT's data center arm plans to use the fuel cells as its main power source, with the relationship meant to reach gigawatt scale across its global portfolio. What the release didn't say matters, too. It gave no dollar value, no project locations, and no timeline beyond first shipments starting in 2027. This deal shouldn't show up in Bloom's 2026 revenue, and Bloom hasn't said how much of it falls in 2027 or later. But 900 megawatts is a lot of fuel cells -- nearly a full year of output at the 1 gigawatt of annual production capacity Bloom's Fremont, California, plant had going into 2026. The company planned to double that capacity by year-end. Bloom needs deals like this, because its quarter-to-quarter growth slowed sharply in the third quarter. Second-quarter revenue of $1.07 billion was 42% above the first quarter's $751 million. Third-quarter revenue then climbed 16% sequentially to $1.24 billion, up 138% year over year. And October's raised outlook (management's third raise this year) implies a sequential gain of 9% to 25% in the fourth quarter. That's still strong growth. Keeping it up into 2027 and 2028, though, depends on deals like NTT DATA's moving from announcement to shipment. Is the price finally reasonable? Based on the midpoint of management's adjusted earnings forecast for 2026 ($3.10 to $3.40 a share), Bloom stock cost around 52 times earnings at its Nov. 5 close. The same forecast had it at around 67 times earnings at the $217.77 close on Oct. 22. On next year's expected earnings, shares now trade at around 31 times earnings. Still, 52 times earnings is a premium price. It assumes Bloom keeps growing quickly well past this year. But Bloom landed a big new deal on Nov. 5 as its shares got much cheaper. Of course, a slower U.S. data center build-out might delay some deliveries. And October's weak spot hasn't gone away. Bloom's operations burned $27 million in cash in the third quarter, mostly because it booked revenue faster than it could bill customers for it. Is Bloom stock worth buying after a 16% one-day drop? I'd consider buying some shares at this price, a few at a time. And I'd maybe add more when billing catches up with revenue. Should you buy stock in Bloom Energy right now? Before you buy stock in Bloom Energy, consider this: The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Bloom Energy wasn't one of them. The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years. Consider when Netflix made this list on December 17, 2004... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $341,966!* Or when Nvidia made this list on April 15, 2005... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $1,146,819!* Now, it's worth noting Stock Advisor's total average return is 852% — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 203% for the S&P 500. We have also spotted 3 other big wins worth knowing about at Morgan Stanley. For a broader view on where money is flowing in AI related build outs, it is worth looking closely at 53 AI infrastructure stocks. Morgan Stanley sits among the largest capital markets groups globally, arranging financing for corporations and institutions that need large, complex funding such as AI focused data center projects. Its role as an intermediary between borrowers and a broad base of investors gives it room to adjust how that exposure is shared across the financial system. We've flagged 1 risk for Morgan Stanley. See which could impact your investment. Why would Morgan Stanley dial back data center construction loans if AI financing is growing? Loan books can get concentrated fast when every AI data center needs billions of dollars and long build times. Morgan Stanley appears to be keeping credit risk in check by arranging financing, then shifting slices of that exposure to private credit funds and asset managers instead of holding everything on its own balance sheet. Does this change the Morgan Stanley Narrative around wealth scale and capital strength? This news lines up with the Narrative that emphasizes Morgan Stanley's capital position and its ability to use balance sheet flexibility to support long duration themes like AI financing and private markets. Recycling data center exposure into broader investor pools fits the idea that CET1 buffers and diversified fees, not concentrated loans, underpin the long term story. See how these catalysts shape Morgan Stanley's path to a $214 fair value. What is the single most important thing to watch next from Morgan Stanley on this theme? Watch how Morgan Stanley describes data center and AI related credit distribution on upcoming quarterly calls, especially any figures on how much of new project lending it keeps versus syndicates or transfers. A clearer split between originate to distribute and loans retained would show whether this risk sharing approach is becoming a consistent model.

artigo.texto: Seyed Madaeni is CEO and co-founder of Verse, an energy software company specializing in battery dispatch optimization for data centers. Even the best-funded project can’t operate without electricity, and the grid often can’t deliver hundreds of new megawatts as quickly as AI developers need them. Access to power has become a competitive advantage, and companies are searching for ways to get it faster. Today, developers see two obvious options. They can wait years for traditional grid upgrades, or they can build private power plants onsite. The first can move too slowly. The second brings fuel-supply, equipment, permitting and community challenges of its own. A third path to data center interconnection is taking shape. Across the country, utilities and grid operators are creating clearer ways for large loads that can reduce the risks they bring to the system. Depending on the market, a data center might guarantee a minimum payment, agree to reduce its grid demand when the system is strained, provide better operating data or contract for new generation and storage. These policies differ, but they share one idea: If a data center wants faster or more certain access to power, it should give the grid greater certainty in return. That is a better approach than advancing projects mainly because they promise jobs or investment. Projects that make their demand more predictable, controllable and financially secure should have a clearer path to service. Ohio is asking data centers to pay for what they reserve Utilities often need to invest in substations, transmission equipment and other infrastructure years before a data center reaches full operation. They are building against forecasts that can change, and their queues may include projects that never get built. Ohio is addressing this problem through financial commitments for large loads. After AEP Ohio proposed a data-center-specific tariff, Ohio regulators approved a settlement requiring large customers to pay for up to 85% of their subscribed capacity, even when they use less. The agreement also includes longer contract terms and additional collateral requirements. In exchange, the connection moratorium was lifted and developers received a defined framework for service. Another utility might choose a different percentage or structure. But a company asking the grid to reserve an extraordinary amount of power should be willing to stand behind that request financially. This protects existing customers from paying for infrastructure built around demand that does not materialize. It also helps serious projects distinguish themselves from speculative ones. Texas and SPP want more predictable operations Other markets are focused on how data centers behave once they connect. A large facility can draw hundreds of megawatts, change its consumption quickly or disconnect during a grid disturbance. At that scale, it’s part of how the power system operates, whether it considers itself a grid participant or not. Texas is responding with clearer technical and operating expectations. A facility that meets the Electric Reliability Council of Texas’ ride-through requirements clears one important gate on the path to energization, alongside required modeling, stability and interconnection reviews. Through controllable-load and bring-your-own-generation pathways in ERCOT's new Batch Zero process, developers can elect dispatchable curtailment under ERCOT’s real-time control in exchange for earlier energization. Meaning, a data center must be able to reduce what it takes from the grid when the system is strained. It could curtail consumption, switch to onsite resources or coordinate several assets. What matters is that the response is available when promised. Southwest Power Pool is making a similar trade through its High Impact Large Load framework. Developers that accept real-time forecast reporting, ramp-rate limits and remote-disconnect capability can have their interconnection study completed within 90 days, clearing the way for an agreement soon afterward. In both markets, developers give the grid better visibility and more control during constrained periods. In return, they receive a faster and more predictable process. PJM asked large loads to help cover the capacity they need PJM Interconnection is approaching the challenge through resource adequacy that prioritizes whether the region has enough capacity to meet demand when the system is under the most stress. Under PJM’s proposed Interim Resource Adequacy Service framework, certain new large loads could connect even when the region doesn’t have enough capacity to serve all forecast demand at its traditional reliability standard. Loads that didn't bring qualifying new capacity or receive an applicable capacity allocation could have been required to reduce their grid consumption during limited emergency conditions. FERC rejected most of the framework in October on jurisdictional grounds, but it encouraged states to decide which retail customers are curtailed when the system is stressed, which keeps the same trade on the table. A data center could reduce that exposure by bringing qualifying generation, storage or demand-side resources. Otherwise, it would accept service that is less firm than what existing customers receive. Bringing new capacity does not make transmission and distribution constraints disappear. A project may still need local upgrades, engineering studies and regulatory approvals. But if the system is short on capacity, a new load should either help fill the gap or be prepared to reduce its demand when the shortage becomes critical. Different rules, one underlying question. Each market is responding to its own constraints, but the question at the heart of these efforts is the same: What can a data center guarantee in exchange for access to power? artigo.texto: ARRAY Technologies, a provider of structural balance-of-system (SBOS) solutions for utility-scale solar, and Shoals Technologies Group, which supplies electrical balance-of-system (EBOS) equipment for utility-scale solar and battery energy storage, said the companies have agreed to combine in a stock-for-stock merger. The firms on Nov. 4 said the deal “creates an integrated energy infrastructure platform that brings together complementary, market-leading solutions across foundations, trackers, fixed-tilt racking, electrical infrastructure, wire management and power delivery systems.” The companies in a news release said ARRAY will serve as the corporate parent of the combined company. Shoals’ shareholders will receive a fixed exchange ratio of 1.6931 ARRAY shares for each Shoals’ share they own. After closing, Shoals’ shareholders are expected to own about 65% of the combined company’s basic shares outstanding, and ARRAY shareholders will own the rest. Officials said the combined company will serve solar and battery energy storage customers through a unified design package, with coordinated purchasing and integrated warranty support across SBOS and EBOS solutions. The groups said the merger supports delivery of “increasing levels of integration over time designed to reduce installation costs, streamline project execution and lower long-term maintenance requirements.” “Today marks an important milestone for Shoals, ARRAY and the customers we serve,” said Brandon Moss, CEO of Shoals. “By bringing together two highly complementary businesses with experienced teams, we are creating an integrated platform with broader capabilities, deeper customer relationships and a stronger foundation for long-term growth. We believe the combined company will be positioned to better service customers, deliver more innovative and integrated solutions, realize meaningful synergies and pursue expansion opportunities across the solar value chain, data center markets and beyond.” Kevin Hostetler, ARRAY’s CEO, said, “This transaction represents a compelling opportunity to create meaningful value for customers of both ARRAY and Shoals by bringing together our complementary strengths. Although structural and electrical systems must operate seamlessly together in the field, they have historically been designed and sourced through separate channels. This combination changes that. Together, we expect to deliver a differentiated, technically integrated and interoperable platform that simplifies project execution, enhances project economics and accelerates innovation for customers.” Strategic and Financial Rationale The companies said the merger will bring several benefits for customers, including more effective service through a unified design package, with coordinated purchasing and integrated warranty support across combined offerings. The combined company intends to offer customers enhanced flexibility and packaging choice across foundations, trackers, electrical infrastructure and wire management solutions, including the solar industry’s best performing ground screw, single-axis tracker, DC wiring solution and cable management hanger. The groups said customer value will be enhanced “by streamlining project execution, reducing installation costs, and lowering long-term maintenance requirements through increased product integration. SBOS and EBOS solutions are highly symbiotic across solar and battery storage projects. By bringing these complementary product categories together, the combined company expects to deliver more integrated solutions that reduce interface complexity, enhance energy yield and reliability, simplify installation and lower customers’ total cost of ownership.” Officials also highlighted both companies technical expertise in their respective markets, which should support innovation. The combined company also expects to realize savings in overhead and other expenses, and noted “Year-one cost synergies are expected to deliver approximately $20 million of incremental, run-rate Adjusted EBITDA [Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization].” The combined company expects to benefit from Shoals’ approximately $1.6 billion of tax amortization and $237 million of Net Operating Losses, which are anticipated to reduce taxable income and limit the cash tax obligations of the combined company for the next several years. Leadership Structure Moss will serve as CEO of the combined company. Hostetler will serve as special advisor. Brad Forth, current chairman of the board of both ARRAY and Shoals, will serve as board chairman after the merger. “Having had the privilege of serving as chairman of both ARRAY and Shoals, I have seen firsthand the complementary products, talented teams and shared commitment to customers offered by both companies,” said Forth. “Together, ARRAY and Shoals are well positioned to deliver enhanced value to customers, shareholders and employees. I also want to thank Kevin for his leadership and important contributions to ARRAY, as well as his valuable insights as he transitions to a Special Advisor role. I look forward to continuing to work with Brandon, who brings proven leadership, deep industry expertise and strategic vision to lead the combined company in this next phase of growth.” The combined company intends to announce a new corporate name and ticker symbol in the coming months to reflect the expanded scope of its products, services and strategic opportunities. —Darrell Proctor is a senior editor for POWER.

artigo.texto: Three separate threads on X this week converged on the same conclusion: Tesla's Cybercab is better positioned than its critics admit. Fresh ride-hailing data dismantles the most common knock on the two-seat design, a closer look at the vehicle's conversational AI reveals something closer to a co-pilot than a voice assistant, and an IRA credit breakdown suggests the battery economics are more aggressive than most analysts have modeled. 1. The two-seat design is backed by actual trip data — not assumptions The loudest skepticism around the Cybercab has always been its passenger capacity: two seats, no more. Critics argue that consumers buying four- and five-seat vehicles signals demand for that space. Sawyer Merritt pushed back hard on that framing this week, citing a Federal Highway Administration study showing that roughly 85% of private ride-hailing trips involve just one or two passengers — with 64.2% of trips carrying a single rider. The distinction matters. What people buy for personal ownership — where occasional family trips, cargo capacity, and optionality all factor in — is a poor proxy for what a robotaxi fleet actually needs to serve. A vehicle optimized for the 85% use case isn't a compromise; it's a deliberate product decision. According to background research, Tesla also targets an operating cost below $0.30 per mile for the Cybercab, a figure that only works at scale with a purpose-built, stripped-down platform. Carrying two seats instead of five is part of how that number gets achieved. 2. The conversational AI goes well beyond voice commands Whole Mars Catalog described the Cybercab's passenger interaction this way: you'll be able to talk to the car like a cab driver — ask it to do whatever you want, as long as it's legal and won't hurt anyone. That framing is more meaningful than it sounds. Most in-car voice systems today are command-and-response: say a specific phrase, get a specific action. What's being described here is a conversational agent — one that can handle open-ended requests, route changes mid-trip, music preferences, and presumably questions about the ride itself. According to background research, the Cybercab's on-board voice interface is powered by a specialized version of ChatGPT, functioning as a multimodal agent capable of anticipating road behavior and interacting vocally with passengers. The system is designed to react to unexpected situations and navigate complex intersections — meaning the AI isn't just listening to passengers, it's also processing the environment in real time. For riders accustomed to awkward, keyword-dependent car interfaces, this represents a meaningful step change in what a driverless ride actually feels like. 3. IRA battery credits could push the pack cost under $3,000 The third data point is the one with the most direct financial implication. Whole Mars Catalog flagged that with the IRA battery production credit factored in, the cost of a full Cybercab battery pack could come in under $3,000. Here's the math behind it. The Cybercab carries a 47.6 kWh usable battery pack built on 4680 cells. The IRA provides a production credit of $35 per kWh for battery cells and $10 per kWh for battery modules — up to $45 per kWh if both apply. On a 47.6 kWh pack, that's a potential credit of roughly $2,142. When stacked against Tesla's already-aggressive 4680 cell cost targets and a stated build cost goal of under $30,000 for the full vehicle, the battery pack becomes one of the cheapest line items on the bill of materials for a vehicle of this capability. A sub-$3,000 pack cost isn't just a talking point — it's the kind of structural cost advantage that makes a $0.30/mile operating target credible rather than aspirational. Taken together, these three threads sketch a Cybercab that is more defensible on design, more capable on software, and more competitive on economics than the skeptic narrative suggests. The real test remains deployment scale — but the underlying numbers are holding up. 🚕 Following the Robotaxi rollout? artigo.texto: Livermore, CA - November 6, 2026 - Your Energy Solutions, a family-owned Bay Area energy company serving the region since 2008, helps homeowners and businesses explore battery storage solutions designed around their energy needs, existing equipment, and property requirements. Changing Solar Credits Make Battery Storage More Valuable California's Net Billing Tariff, commonly known as NEM 3.0, took effect in April 2023 for customers of Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E), Southern California Edison (SCE), and San Diego Gas & Electric (SDG&E). Under this policy, excess electricity exported to the grid receives compensation based on lower, time-dependent export rates rather than the retail electricity rates available under the previous net metering structure. This change has made it more important for solar owners to consider when electricity is generated and when it is consumed. Solar panels typically produce the most electricity around midday, while household energy demand often increases during the evening. Without battery storage, surplus daytime electricity may be sent to the grid for comparatively low compensation, leaving homeowners to purchase electricity later when household demand rises. A battery system can store some of that excess solar energy for use after sunset. This allows homeowners to increase the amount of solar-generated electricity consumed on-site and reduce reliance on grid electricity during higher-demand periods. Industry reporting has also highlighted a significant increase in battery adoption among California solar installations following the introduction of the new billing structure. Backup Power Remains an Important Consideration Solar economics are not the only reason homeowners are considering battery storage. Power outages associated with wildfire-prevention measures and other grid events remain a planning consideration across parts of California. Pacific Gas and Electric has conducted Public Safety Power Shutoffs in areas near Livermore and Altamont Pass to reduce wildfire risks. Although recent shutoffs have affected smaller areas than some past events, these situations demonstrate why household energy preparedness remains relevant for Bay Area residents. A properly designed battery system can provide backup electricity during an outage, depending on battery capacity, electrical configuration, and household energy consumption. The amount of power available and the appliances supported depend on the system selected and the home's specific electrical requirements. Battery Storage Solutions from Your Energy Solutions Your Energy Solutions provides battery storage design, installation, and service for residential and commercial properties. Battery systems can be incorporated into new solar installations, added to existing solar systems, or integrated with solar equipment originally installed by another contractor. Residential battery options include Tesla Powerwall, SolarEdge, Enphase, and FranklinWH. Commercial customers can explore solutions from SolarEdge, Enphase, and Fortress Power. For homeowners interested in whole-home backup, the company evaluates the property's electrical requirements and available equipment to determine whether a single battery or a different configuration can support the desired loads. Existing solar owners also receive compatibility reviews, including guidance about potential system changes that could affect their current Net Energy Metering status. Financing options are available to help qualified customers explore battery storage investments. A Family-Owned Bay Area Company with In-House Expertise Since 2008, Your Energy Solutions has served communities throughout the Bay Area with an emphasis on personalized project support. The company manages design, installation, and service entirely in-house, without relying on subcontractors. Each project receives a dedicated point of contact, and the team avoids high-pressure sales practices. Additional support includes assistance with manufacturer warranty claims and a 10-year workmanship warranty on battery installations. Quadrilhas organizadas estão interceptando caminhões para roubar cargas valiosas de componentes para data centers, como servidores, cabos de cobre e chips de memória. Com ataques altamente planejados antes dos veículos deixarem os depósitos, os prejuízos com os roubos já somam US$ 110,6 milhões desde junho, registrando perdas que variam entre US$ 2 milhões e US$ 38 milhões por ocorrência. A corrida do ouro da inteligência artificial está recriando uma espécie de "Velho Oeste do século XXI", reunindo todos os elementos de um faroeste clássico. De um lado, estão as minas de ouro — os data centers — e investidores com bolsos cheios, dispostos a comprar as pás e todo o material necessário para extrair o metal precioso, que agora assume a forma de dados. Faltavam apenas os saqueadores de estradas para completar o cenário, mas eles acabaram de chegar. Desta vez, a diligência é um caminhão semirreboque carregado de peças para equipar data centers. Conforme revelou a emissora norte-americana NBC News, a nova carga cobiçada reúne servidores, cabos de cobre para instalações e chips de memória. E as quadrilhas não improvisam: escolhem a carga de maneira calculada muito antes de o veículo deixar o depósito e o interceptam antes que chegue ao destino final. Prejuízos passam de US$ 100 milhões desde junho Estima-se que, desde 3 de junho, os roubos registrados de cargas de tecnologia somaram **US$ 110,6 milhões**. artigo.texto: Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has defended the anti-data center movement. He argues that slower compute growth would buy time to harden the world against AI-driven cyber and bio risks. The timing matters for markets. AI chip stocks and Bitcoin miners that now rent power to AI labs depend on a fast data center buildout. Why Buterin Isn't Worried About the Anti-Data Center Movement Buterin said in an X post on Nov. 8 that he disagrees with the strong emotional reaction to anti-data center groups. His case rests on algorithmic progress. By his estimate, whatever bigger data centers could do in two years, today's will manage in four, or sooner. Even extreme success for the anti-data center movement would therefore cause nothing close to a disaster, the Ethereum co-founder argued. Cybersecurity problems are already visible, he noted, and bio risks may follow soon. The world needs every bit of time to prepare. He added that science faces many bottlenecks besides AI. As a result, delaying AI by one year would slow research by far less. Buterin stressed that his view needs no doomer claims about recursive self-improvement (RSI), where AI systems upgrade themselves. The post fits his recent warnings. At Devcon 8, he said AI could crack crypto by finding shortcuts through its cryptography. Who Pays if the AI Buildout Slows? The anti-data center movement has spread from protests to policy. Sen. Bernie Sanders has called for a national data center moratorium after Democrats won Congress. In Europe, several hundred activists occupied a Microsoft construction site in Amsterdam on Nov. 6, Al Jazeera reported. Police detained 150 to 200 people. However, not everyone agrees with Buterin. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink has warned that halting data center construction would push the US into recession. Bitcoin miners carry their own exposure. Riot Platforms sold most of its Bitcoin to fund Texas AI data centers. The state's governor-elect has pledged a permit freeze. Still, Buterin said that even if the anti-data center movement's success proved net-bad, it would be no worse than many other political fights. For AI-linked assets, the debate is shifting from whether the buildout continues to how fast. artigo.texto: All eyes were on Texas during the midterms, and artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, especially the neoclouds, took a beating when a Democrat governor won the state. The main fear is that increased AI regulations will make it harder to build data centers in the future, and existing projects may get delayed. It's a legitimate concern, and Texas isn't the only state that was affected. Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona also saw Democratic victories, and they have been instrumental states for the AI boom. Bears will argue that Democratic victories can turn into a major bottleneck for AI as construction projects are delayed or canceled. Here's what investors should consider. Governors still answer to the House and Senate While governor victories capture headlines, each governor must still answer to their state's House and Senate. Those two political arms introduce more variety that can result in gridlock instead of sweeping AI regulations. Here's how it varies for the four states that have played a vital role in artificial intelligence: - Texas: Republicans lost the House but have the Senate. - Ohio: Republicans maintained the House and the Senate. - Georgia: Republicans lost the House but have the Senate. - Arizona: Democrats won the House and the Senate. Ohio has the best political profile for tech companies. A gridlock essentially lets existing data center projects continue. Texas and Georgia can still create a gridlock due to Republicans controlling the Senate, but their political leverage isn't as good as Ohio's. Data centers in Arizona won't face the same political gridlock since Democrats have secured the House and the Senate. Arizona Democrats are in the best position to act swiftly. Job cuts are a real risk Although activism and protests toward data centers have gotten louder in recent months, delaying and canceling these projects comes with downsides that extend beyond lost innovation. While an anti-big tech stance may cause people to look the other way when hyperscalers face roadblocks, those same data center delays and cancellations have a real impact on jobs. Politicians on both sides of the aisle love to tout job growth. For instance, former President Biden was enthusiastic about a $3.3 billion data center in Wisconsin since it could create 2,000 permanent jobs once built. If many data centers are delayed or canceled, it can lead to thousands of people losing their jobs. While regulation may become stricter, kneecapping the industry also translates into lost jobs. Democrats may not care as much about GDP during this cycle since Trump is still the president, but slowing down AI infrastructure can result in negative GDP growth, since it's the main catalyst powering the economy. A negative GDP growth reading won't be a good look. The Democrats can introduce measures that make their voters happy without uprooting the entire AI trade. Local engagement will become more valuable Good PR will be incredibly valuable for neoclouds as the Democrats gain more control of the government in January. Investors can expect to see companies take more steps to financially support local communities beyond new jobs. These initiatives can help them win over residents and provide tangible benefits to the entire community. Part of that may mean reduced tax breaks, a point of contention that was gaining steam before the midterm results. Some tech companies are also acquiring old infrastructure and converting it into AI data centers. For instance, Terawulf is turning a retired coal plant into an AI data center. Those types of changes are less disruptive and let AI data center developers focus on job creation. If more neoclouds and colocation developers take this approach, it will be harder for Democrats to issue sweeping changes that stall out the industry. Investors should pay attention to how data center developers are enhancing local communities, because winning over locals will reduce uncertainty with their gigawatt pipelines.

artigo.texto: Building AI Kill Switches in Data Centers Data center-level AI “kill switches” are more feasible than agent-level ones, but they need early detection and global regulatory alignment to work. As businesses – and societies more broadly – grapple with the risks posed by advanced AI systems, one proposed safeguard is an AI “kill switch”: a mechanism designed to shut down an out-of-control model or agent before it can cause serious harm. More than a few observers (including me) have noted that implementing a kill switch of this type is a lot harder than many proponents assume. One major reason is that most AI systems run on distributed infrastructure. You cannot simply turn off one server or issue a process-level command to stop a large-scale AI deployment that spans clusters, facilities, or regions. That said, there may be a realistic approach: building AI kill switches at the data center level. While such a strategy would not solve every problem, it could offer a practical way to isolate certain AI workloads quickly in an emergency. What a Data Center-Level Kill Switch Would Actually Do A kill switch implemented at the data center level would allow operators to shut down or isolate AI workloads on a facility-by-facility basis. If an AI model or agent began to behave unpredictably, operate outside its intended scope, or otherwise pose a threat, the facility hosting it could be taken offline or disconnected to contain the risk. This type of kill switch would not provide fine-grained control over individual AI agents or models inside a data center. It would also not necessarily stop every process immediately. But it could offer a relatively fast and effective way to contain a rogue system by cutting it off from power, connectivity, or both. Where Data Center Kill Switches Fall Short Before considering how to build an AI kill switch into a data center, it is important to note the approach’s limitations. One challenge is scale. Some AI models are distributed across multiple data centers, so shutting down a single facility would not stop the entire system. In those cases, a kill switch would only be effective if every facility supporting the workload could also be disabled or isolated. Even then, partial shutdowns could still matter because they would reduce the compute and storage resources available to the model. Another concern is propagation. A sufficiently sophisticated rogue AI system might attempt to replicate itself beyond its original environment by deploying copies of models, agents, or data to external infrastructure. A data center-level kill switch would do little to address that problem once replication had already occurred. For that reason, early detection would be essential. The sooner operators can identify signs of anomalous or unauthorized AI behavior, the more useful any kill switch mechanism becomes. Two Ways to Isolate a Rogue AI Workload There are two basic ways to shut down or isolate a rogue AI workload at the data center level: cutting power or cutting connectivity. Both approaches are difficult because data centers are engineered to resist exactly these kinds of failures. Option #1: A Power-Based Kill Switch The first option is to shut off the power supply to the facility. In theory, this is the most direct way to turn off AI infrastructure. In practice, it is not so simple. Most data centers are designed with redundant power systems, including UPS units and backup generators. If the primary utility power is interrupted, workloads are supposed to stay online. That resilience is a feature, not a bug, but it complicates any attempt to create a deliberate shutdown mechanism. Backup systems are not designed to distinguish between a routine grid outage and an intentional “kill switch” event, so cutting the main power alone is unlikely to stop servers from operating. There is also the issue of hardware risk. Abrupt power loss can create operational and equipment problems, especially in environments filled with expensive GPU-based servers. For that reason, most data center operators would be reluctant to support any mechanism that could damage infrastructure during an emergency shutdown. Option #2: A Network-Based Kill Switch The other option is to sever the data center’s network connectivity. This would not necessarily stop AI workloads from continuing to run inside the facility, but it could prevent them from communicating externally, accessing remote resources, or interacting with users and other systems. Here too, however, resilience makes implementation difficult. Most modern facilities have multiple upstream carriers, redundant network paths, and diverse interconnection points. To isolate a rogue AI workload at the facility level, operators would need a way to turn off all relevant external connectivity paths, not just one. Could Regulation Make AI Kill Switches Mandatory? Data center operators are unlikely to make it easy to power off or disconnect their own facilities on demand. Their business model depends on uptime, resilience, and fault tolerance, so voluntary adoption of AI kill switches does not seem especially likely in the near term. A regulatory path is easier to imagine. Governments could require facilities that host certain classes of AI workloads to maintain a standardized mechanism for isolating those workloads in an emergency, most likely through network disconnection rather than power interruption. Such a requirement would still be difficult to implement, but it is more feasible than expecting operators to redesign facilities around rapid shutdown capabilities on their own. The effectiveness of that model would depend heavily on consistency across jurisdictions. If only a handful of regions required kill switches, AI companies could simply place high-risk workloads in facilities elsewhere. But if regulators adopted broadly aligned rules, data center-level kill switches could become a practical part of the AI safety conversation.

artigo.texto: The dust from the midterms had hardly settled Wednesday when OpenAI leaders began reckoning with an urgent question: would the outcome make it harder to secure the vast amounts of computing power the company needs to keep growing? During a Q&A with employees, OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman fielded questions about data centers and public sentiment on AI, according to people familiar with the matter. A day earlier, a wave of data-center opposition had helped candidates promising to freeze development win statehouses in Texas, Georgia, Ohio and Michigan—all major states for data-center sites. Altman acknowledged that the public is concerned about water use and said that whatever the reason, he understood why people might not want to live near data centers, the people said. At one point, he mused that the company should perhaps look to build data centers in the desert. Meanwhile, senior leaders were busy discussing whether the company would need to reset expectations for its data-center capacity next year, The Wall Street Journal previously reported. And employees involved in OpenAI’s data-center development were exchanging intelligence on newly elected Democratic politicians in key states and discussing how best to engage with them, according to messages viewed by the Journal. Across Silicon Valley, similar scenes played out as tech companies that have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to the artificial-intelligence race, and carefully cultivated relationships with AI-friendly officials at all levels of government, rushed to plan for a changed reality. Overnight, they found themselves facing the prospect of blanket moratoriums, tighter environmental regulations and longer review timelines, along with potential new AI-safety regulations that could further bog them down. The tech investor Brad Gerstner said on the “All-In” podcast that as much as 35% of the U.S. data-center construction planned for next year is now at risk. Executives in charge of government relations for so-called hyperscaler companies moved quickly to open lines of communication with incoming governors and their transition teams, seeking an understanding of how their campaign-trail rhetoric would translate into policy actions. Dina Powell McCormick, who as president of Meta Platforms oversees its AI-infrastructure operations, said at the WSJ Tech conference Wednesday night that the company had already found one incoming governor prepared to parley. “We did have a governor that won last night who did make data centers a big part of their platform say, ‘As soon as we get past the inauguration, let’s meet, because we don’t want to lose this investment in our town. We don’t want these jobs to go elsewhere,’ ” she said. But on the whole, Powell McCormick said, Meta assumes that building data centers in the U.S. is “going to be harder” and getting new ones done from scratch will be “very challenging.” She said Meta and other tech companies are increasingly considering building new data centers outside the U.S. as one way around the new hurdles. Another avenue, she said, is to scale up existing data centers, where surrounding communities that have seen benefits in the form of job creation and tax revenue don’t require as much persuasion. To have any hope of winning over the public, Powell McCormick said, the AI industry will have to get much better at talking about its product and the potential societal benefits. “I think we have to double and triple down on telling the story,” she said. OpenAI President Greg Brockman , also speaking at the conference, echoed that point, saying, “We need to do a better job of really communicating to local communities about why data centers are something that can be beneficial to them.” On Thursday, OpenAI became the latest AI giant to unveil a broad commitment governing how it approaches building new data centers. The company said it would not require public officials to sign nondisclosure agreements to engage in data-center negotiations and that it would solicit community input and provide clear public information about the energy, water and noise impacts of its infrastructure investments. Anthropic, in an S-1 filing last week for a planned initial public offering, previewed for investors the risk that local and state governments might adopt data-center moratoriums. “Such moratoriums, or similar actions, could delay or prevent the construction or expansion of facilities on which we depend for compute,” the filing said. Anthropic said it was pursuing projects in several “non-U.S. jurisdictions” as part of a plan to “reduce concentration risks associated with operating a significant portion of our compute infrastructure in the United States.” The S-1 detailed approximately $895.4 billion of AI computing and infrastructure commitments through 2045. The company has separately announced plans to build data centers in Texas and New York, with sites coming online this year. artigo.texto: North Dakota Town Bucks Backlash, Welcomes Data Center In a year when voters across the country largely tried to slam the brakes on new data centers, one tiny North Dakota town hit the gas, the Washington Post reports. Residents of Harwood, population 845, rejected a ballot measure that would have forced independent reviews and public hearings for big industrial projects, effectively clearing the way for a $3 billion, 1.8-million-square-foot data center on the edge of town. The measure failed by roughly 3-to-1, Fortune reports, even as national exit polls showed 76% of voters opposed to new data centers in their communities and most skeptical of AI's impact. Harwood's mayor argued the project was inevitable—if not in Harwood, it would likely still have ended up nearby—that the town should be the one to capture its projected $1.65 million in annual property taxes and 200 or so new jobs. Opponents warned of environmental risks, noise, and future cleanup costs—but were decisively outvoted. Per CNBC and Business Insider, the Harwood ballot measure appears to have been the only one across the nation that went favorably for data centers. - Hegseth's defensive video draws Hatch Act criticism. - GOP senator says there's corruption in administration. - The most dangerous footwear are ... slippers? - South Africa is in for coalition rule after ANC's worst setback.

artigo.texto: A new database of local government meeting records puts a hard number on something planners have heard in hearing rooms all year. Prophecy Gov, a San Francisco AI startup, operates a tool called American Sentiment, and it classified 90.5% of 10,202 public comments about data centers as negative, according to TechRadar’s coverage of the report. The comments came from 906 public meetings held by 417 local governments across 48 states during 2026. Headline writers boiled that down to “America hates data centers.” That phrase is headline wording, not an on-record statement from a named person, and the data does not say 90.5% of Americans oppose data centers. It says that when residents speak at the microphone, they mostly speak against. The finding arrives in a year when siting fights have moved from zoning footnotes to front-page politics. Our earlier look at the 41 data center ballot measures that put the AI boom on notice covered the voting side. This story covers the hearing-room side, and for anyone who buys or builds cloud capacity, it matters just as much. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What American Sentiment Actually Measured American Sentiment is a database, not a survey. Prophecy Gov collected public comments made at local government meetings, then classified each one by tone. The comments were not solicited, weighted, or balanced against a population sample. Residents chose to speak, and the tool recorded what they said. That design has real strengths. Public comment is where land-use decisions get shaped, and local boards often cite what they hear from residents when they vote on rezoning, tax abatements, or utility agreements. A dataset of 10,202 comments across 48 states gives researchers something they rarely had before: a searchable record of the arguments people actually make in the room. The classification split is stark. Beyond the 90.5% negative share, 7% of comments expressed support for a potential nearby data center, and 2.5% asked questions. Those three buckets account for the whole dataset. In other words, almost nobody in these meetings arrived undecided and left with a neutral note on the record. TechRadar framed the result with the “America hates data centers” headline, and other outlets echoed the sentiment. The underlying dataset is more careful than the headline. It measures comment tone at 2026 meetings, nothing more. Keep that boundary in mind through the rest of this analysis, because the gap between “comments” and “public opinion” is where most of the debate will happen. The Numbers at a Glance The table below collects every figure reported so far from the American Sentiment database. No price data, technical specifications, or named speaker quotes have surfaced in the coverage, so this is the full quantitative picture as of November 09, 2026. Two details deserve a second look. First, the 73% figure describes meetings, not comments, so it measures how often a hearing featured zero supporters. Second, water is named as the top concern, but the reports available so far do not give a percentage for it. Anyone citing a specific water share is guessing. Why 90.5% Is Not a National Poll The most important caveat is also the simplest. The dataset measures the comments collected, and those comments are not a representative national opinion poll. A poll draws a sample that mirrors the population. A public comment period draws whoever shows up, and showing up takes time, motivation, and often a personal stake. Who shows up at the microphone People who live next to a proposed site have the strongest reason to attend. They worry about noise, traffic, property values, and power lines. People who might benefit from a data center, such as future employees, local suppliers, or residents who like lower property tax rates, have a diffuse stake and little reason to give up an evening. That asymmetry is old, and planners know it well. The self-selection problem cuts both ways Self-selection inflates opposition in the raw numbers, but it does not make the opposition fake. Local boards act on what they hear. If 9 in 10 speakers oppose a project, elected officials feel that pressure whether or not a silent majority would have voted differently. For developers, the comment record matters as a political force even if it fails as a statistical sample. The sensible reading: American Sentiment tells us what local decision-makers are hearing, not what the country thinks. Those are different questions, and only the first one drives permit votes. The 7% Support Gap and the 73% of Empty Support Benches Seven percent of comments backed a nearby data center. That sounds small, and in raw terms it is. Using the reported shares, it works out to roughly 714 supportive comments out of 10,202. The more telling number is the meeting-level one: 73% of tracked meetings had no supporters at all. Run the arithmetic and the picture sharpens. About 661 of the 906 meetings featured no one speaking in favor, which leaves roughly 245 meetings with at least one supportive voice. In those 245 hearings, supporters were still outnumbered overall, since the 90.5% negative share holds across the whole dataset. total_comments = 10202 meetings = 906 negative = total_comments * 0.905 # ~9,233 support = total_comments * 0.07 # ~714 questions = total_comments * 0.025 # ~255 mention_ai = total_comments * 0.21 # ~2,142 no_support_meetings = meetings * 0.73 # ~661 with_support = meetings - no_support_meetings # ~245 comments_per_meeting = total_comments / meetings # ~11.3 These counts are our own rounding of the reported percentages, so treat them as approximations rather than figures published by Prophecy Gov. They still show the scale: a few hundred supportive comments set against more than nine thousand negative ones. The practical lesson for the industry is blunt.
