artigo.texto: The European Union and the United Kingdom are preparing to reconnect their carbon markets, a move that could spare manufacturers on both sides of the Channel from additional carbon border charges, according to a draft document seen by Euronews. The two sides are expected to announce the conclusion of negotiations to link their respective Emissions Trading Systems (ETS), allowing EU and British carbon allowances to be mutually recognised. The agreement, set to be announced at the EU-UK summit in Brussels on 20 November, would also pave the way for goods originating in the EU and UK to be exempted from their respective Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms (CBAM). "We welcome the conclusion of the negotiations on linking the EU’s and the UK's ETS agreement. This would allow mutual recognition of EU and UK allowances and exempt EU and UK goods from respective CBAM subject to respective laws and procedures that we plan to launch without delays," reads the draft document, which could still change until its publication. The move would address a growing trade concern following the introduction of the EU's carbon border mechanism in January 2026 and Britain's plans to introduce its own system in January 2027. Without a formal link between the two carbon markets, manufacturers could face additional carbon costs when exporting goods across the Channel, despite already operating under domestic emissions pricing systems. Protecting industrial competitiveness? Some EU and UK officials have argued that energy-intensive industries such as steel, aluminum, cement and fertilisers could avoid additional charges, which could help protect competitiveness and reduce the administrative burden of trading between the two markets. But the proposed linkage has its critics. British MP David Tufnell said the country's industry is at a "critical juncture," blaming high carbon costs for the industrial decline. "Pursuing UK-EU ETS linkage threatens to push UK carbon prices up even further towards EU levels," Tufnell told Euronews. Carbon markets are designed to encourage industries to invest in decarbonisation by putting a price on emissions. But the global energy crisis and high inflation have intensified concerns about the costs of the green transition for businesses and households. Tufnell also argued that the UK gives its industries fewer free carbon allowances than the EU, potentially leaving British manufacturers facing higher emissions costs than their European competitors. Related "This matters greatly for industrial communities like mine in Pembrokeshire and for British industrial competitiveness and national resilience more broadly. If carbon costs rise faster in the UK than in competing jurisdiction then production, investment and employment move overseas while global emissions remain unchanged,” Tufnell said. The deal would represent a significant step in the post-Brexit rapprochement between London and Brussels, demonstrating how both sides are seeking to reduce economic barriers without reversing Britain's departure from the EU. Analysts say that linking the systems would create a larger carbon market, potentially improving the availability of allowances and making it easier for companies to trade emissions permits. But closer integration would also bring regulatory obligations, a politically sensitive issue in Britain, where Brexit was partly driven by the desire to escape EU rules. The two carbon markets have different rules and sectoral coverage, including differences over the treatment of transport and buildings. Carbon pricing for road transport and buildings Moreover, the second EU ETS iteration, which will mandate oil and gas operators to pay for the emissions linked to heating in buildings and road transport fuels, is due to kick in in 2029. The new carbon tax will likely pass on to consumers' bills, which has led to greater social scrutiny of the ETS2. If the EU and the UK link their carbon markets, Britain would be required to keep its carbon pricing sufficiently aligned with EU requirements. EU officials are keen to extend the reach of its carbon-pricing system beyond the bloc's borders, while protecting the integrity of its market against carbon leakage. The UK sees it as an opportunity to reduce trade costs and preserve access to the European market without formally rejoining the EU's regulatory structures. According to the October Messina Group Megapoll, 49% of Britons backed rejoining the EU, with 28.5% against.

artigo.texto: TREX Energy Commissions Lithium Battery Manufacturing Facility in Hyderabad The line is designed to manufacture battery packs for 261 kWh and 5 MWh energy storage systems November 6, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights Hyderabad-based energy storage solutions company TREX Energy has commissioned a lithium battery manufacturing facility at E-City in Hyderabad, Telangana. The company also plans to expand its manufacturing operations with a second facility in Madhya Pradesh. The state government has allotted four acres of land to TREX Energy for the proposed second phase of its manufacturing expansion. The commissioned facility features an automated module assembly line with a production rate of 12 parts per minute. The line is designed to manufacture 52S battery packs for 261 kWh and 5 MWh battery energy storage systems (BESS). TREX Energy’s energy storage portfolio ranges from 5 kWh to 5 MWh, catering to residential, commercial and industrial, and utility-scale applications. The company said the automated assembly line would support manufacturing efficiency, production consistency, and quality control. TREX offers battery storage systems for factories, offices, and commercial facilities to manage electricity consumption, provide backup power, and improve operational resilience. Its utility-scale battery storage solutions cater to grid applications and renewable energy projects. The company also manufactures residential energy storage systems and home inverter batteries. Bharat S. Chhittarka, Director of TREX Energy, said the company was focusing on reducing financing costs to make BESS more affordable for the Indian market. According to Mercom India’s Energy Storage Manufacturing Ecosystem Report, the country’s operational battery energy storage manufacturing capacity is heavily concentrated in downstream manufacturing, which accounts for 92% of the total, while cell manufacturing represents just 8%. India’s downstream battery storage manufacturing capacity, including battery packs, containers, and integrated energy storage systems, stands at approximately 86 GWh. The downstream buildout reflects the strong pipeline for BESS in India. The country’s energy storage pipeline has crossed 110 GWh across the under-development and pre-construction stages, according to data from the Mercom India Renewable Energy Project Tracker. The pipeline includes BESS and pumped storage projects.

artigo.texto: Can Optical AI Cut Data Center Inference Power Use? Lumai is testing optical AI servers in a UK lab to see whether shifting inference prefill off GPUs can ease data center power constraints. Power is always a limiting factor for data centers, and AI inference is increasing that strain more than ever. Lumai, an optical compute company spun out of the University of Oxford in 2021, says it can ease that pressure by using light rather than transistors to perform the core math of inference. The company is now putting that claim to a real-world test. Lumai is deploying its Iris Nova servers in the Scaling Inference Lab, a UK facility that evaluates new AI hardware on real workloads in a live commercial setting. Iris Nova is Lumai’s first server, an optical AI accelerator built for data center inference, and it will be the first optical inference platform deployed in the lab. The UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA), a government-backed R&D funding agency, supports the lab, while CommonAI CIC, a non-profit focused on collaborative AI development, operates it. Researchers will use the deployment to evaluate how optical compute performs in a commercial data center environment. The problem the hardware is designed to address is power. “Power is the biggest challenge,” Phillip Burr, director of product at Lumai, told Data Center Knowledge. “Data centers have a fixed power budget, and inference demand is growing faster than the available power.” How Optical Inference Could Ease Data Center Power Constraints Matrix multiplication, the process of multiplying large grids of numbers together, sits at the center of AI inference. According to Burr, that is an area where optical compute can operate very efficiently. To understand why optical hardware may have an advantage, it helps to look at how GPUs and optical systems perform that arithmetic differently. “GPUs are silicon chips that use transistors to perform the matrix multiplications at the heart of AI inference,” Burr explained. “Optical compute uses the properties of light to perform the same matrix multiplications, completing millions of operations in a single optical cycle.” Lumai said Iris encodes numbers as light intensity and uses passive optical components, such as lenses, to perform the math. The company said the computation itself uses negligible amounts of energy, with power use rising only minimally as performance scales. That does not mean the system abandons traditional electronic components altogether. Burr said Lumai’s architecture is hybrid: optics handle matrix multiplication, while memory, control, and nonlinear functions are performed electronically. There are two main phases of inference, and optical compute targets one of them. Burr said the prefill phase is where the prompt and context are processed. The second phase, decode, is where the output tokens are generated. “Prefill is compute-bound; each model weight is reused across every token in the prompt, so arithmetic dominates,” Burr said. “This is where optical compute boosts performance.” In practical terms, compute-bound means the speed of the arithmetic determines overall performance. A token is a small unit of text, such as a word or part of a word. Decode works differently because tokens are generated one at a time. Burr said decode is limited by memory bandwidth, so faster arithmetic does not provide the same benefit. He added that model training is also not a strong fit for optical compute today, as it requires higher precision and continuous weight updates. “GPUs remain a good fit for training and decode,” Burr said. The Lumai Iris Nova server is designed to handle the prefill phase and leave decode to other hardware. “Iris is designed for the prefill stage, while GPUs or other decode-optimized hardware are used for decode,” Burr said. “Moving prefill off GPUs also frees that GPU capacity for decode.” How Iris Nova Fits into Existing Data Center Infrastructure For operators that split inference by running prefill on Iris Nova and decode on GPUs, software is needed to route those tasks to separate hardware. That approach is known as disaggregated serving, and Burr said Iris Nova is designed to work with the frameworks that support it. “For integration, Iris works with standard software frameworks such as PyTorch, standard networking interfaces, and disaggregated inference serving frameworks such as vLLM and SGLang,” Burr said. Whether that split pays off depends on the work a data center is handling. “The deciding factor for an operator is how much of their compute goes to prefill,” Burr said. “Prefill dominates with long prompts and agentic workloads, where models repeatedly process large contexts. This is where optical compute delivers the most.” Another practical consideration is facility requirements, and Burr said the hardware is built from familiar components. “Lumai Iris servers are built from components already manufactured at high volume for data center communications, rather than novel materials or bespoke fabrication,” Burr said. The cooling requirements are similarly conventional. The Scaling Inference Lab, where Iris Nova is being deployed, tests hardware in a live commercial setting with standard power, cooling, and rack integration, giving Lumai a trial under typical data center conditions. “Iris Nova operates in standard air-cooled racks and does not need liquid cooling,” Burr said. Lumai said the goal of the ARIA-backed deployment is to validate the system further and generate data to help shape its next product for production deployment. “The ARIA deployment will put a cluster of Iris Nova servers into an independently run lab, ARIA’s Scaling Inference Lab,” Burr said. “It will show that optical compute can run real AI workloads outside a research setting, and it will provide system-level data on performance.”

artigo.texto: A Crusoe, desenvolvedora de data centers com sede em Denver e avaliada em US$ 30,9 bilhões, confirmou nesta sexta-feira a venda de um projeto inacabado no sudeste do Wyoming para o Google. O Google prevê investir US$ 17 bilhões para concluir o campus, mas não revelou quanto desembolsou pelo ativo. Por que o Google tomou as rédeas do projeto O Google já havia tentado fechar com a Crusoe um contrato como cliente desse mesmo empreendimento, sem sucesso. Agora assume o desenvolvimento depois de, segundo informações divulgadas, demonstrar preocupação com o custo e o cronograma de obra sob a gestão da companhia de Denver. O projeto foi anunciado no ano passado em parceria com a Tallgrass, empresa de infraestrutura apoiada pela Blackstone, com a meta de chegar a 10 gigawatts de potência, unidade que equivale a um bilhão de watts. Os números da operação A venda havia sido antecipada por outro veículo de imprensa em junho. Mesmo assim, o revés no estado não impediu a Crusoe de levantar US$ 3,9 bilhões em setembro. Como a Crusoe ganha dinheiro e quem são seus clientes A receita vem de três frentes: alugar espaço a clientes que levam os próprios chips de IA, alugar as GPUs (unidades de processamento gráfico) da própria empresa e vender capacidade computacional para rodar modelos de IA. Essa última atividade é chamada de inferência, isto é, o uso de um modelo já treinado para responder às consultas dos usuários. Os projetos mais robustos atendem nomes de peso do setor. Em Abilene, no Texas, o campus avança por fases para a Oracle e para a OpenAI, enquanto um complexo separado de 900 megawatts, vizinho ao primeiro, será usado pela Microsoft. A Meta também figura entre os clientes. A companhia nasceu das mãos de Chase Lochmiller, atual CEO, e Cully Cavness, como um negócio de mineração de criptomoedas movido a gás natural que, de outra forma, seria queimado. Em setembro, com a rodada de captação, entraram três conselheiros, entre eles JB Straubel, fundador da Redwood Materials e membro do conselho da Tesla, que já havia investido na Crusoe em 2021. A empresa também foi a primeira cliente do negócio de armazenamento de energia de Straubel. Leitura para o investidor O episódio do Wyoming expõe o principal gargalo da infraestrutura de IA em grande escala: equipamentos, acesso a energia e oposição de comunidades locais podem atrasar obras e encarecer orçamentos. Para desenvolvedores independentes, que dependem de capital externo e de contratos com clientes, um projeto de gigawatts que sai do controle se transforma em risco de difícil absorção. Há duas leituras possíveis. De um lado, a Crusoe segue com avaliação elevada e conseguiu captar recursos após o revés, o que sinaliza apetite do mercado pela carteira da empresa. De outro, a perda do ativo e a não conquista do Google como cliente naquele projeto indicam que a execução pesa tanto quanto a tese de crescimento. A relação, contudo, não foi encerrada: a Crusoe segue desenvolvendo para o Google outro data center, perto de Amarillo, no Texas. O caso reforça que o retorno de campus de IA depende de cronograma, custo e energia, variáveis que nem sempre aparecem nos anúncios de capacidade. Entre os pontos a acompanhar estão o valor da transação, ainda não divulgado, e o andamento das obras nos demais campi.

artigo.texto: On Wednesday afternoon, Jamie Robins strolled up to the entrance of Google’s UK headquarters in Kings Cross, London. He brandished a letter containing details of a petition signed by almost 55,000 people, calling for Google to abandon plans to build a large new data center in Thurrock, 15 miles to the east of London. Robins works for wildlife conservation trust Buglife, part of an unlikely alliance of special-interest groups trying to block the Thurrock development. Buglife and local wildlife groups fear for an endangered plant, rare bumblebee, and other invertebrates whose habitat they say will be destroyed. Nonprofit Foxglove says the data center will emit too much pollution. The Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club wants to return to racing on the site. Members of the various groups joined Robins outside Google’s office last Wednesday, holding placards demanding the company “search elsewhere” for somewhere to put its facility. Across the UK, companies like Google are preparing to build industrial-scale data centers, part of a scramble to meet the swelling demand for the compute needed to run artificial intelligence models and other digital services. The UK government is eager to encourage them, hoping to capture a share of the hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into the AI industry and minimize the country’s dependence on foreign partners for compute. But like in the US, people living near to the proposed developments are making their objections known and trying to gum up the works. Google says its plans for the Thurrock site prioritize biodiversity and the reduction of emissions. “We share the concerns that Buglife and others have—and their expectation that this site should be developed sustainably,” Adam Elman, director of sustainability EMEA at Google, tells WIRED. But the situation in Thurrock underscores the level and breadth of resistance that data center developers face as the public mood towards them appears to sour. Though small, the demonstration outside Google was one of a number of anti-data center protests that took place across Europe last week. In Amsterdam, protesters scaled a crane at a Microsoft data center site and unfurled a “fuck AI” banner. “There’s local campaign groups against data centers popping up every week,” says Robins. “People are angry about data centers turning up in their back gardens. They’re angry about data centers flouting local opinion—and about the impact it has on wildlife.” The Thurrock site is located next to a fuel stop, where an arterial road meets the highway that encircles London. On the plot, the remnants of Arena Essex, a disused motorcycle racing stadium, border grassland scribbled with old footpaths, and a lake. Google acquired the site through a subsidiary in 2023. In May last year, it applied for permission to build a data center campus there. When locals caught wind, they coordinated with national wildlife and environmental groups and began to kick up a fuss. Of the 1,000 responses submitted by members of the public to the planning authority, only one supported the project. (Thurrock Council says that many of the responses were submitted by people living outside the local area.) The protest group argues that Google’s proposal fails to properly account for the negative effects of the data center development: the loss of the raceway sporting facility, the destruction of habitat for rare flora and fauna, and the up to 570,000 tonnes of emissions it could produce each year—which Foxglove claims cannot be accommodated under the UK government’s carbon budget. “We’re an outlier. We object on different grounds. I think that’s why I think we’re quite useful to the whole campaign,” says Mark Sexton, director at the Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club. “The unlikely alliance has got some attention.” Google says the objections are grounded in misconceptions about its plans. The company claims it will achieve a net gain in biodiversity by retaining habitat and transplanting endangered plants to another location; and that it will offset the emissions by financing new sources of renewable energy generation, with a view to becoming carbon-neutral by 2030. Google argues that razing the motorcycle stadium will not result in the loss of an invaluable community facility because the track has already been out of use for a number of years. “We want to be good neighbors,” says Elman. “We recognize the ecological value of these sites. Our goal is to minimize the impact as much as possible.” Unconvinced by Google’s reassurances, the protesters intend to continue to fight the development—one small act of protest at a time. “Do I think we’ve got much hope? Not right now,” says Rob Pownall, founder of nonprofit Protect The Wild, who attended Wednesday’s demonstration. “But this is another chip off that massive ice block.” There are some signs the grassroots anti-data center movement is starting to win concessions. In the US, some states have instituted permitting freezes and data center moratoria, and pro-data center candidates were roundly crushed in this week’s midterm elections. In the UK, Foxglove recently succeeded in a legal challenge that forced the government to withdraw planning permission for a data center to the west of London. Thurrock Council tells WIRED it expects to rule on Google’s initial planning application early next year. After that, the company will need to come up with a more granular plan for developing the site, which will be subject to another lengthy vetting process. The protesters say they intend to make life hard for Google at every step. “These planning campaigns can go on for years,” says Robins. “It’s a war of attrition.”

artigo.texto: Gumi City Launches Battery Demonstration Center to Expand Advanced Industries Following semiconductor and robot complexes, Gumi strengthens secondary battery sector with new infrastructure A demonstration center for comprehensively managing batteries, secondary batteries, will be established in Gumi, North Gyeongsang Province. On October 28, the groundbreaking ceremony for the BaaS, Battery as a Service, test demonstration center was held at the First Industrial Complex of the Gumi National Industrial Complex, hosted by the Korea Testing & Research Institute (KTR). Approximately 300 attendees, including Gumi Mayor Kim Jang-ho, Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan, Gyeongbuk Vice Governor for Economy Yang Geum-hee, and KTR President Lee Seung-ryeol, participated. BaaS is a business model that provides various services related to batteries, including repair, rental, charging, and reuse. The BaaS test demonstration center, built on a 24,576-square-meter site within the First Industrial Complex, spans a total floor area of 4,231 square meters and consists of six buildings. The total project cost amounted to 27.2 billion Korean won. The center evaluates the performance and safety of used batteries and supports their reuse in energy storage systems, ESS. KTR plans to provide full-cycle services for secondary batteries—from manufacturing to reuse—by integrating the center with its existing testing and certification systems. artigo.texto: Na tarde de 5 de novembro, o Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente de Hai Phong, em colaboração com a Allotrope Vietnam Co., Ltd., organizou uma conferência de treinamento sobre simulação de sistemas de comércio de emissões (SCE). Capacitar agências reguladoras e empresas com o conhecimento necessário para operar um mercado de carbono. Pesquisar, acessar e preparar gradualmente as condições para participar do mercado de carbono é um aspecto importante que visa apoiar a cidade de Hai Phong na adaptação proativa às novas tendências de desenvolvimento. Além de aprenderem sobre os princípios básicos do Sistema de Comércio de Emissões (SCE), os participantes participaram diretamente de três rodadas de simulações de cenários de negociação, tomando decisões sobre a gestão de cotas de emissão, escolhendo opções de conformidade e equilibrando os custos de redução de emissões sob a perspectiva tanto de agências governamentais quanto de empresas. Isso proporcionou uma oportunidade para melhor compreender os princípios de funcionamento, os métodos de negociação e o impacto do mercado de carbono na gestão, na produção e nas operações comerciais. Em seu discurso na conferência, o Sr. Pham Van Thuan, Diretor Adjunto do Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente, sugeriu que as agências de gestão estatal pesquisem e compreendam proativamente os princípios de funcionamento do sistema de comércio de emissões. Ele também enfatizou a necessidade de aumentar a conscientização sobre o papel e as responsabilidades das agências de gestão na organização dos inventários de gases de efeito estufa, no monitoramento dos resultados da redução de emissões e na preparação das condições necessárias para a implementação de mecanismos de gestão de emissões no futuro. Para a comunidade empresarial, especialmente para as instalações sujeitas a inventários de gases de efeito estufa, é crucial reconhecer que o inventário e a redução de emissões não são apenas uma exigência para o cumprimento da lei , mas também uma oportunidade para revisar os processos de produção, economizar energia, inovar em tecnologia, melhorar a eficiência no uso de recursos e aumentar a competitividade. As empresas precisam aprimorar proativamente suas capacidades de gestão de emissões e acessar gradualmente as ferramentas e os métodos operacionais do mercado de carbono. Especialistas e unidades colaboradoras organizaram sessões de treinamento com foco na transmissão de conhecimento essencial, na conexão da teoria com situações práticas, no fornecimento de orientações específicas e fáceis de entender durante exercícios de simulação e no compartilhamento de experiências e questões internacionais a serem consideradas ao aplicá-las às condições reais do Vietnã e à situação prática na cidade de Hai Phong. A transformação verde e a redução das emissões de carbono são processos de longo prazo que exigem o envolvimento sincronizado de todos os níveis, setores, da comunidade empresarial e da sociedade como um todo. Capacitar proativamente empresas e organizações com conhecimento, aprimorar suas capacidades e fornecer acesso antecipado a ferramentas de gestão de emissões ajudará Hai Phong a evitar ser pega de surpresa por novas demandas e a aproveitar efetivamente as oportunidades de desenvolvimento no período vindouro. artigo.texto: Next week, much of the industry will gather in Las Vegas for RE+ to talk about what gets built next. It’s an important conversation, but I’d encourage asset owners to bring a second question with them: what more can we get from what’s already been built? This question matters more than ever as electricity demand climbs and customers feel it on their monthly bill. EIA expects consumption to grow another 3.1% in 2027, driven largely by data centers and other commercial loads, while residential customers will pay nearly 5% more for power this year. The industry is working hard to add capacity, but getting it built takes time. According to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and GridTracker, the median project built in 2025 spent more than five years moving from interconnection request to commercial operation and only 13% of the capacity that requested interconnection between 2000 and 2020 had come online by the end of 2025. New generation is essential, but the fleet already operating is an opportunity we can’t afford to pass up. With nearly 52 gigawatts (GW) of utility-scale battery storage operating in the U.S. as of mid-2026, the installed base is too large to overlook and performance across it varies widely. When a battery energy storage system (BESS) falls short, the instinct is often to blame the battery and reach for augmentation or replacement, but in many cases the bottleneck is the controls, software and integration around it. Operating assets are under more pressure Higher prices should raise the value of delivering power when and where the grid needs it, yet revenues for many operating assets are moving in the other direction. In ERCOT, the average battery earned 84% less in 2025 than at its 2023 peak, as more storage competed for the same services. With incentive economics shifting too, asset managers face real pressure to get more from existing assets. At the same time, utilities are leaning on storage for grid stability. As more gas units face revenue pressure and retirement, the grid loses the spinning mass that provides inertia in the first moments of a disturbance. Grid-forming inverters can replace that inertia, often by upgrading existing storage rather than building new. Providing that support, alongside peak shaving, load shifting and voltage and frequency regulation, takes controls that respond faster than many legacy SCADA and EMS platforms were built to handle. Compliance requirements are moving just as quickly, with FERC Order No. 901 directing NERC to develop new reliability standards for inverter-based resources, including batteries, through 2030. Many plants operating today were designed before those requirements existed, increasing the importance of controls that can evolve as grid codes change. The same logic also applies to solar and wind plants. Once control functions are proven in the field they can easily be applied to other assets across the whole market. The battery isn’t always the bottleneck A recent Gridmatic study of 30 California batteries shows what’s at stake, with fleetwide availability averaging just under 80% and execution and bidding strategy driving a wide gap between top and bottom performers. Had every asset matched the leader, the group would have earned an estimated $98 million more over two years. The lesson isn't that every performance gap can be solved with software. It's that owners shouldn't assume the battery itself is the limiting factor. Before committing additional capital, owners should examine the full system: controls, software, market strategy, integration and plant-level coordination alongside battery health and hardware performance. Think about the smartphone in your pocket. Its hardware may be several years old, but software updates can improve how it performs and add capabilities that weren’t available when you bought it. Storage assets aren't so different: the physical equipment may still have years of useful life, while the controls and software around it can evolve to meet new market and grid requirements. A modern energy management and plant control platform layered onto existing assets can help owners: - Respond faster and more precisely to grid signals and market opportunities - Meet new grid code requirements through software rather than hardware - Expand operational flexibility and support additional value streams - Maximize usable energy through balancing and intelligent power allocation - Extend the competitive life of existing assets A controls retrofit in practice We saw this firsthand in the U.K., where our team, then part of Wärtsilä, worked with Zenobē to retrofit an existing 100 MW/100 MWh battery site with a new GEMS power plant controller. The upgrade took over energy management, secured grid compliance and added stateful grid-code functions such as de-load, along with control for multiple tenants sharing one point of interconnection. The batteries stayed in place, but the site gained new capabilities and is better prepared for future requirements. That same approach translates to U.S. markets, where interconnection rules and local regulations are evolving quickly. New deployments will remain critical, but the next wave of value may come from making today’s fleet work harder. As the industry gathers at RE+, owners should ask not just what they need to build next, but what more the assets already on the grid could deliver. Before replacing hardware or adding capacity, diagnose the whole plant. The constraint may not be the battery cells.

artigo.texto: GM to close Detroit battery assembly plant, but not for reasons you might think GM is closing a battery-assembly plant south of Detroit, a spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch. The Brownstown Battery Assembly Plant assembled battery packs for Cadillac’s flagship EV, the Celestiq, and both electric drive units (the motors that power the car) and battery packs for the Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray, a plug-in hybrid version of its famous sports car. Automotive News first reported the closure. The closure is not related to GM’s electric vehicle strategy, the spokesperson said. Instead, GM leased the site, and the lease was nearing its end. The employees and work at Brownstown will be moved to other GM facilities, though the company would not confirm which ones. Like many automakers, GM’s electrification strategy was thrown a curveball after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the sweeping federal law signed last year, repealed incentives to produce and sell EVs. Since then, the company has pared back its public comments on EVs, though it hasn’t given up on full electrification. GM continues to produce a range of EVs, including the Chevrolet Silverado EV and the limited-time-only Chevrolet Bolt. It also continues researching new battery chemistries, including lithium-manganese-rich and sodium-ion, and it’s rolling out a new $900 million facility to speed commercialization. artigo.texto: A movimentação também ocorre em um momento em que o Brasil tenta preservar sua competitividade na atração desse tipo de empreendimento, diante da disputa com países como Chile e Argentina, que também oferecem incentivos e desenvolvem infraestrutura para receber data centers. Procurada pela Bloomberg, a ByteDance não respondeu ao pedido de comentários. A expansão da infraestrutura está ligada aos planos da companhia de fazer da inteligência artificial (IA) um novo motor de crescimento. Para isso, a empresa vem ampliando os gastos com equipamentos e capacidade de processamento. Ao mesmo tempo, a resistência de eleitores americanos aos projetos de data centers nas eleições legislativas de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos pode desacelerar novas construções no país e levar desenvolvedoras a procurar outros mercados, como o Brasil. Ceará concentra projetos de data centers A ByteDance anunciou no ano passado um investimento de R$ 200 bilhões (US$ 36 bilhões) para construir um complexo de data centers no Pecém, em etapas. As obras da primeira fase começaram no início de 2026. A localização é considerada estratégica pela proximidade com Fortaleza, que concentra o maior hub de cabos de fibra óptica da América do Sul. A infraestrutura permite conectar o Brasil a outros mercados e facilita a exportação de dados. “A região de Fortaleza e o Nordeste em geral se destacam porque é justamente ali que chegam os cabos submarinos do Brasil”, afirmou Affonso Nina, presidente da Brasscom, associação que representa empresas do setor de tecnologia. “É uma localização privilegiada.” O Ceará também reúne condições favoráveis para o fornecimento de energia renovável. O estado está em uma das regiões brasileiras com maior potencial de geração eólica e solar, característica importante para data centers, que demandam grandes volumes de eletricidade. A capacidade instalada de data centers no Brasil mais do que dobrou desde 2022 e ultrapassou 1 gigawatt, segundo a Brasscom. A associação estima que o volume cresça cerca de 20% ao ano até 2031, quase triplicando em relação ao patamar de 2025. Incentivos fiscais e desafios de infraestrutura A construção de data centers no país deve ganhar impulso com os incentivos fiscais sancionados pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva em setembro. As medidas reduzem em cerca de um terço a carga tributária sobre a importação de servidores, processadores e equipamentos de rede, com o objetivo de tornar o Brasil mais competitivo na disputa por esses empreendimentos. O setor, porém, ainda aguarda a publicação das normas que vão detalhar quais produtos poderão receber os benefícios. Os projetos de data centers contam com apoio de diferentes partidos no Brasil e enfrentam resistência local limitada, ao contrário do que ocorre nos Estados Unidos. No discurso de vitória após sua reeleição, em outubro, Lula prometeu atrair mais empreendimentos do setor para o país. Apesar dos incentivos, a expansão depende de melhorias na infraestrutura elétrica. Um dos desafios é ampliar as linhas de transmissão para transportar energia renovável até os centros de consumo, especialmente no Sul do país. “Ainda temos outros desafios. Nossa rede de transmissão não consegue absorver todas as usinas que buscam conexão ao sistema”, afirmou Bruna de Barros Correia, sócia da área de energia do escritório BMA Advogados.

artigo.texto: O governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva destinou R$ 46,3 milhões para a criação de uma rede nacional de data centers. Anunciado nesta sexta-feira (6), o projeto pretende conectar centros de processamento de dados espalhados pelo Brasil, com atenção especial a estruturas de pequeno porte e localizadas no interior do país. Batizada de Prisma, a iniciativa será desenvolvida pelo Centro Brasileiro de Inovação em Tecnologias da Informação e da Comunicação (CPQD), em Campinas (SP), ao longo de 36 meses. A proposta é utilizar inteligência artificial (IA) para distribuir automaticamente tarefas de processamento entre os centros conectados, considerando a eficiência energética e a capacidade disponível em cada unidade. Como vai funcionar a rede nacional de data centers A plataforma deverá permitir que desenvolvedores encaminhem arquivos para processamento sem precisar escolher manualmente qual data center será responsável pela tarefa. O sistema identificará a central com as melhores condições de eficiência energética naquele momento e direcionará o trabalho para ela. A distribuição será administrada por inteligência artificial, que levará em conta a disponibilidade de capacidade de processamento e conexão das estruturas participantes. Outro recurso previsto é a possibilidade de transferir operações que já estejam em andamento. Caso outro data center apresente condições mais favoráveis durante o processamento, a plataforma poderá deslocar a tarefa para essa unidade. Segundo Gustavo Correa Lima, diretor de Tecnologia e Inovação do CPQD, essa capacidade também está relacionada à continuidade das operações. A intenção é reduzir a dependência de uma única central e permitir que o processamento seja mantido mesmo quando houver mudanças nas condições de funcionamento de determinado data center. Projeto busca fortalecer a soberania digital brasileira A proposta também pretende ampliar o controle nacional sobre a infraestrutura de processamento e armazenamento de dados. Para isso, a rede poderá reunir servidores de diferentes tipos de organizações instaladas no Brasil. Além das empresas especializadas em data centers, poderão participar operadoras de telecomunicações, indústrias, provedores de internet e outras companhias que tenham servidores com arquitetura de processamento de borda. Essa integração é apontada como uma das formas de fortalecer a soberania digital, já que permitirá utilizar estruturas distribuídas dentro do território brasileiro. Entre os resultados esperados estão a redução do consumo de energia elétrica e da pegada de carbono dos data centers, além da expansão da infraestrutura digital para regiões que atualmente recebem menos investimentos nesse setor. A iniciativa também pretende aumentar a capacidade de resposta a falhas no fornecimento de energia e a ataques cibernéticos. Finep será responsável pelos recursos O financiamento de R$ 46,3 milhões será administrado pela Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep), empresa pública vinculada ao Ministério da Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação (MCTI). A liberação dos recursos foi assinada pela instituição nesta sexta-feira (6). O dinheiro virá do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel), cuja iniciativa já recebeu aprovação do Ministério das Comunicações, pasta à qual está subordinado o conselho gestor do fundo. De acordo com Joana Meirelles, superintendente da Área de Saúde e Transformação Digital da Finep, a plataforma deverá ser nacional, segura e sustentável. A expectativa é que a infraestrutura possa atender setores considerados estratégicos, como saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações, apoiando a transformação digital dessas áreas. Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

artigo.texto: Carro da BYD chega a 503 km/h e bate recorde mundial de velocidade Modelo elétrico superou marca anterior, de 496,22 km/h, registrada em setembro de 2025, na Alemanha O carro superesportivo da BYD, Yangwang U9 Xtreme, atingiu 503,17 km/h e bateu o recorde mundial de velocidade. O marco foi comunicado pela fabricante nesta 6ª feira (06.nov.2026) e reconhecido pelo Guinness e pela FIA (Federação Internacional de Automobilismo). O teste feito foi registrado em 1º de novembro, durante um teste em uma estrada de Abu Dhabi, nos Emirados Árabes Unidos. O veículo superou seu próprio recorde anterior, de 496,22 km/h, estabelecido em setembro de 2025, na Alemanha. Segundo a BYD, o resultado garantiu ao modelo 2 recordes oficiais: - maior velocidade alcançada por um carro de produção em uma única direção; - maior velocidade registrada por um carro elétrico de produção nas mesmas condições. Para a realização do teste, as autoridades locais autorizaram o fechamento de um trecho de 10km de estrada. A maior reta disponível tinha 7km de extensão. #vídeo 🎥 Carro da BYD chega a 503 km/h e bate recorde mundial de velocidade publicidade 🚘 O carro superesportivo da BYD, Yangwang U9 Xtreme, atingiu 503,17 km/h e bateu o recorde mundial de velocidade. O marco foi comunicado pela fabricante nesta 6ª feira (06.nov.2026) e reconhecido pelo Guinness e pela FIA (Federação Internacional de Automobilismo). ⬇️ Assista ao vídeo: — Poder360 (@Poder360) November 6, 2026 SOBRE O CARRO O Yangwang U9 Xtreme tem 4 motores elétricos, um em cada roda, com potência combinada de 3.019 cavalos. O veículo também conta com suspensão inteligente e pneus desenvolvidos para altas velocidades. A suspensão hidráulica permite que o carro salte sobre obstáculos em meio segundo, segundo a BYD. Em uma demonstração, o U9 atingiu 120 km/h e percorreu cerca de 6 metros no ar. O sistema também permite movimentos sincronizados com música e luzes. O U9 convencional não é vendido no Brasil. Na China, custa a partir de 1,68 milhão de yuans (cerca de R$ 1,38 milhão). O U9 Xtreme terá produção limitada a 30 unidades.

artigo.texto: A comprehensive academic review published in Frontiers in Chemistry outlines how precise chemical fluorination transforms carbon nanotubes from inert conductive platforms into highly reactive components for advanced electrochemical energy storage. Writing across a framework linking synthesis routes, chemical bonding, structural evolution, and device performance, the researchers show that attaching fluorine atoms to one-dimensional carbon tubular lattices provides an exceptionally direct mechanism for manipulating electronic structure, surface polarity, and interfacial reactivity. The incorporation of fluorine replaces sp2-hybridized carbon networks with fluorinated sp3 local environments, generating a spectrum of semi-ionic and covalent carbon-fluorine bonds. Because pristine carbon nanotubes inherently feature chemically inert surfaces, restricted electrochemically active sites, and poor wettability toward polar ether- and carbonate-based battery electrolytes, chemical modification has become essential for expanding their roles beyond standard passive conductive additives. The structural characteristics and electrochemical utility of fluorinated carbon nanotubes depend decisively on the synthetic route used to introduce the halogen atoms, as different fluorination methods operate under distinct kinetic, thermal, and mass-transport regimes. Direct gas-phase fluorination utilizing pure fluorine gas or diluted fluorine-nitrogen mixtures at elevated temperatures between 200 °C and 600 °C remains the most common industrial method, enabling high fluorine loadings with fluorine-to-carbon atomic ratios approaching 0.8 to 1.0. However, because molecular fluorine has a kinetic diameter of approximately 0.35 nanometers, diffusion within tightly packed nanotube bundles is restricted, leading to localized over-fluorination, outer-wall exfoliation, and severe lattice disruption. Conversely, atomic fluorination driven by the thermal decomposition of xenon difluoride or terbium tetrafluoride releases atomic fluorine radicals with a van der Waals radius of roughly 0.147 nanometers. These smaller species access nanotube surfaces without mass-transfer barriers, yielding exceptionally homogeneous fluorine distributions dominated by semi-ionic configurations while preserving the structural integrity of the graphitic core. Alternative low-temperature and liquid-phase fluorination techniques offer further synthetic control by tailoring reactive species and functional penetration depths. Radio-frequency or microwave plasma fluorination using carbon tetrafluoride operates below 150 °C, generating reactive radicals and ionic fragments that are confined to the outermost atomic shells of the carbon nanotubes. This selective surface modification introduces carbon-fluorine, difluoromethylene, and trifluoromethyl groups while keeping the conductive inner graphitic channels intact, yielding modest fluorine contents below a fluorine-to-carbon ratio of 0.3 that enhance interfacial polarity without degrading electrical pathways. Liquid-phase routes, including solvothermal treatments with electrophilic Selectfluor at temperatures from 140 °C to 200 °C or nucleophilic room-temperature reactions with aqueous hydrofluoric acid, provide milder reaction environments that favor semi-ionic bond configurations. Additionally, solid-state pyrolytic techniques employing fluorine-donating precursors such as polytetrafluoroethylene or ammonium fluoride at 400 °C to 700 °C introduce low concentrations of fluorine without requiring corrosive gaseous reagents. Spectroscopic investigations resolve the intricate evolution of local chemical environments as fluorine accumulates on the carbon nanotube framework. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy distinguishes semi-ionic carbon-fluorine vibrations near 1110 reciprocal centimeters from covalent carbon-fluorine stretching bands appearing at 1210 to 1220 reciprocal centimeters, alongside difluoromethylene features emerging near 1340 reciprocal centimeters under deeper fluorination conditions. Complementary X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy identifies semi-ionic species by carbon 1s binding energies between 288.2 and 288.8 electronvolts and fluorine 1s peaks between 685.5 and 687.0 electronvolts, whereas covalent bonds emerge at higher carbon 1s energies of 289.4 to 290.4 electronvolts and fluorine 1s signals between 688.0 and 689.0 electronvolts. Solid-state fluorine-19 magic-angle-spinning nuclear magnetic resonance tracking demonstrates that semi-ionic configurations resonate near minus 152 parts per million, whereas strong covalent bonds appear near minus 190 parts per million and undergo downfield shifts toward minus 188 parts per million when fluorination temperatures increase from 350 °C to 430 °C, directly reflecting a progressive loss of ionic character and a strengthening of covalent bonding. Lattice alterations and morphological reconstructions driven by fluorination fundamentally reshape both physical dimensions and electronic transport within carbon nanotubes. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy reveals that fluorination expands the pristine graphitic interlayer spacing of 0.33 nanometers up to 0.67 nanometers in heavily treated outer walls while inner shells retain their native graphitic dimensions. Raman spectroscopy reflects this structural reorganization through increases in the defect-associated D-band to graphitic G-band intensity ratio, caused by the conversion of sp2 carbon into sp3 hybridization. artigo.texto: Transforming agricultural by-products into a resource. National Assembly Deputy Nguyen Thi Lan expressed strong agreement with the Government's submission and the verification report of the Committee on Science , Technology and Environment; and highly appreciated the meticulous and constructive work of the drafting agency and the verification agency. According to the deputy, the bold move to significantly reduce pre-approval procedures, thoroughly decentralize power, and shift to data-driven risk management is a crucial institutional breakthrough. National Assembly Deputy Nguyen Thi Lan ( Hanoi ). Photo: Quang Khanh Based on practical experience in scientific research and the agricultural and environmental fields, delegates proposed three key groups of solutions. Regarding the removal of bottlenecks in the management of agricultural by-products under Articles 72 and 72a, National Assembly delegate Nguyen Thi Lan highly appreciated the regulation allowing the management of waste that meets technical standards as products and goods. However, in reality, Vietnam generates more than 150 million tons of by-products annually, while there are still no complete legal criteria to determine when by-products are no longer considered waste. According to the delegates, this situation means that large biomass resources from straw, rice husks, shrimp pond mud, and livestock manure are still controlled as waste. Even the transportation of straw and rice husks for mushroom cultivation and animal feed must comply with waste transportation regulations, hindering production and the circular economy . Citing the European Union's experience in applying the "waste attribute termination" standard, the delegate argued that a clear legal mechanism is needed to transform by-products that meet technical requirements into marketable goods. In agreement with the verification report, National Assembly delegate Nguyen Thi Lan proposed adding to Clause 4, Article 72a the principle that the Government shall regulate the criteria for terminating waste attributes and issue technical safety standards for agricultural by-products. Once the standards are met, by-products can be circulated as goods, without the need for waste management procedures; the regulatory agency then switches to post-inspection control. According to the delegates, this is an important solution to remove legal barriers, effectively exploit biomass resources, and promote the circular economy in agriculture. Stratified greenhouse gas inventory, ensuring it aligns with implementation capacity. Regarding the regulations on greenhouse gas inventory in Article 91, National Assembly Deputy Nguyen Thi Lan agreed with the goal of shortening the emission inventory cycle to annual levels to standardize national data. The Deputy also noted that the draft initially delineates the reporting responsibilities of facilities on the list, requiring independent assessment for facilities allocated quotas. However, according to the delegates, the number of organizations qualified to conduct independent assessments in our country is currently limited. If the requirement for annual inventory and assessment is applied on a large scale immediately, while the infrastructure is not yet adequate, businesses will face significant pressure regarding compliance costs and risk delays in fulfilling their obligations. Therefore, legal requirements need to be linked to the conditions and capacity for implementation. A view of the discussion in the assembly hall. Photo: Quang Khánh Drawing on the experiences of Japan and South Korea regarding hierarchical management, delegates proposed amending Clauses 2 and 7 of Article 91 to require only annual independent inventory and assessment for facilities allocated quotas, such as coal-fired power plants, cement factories, and steel mills. For other facilities, such as agricultural, forestry, and aquatic product processing plants and textile factories, a biennial cycle should be maintained during the transitional period. In addition, delegates proposed combining a common online reporting tool and shifting strongly towards post-audit methods. A tiered approach would help ensure the goal of standardizing emission data, while being more aligned with implementation capacity and avoiding creating additional cost burdens for businesses. Regarding the carbon market in Article 139, National Assembly Deputy Nguyen Thi Lan stated that the draft has initially established a legal framework for this market. However, some programs and projects with significant emission reduction potential, such as the project to cultivate 1 million hectares of high-quality, low-emission rice or mangrove reforestation projects, still face difficulties in accessing long-term funding. According to the delegates, one of the obstacles is that carbon credits are not clearly defined as assets under the Civil Code, making them unsuitable for use as collateral. While cooperatives have emission reduction certifications and banks are interested in lending, the lack of a legal basis for property rights prevents the flow of financial resources. Citing New Zealand's experience in legalizing carbon credits as a special property right, allowing for the registration of security measures on the national data system, the delegate proposed adding to Clause 1 of Article 139 the principle that carbon credits and emission quotas are special assets, permitted to be mortgaged and registered as security measures when the conditions are met as prescribed. At the same time, the Government needs to be tasked with guiding the mechanisms for valuing and handling collateral assets, and establishing fair benefit-sharing mechanisms for farmers and cooperatives directly involved in forest conservation and low-emission rice production. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Por que o Brasil está atraindo investimentos bilionários em data centers? Publicado 07/11/2026 • 09:00 | Atualizado há 2 dias KEY POINTS Foto: pexels Ações de empresas de centros de dados de IA ficaram sob pressão após democratas conquistarem vitórias expressivas nas midterms. O Brasil vem ganhando espaço na disputa global por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial (IA). Enquanto comunidades nos Estados Unidos pressionam contra a construção de novos data centers, o país oferece incentivos fiscais, energia elétrica mais barata e um mercado consumidor em expansão para atrair gigantes como Amazon, Google e Microsoft. Uma reportagem publicada pela Revista Fortune, destaca que essa combinação favorece a expansão do setor no país. Além disso, a Lei REDATA, sancionada pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva em setembro, reduziu impostos sobre equipamentos de data centers e estabeleceu contrapartidas para estimular a pesquisa e o desenvolvimento no Brasil. Leia também: Imposto Seletivo deve começar em fevereiro de 2027; governo prevê manter IPI na transição O tamanho do mercado brasileiro já aparece nos planos das grandes empresas de tecnologia. A Amazon Web Services (AWS) investiu mais de US$ 3,8 bilhões (cerca de R$ 20,7 bilhões) em infraestrutura de data centers na região desde 2011. A companhia também prometeu investir outros US$ 1,8 bilhão (R$ 9,8 bilhões) até 2034. O Google pretende dobrar sua infraestrutura de computação em nuvem no Brasil até 2030, em resposta ao aumento da demanda. Já a Microsoft comprometeu US$ 2,7 bilhões (R$ 14,7 bilhões) para ampliar sua infraestrutura de nuvem e inteligência artificial ao longo de três anos. Embora a demanda local ainda impulsione grande parte da expansão na América Latina, Carlos Barrera, CEO da Atlas Renewable Energy, avalia que a região também pode receber investimentos que encontram dificuldades para avançar nos Estados Unidos. Outro atrativo é o custo da eletricidade. A energia no Brasil custa menos da metade do preço praticado nos Estados Unidos. De acordo com dados do Ministério de Minas e Energia, quase 87% da eletricidade brasileira vem de fontes renováveis. A expansão das usinas eólicas e solares também contribuiu para gerar excedentes de energia. Esse cenário favorece os data centers, que precisam de fornecimento constante de eletricidade para manter servidores e equipamentos de processamento em funcionamento. Entretanto, a vantagem pode enfrentar obstáculos. O Brasil precisará ampliar as linhas de transmissão para conectar os grandes empreendimentos à rede elétrica. Além disso, autoridades discutem os possíveis efeitos desses projetos nas contas de luz dos consumidores. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC A carga tributária brasileira também representava um desafio para o setor, já que os impostos federais sobre equipamentos importados elevavam os custos de construção. Para enfrentar o problema, Lula sancionou, em 15 de setembro, a Lei REDATA, que reduz impostos sobre equipamentos destinados a data centers que cumpram os requisitos legais. Em contrapartida, as empresas precisam oferecer pelo menos 10% dos serviços de computação qualificados a clientes brasileiros e investir 2% do valor dos equipamentos beneficiados em pesquisa e desenvolvimento no país. A iniciativa busca fortalecer a soberania digital. Segundo o Ministério do Desenvolvimento, 60% dos dados digitais brasileiros ainda são processados no exterior. Com mais capacidade computacional instalada localmente, o governo espera estimular empresas nacionais a desenvolver soluções de IA e reduzir a dependência de serviços estrangeiros. Apesar das oportunidades, a expansão dos data centers também enfrenta resistência. Poucos dias antes da entrada em vigor da REDATA, procuradores federais acionaram a Justiça contra um projeto ligado ao TikTok. Leia também: Ibovespa abre em queda e recua aos 165 mil pontos, com dólar a R$ 5,50 e juros em alta A ação exigiu um estudo de impacto ambiental e consulta ao povo indígena Anacé antes do início das operações. O episódio mostra que a atração de investimentos precisa considerar os efeitos dos empreendimentos sobre o meio ambiente e as comunidades próximas. Assim, o Brasil reúne condições para ampliar sua participação no mercado global de inteligência artificial. artigo.texto: TREX Energy Opens Lithium Battery Manufacturing Facility in Hyderabad TREX Energy's new Hyderabad facility is equipped with a 12 PPM automatic module assembly line to support the production of battery packs for energy storage applications. November 06, 2026. By News Bureau TREX Energy, an Indian energy storage company, has announced the opening of its lithium battery manufacturing facility at E-City, Raviryal, Maheshwaram, Hyderabad. Equipped with a 12 PPM automatic module assembly line, the line is designed to produce 52S battery packs used in 261 kWh and 5 MWh Energy Storage Systems (ESS). As India expands its renewable energy capacity, the need for reliable energy storage is growing across industries, utilities, and households. Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and other ESS solutions can help manage fluctuations in power supply, support peak-load management and provide backup power across a range of applications. The company's Hyderabad facility is intended to support this evolving demand through local manufacturing. The company aims to develop energy storage solutions suited to Indian operating conditions while helping reduce dependence on imports and improve delivery timelines. Bharat S. Chhittarka, Director, TREX Energy, said, "We're focused on reducing financing costs to make BESS more affordable and reliable for the Indian market. Energy must be available when it's needed, and BESS is a key solution." The Hyderabad facility features a 12 PPM automatic module assembly line, designed to manufacture battery modules at a rate of 12 parts per minute. Automation is intended to support production consistency, manufacturing efficiency and quality control as demand for energy storage solutions grows. The facility will manufacture battery packs for applications including 261kWh BESS configurations and larger energy storage systems. The company's offerings are designed to address the requirements of customers across residential, Commercial & Industrial (C&I) and utility-scale segments. Roshan Shaik, Technical Director, TREX Energy, said, "Our 12 PPM automatic module assembly line marks a significant step forward in TREX Energy's manufacturing capabilities. It enables us to produce battery modules efficiently and consistently, supporting BESS solutions ranging from 5 kWh to 5 MWh. This facility strengthens our ability to meet India's growing energy storage demand with scalable, reliable, and high-quality solutions." TREX Energy's product portfolio includes BESS ranging from 5 kWh to 5 MWh, catering to energy storage requirements across residential, commercial, industrial and utility-scale applications. Its offerings include C&I BESS solutions for factories, offices and commercial facilities to manage energy consumption, support backup power and improve operational resilience. The company also provides utility-scale BESS for grid-related applications and large renewable energy projects, along with residential energy storage systems and home inverter batteries for household backup requirements. Its battery pack and ESS solutions include configurations such as 52S battery packs designed for 261 kWh BESS and 5 MWh systems. By serving both residential customers and larger energy users, TREX Energy aims to address a broad range of energy storage requirements through its expanding product portfolio. The company is also planning the next phase of its manufacturing expansion. The Madhya Pradesh Government has allotted four acres of land to the company for its proposed Phase 2 facility. The planned expansion is expected to increase the company's manufacturing footprint and support its efforts to serve customers across additional markets in India. Further details regarding the facility's capacity, development timeline and commissioning are subject to confirmation. The Hyderabad facility represents TREX Energy's commitment to developing local manufacturing capabilities for India's evolving energy storage ecosystem. Through its focus on C&I applications, residential energy storage and utility-scale BESS solutions, the company aims to serve the varied requirements of businesses, households and energy infrastructure providers. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Regulamentação do Redata fica para depois de viagem de Lula à COP Miriam Belchior (Casa Civil) afirma que governo já encaminhou diretrizes da nova política para data centers A regulamentação do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) ficará para depois da viagem do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) à COP31 e à Cúpula da Asean, disse nesta 6ª feira (6.nov.2026) a ministra da Casa Civil, Miriam Belchior. Segundo a ministra, já está avançada a elaboração do decreto com as regras de acesso aos benefícios fiscais da nova política, mas o governo teve de priorizar nos últimos dias discussões relacionadas à transição energética, com vistas à ida de Lula à Conferência do Clima da ONU. “Está praticamente finalizado, mas nós tivemos que priorizar com o presidente outros temas, inclusive essa viagem dele da COP31. Essa discussão deverá se dar com ele na outra semana, quando a gente espera, então, anunciar a regulamentação”, disse Belchior a jornalistas depois da reunião do CNPE (Conselho Nacional de Política Energética). Lula embarca na 2ª feira (9.nov) para Antália, na Turquia, onde participa da COP. Depois, vai a Filipinas para a cúpula da Asean. Deve voltar ao Brasil em 16 de novembro. O projeto de lei que institui o Redata foi sancionado pelo presidente em 15 de setembro, mas o texto aprovado pelo Congresso ainda tem uma série de pontos pendentes de regulamentação. O principal é a definição das fontes de energia que serão exigidas para empreendimentos interessados no programa. O texto original estabelecia que só data centers abastecidos por energia 100% renovável poderiam receber os incentivos fiscais, mas uma alteração no Senado incluiu também fontes “consideradas de baixa emissão”. Isso abriu brecha para o uso de gás natural, defendido por representantes da indústria, governadores, congressistas e pelo ministro de Minas e Energia, Alexandre Silveira (PSD). Segundo o MME, a regulamentação do programa deve incluir “diversas fontes de energia” para que a lei garanta a atratividade de grandes centros de processamento de dados. Na avaliação da pasta, a inclusão do gás pode contribuir para dar previsibilidade a investidores internacionais e nacionais. A inclusão do gás natural não é consenso dentro do governo. Nas últimas semanas, integrantes do Ministério da Fazenda, da Casa Civil e de Minas e Energia participaram de uma série de reuniões sobre o tema. Segundo apurou o Poder360, atualmente já há convergência sobre o tema e a tendência é que o gás seja incluído na regulamentação. GÁS NATURAL NO REDATA Feita poucas horas antes da votação do texto no Senado, a alteração que abriu caminho para outras fontes de energia é resultado de uma articulação do setor de gás natural. O movimento também foi apoiado por congressistas que atuavam pelo avanço do texto, inclusive com sugestões de inclusão de outros tipos de fontes, como energia nuclear. Durante a tramitação no Senado, o senador Esperidião Amin (PP-SC) apresentou uma emenda para incluir expressamente geradores movidos a gás natural ou biometano entre as fontes admitidas. O trecho foi rejeitado pelo relator Cid Gomes (PSB-CE). Defensores do uso do gás natural argumentam que o combustível atua como fonte de transição para evitar instabilidade no fornecimento de energia aos data centers. As fontes eólica e a solar, duas das mais usadas no segmento de data centers ao redor do mundo, são intermitentes, ou seja, dependem de variáveis ambientais e não asseguram fornecimento constante ao longo do dia. Como os data centers precisam funcionar ininterruptamente para sustentar o processamento de dados de sites, redes sociais e ferramentas de inteligência artificial, é comum que esses empreendimentos usem sistemas secundários com outros tipos de abastecimento para situações de emergência ou interrupção de fornecimento. Já os críticos da medida afirmam que a inclusão de fontes não renováveis, mesmo que de baixa emissão, contraria as metas de descarbonização e pode reduzir a competitividade do país na atração de empresas de tecnologia.

artigo.texto: [SMM ESS Flash] A Revolta da Alemanha comissiona a primeira bateria doméstica de íons de sódio de 10 kWh, alocação de 2026 esgotada A startup Revolta, sediada em Frankfurt, instalou e comissionou a primeira bateria doméstica de íons de sódio de 10 kWh da Alemanha em uma propriedade perto de Aschaffenburg, um sistema com tensão nominal de 450 V composto por cinco módulos de 2 kWh combinados com um inversor SMA. Cada módulo pesa 18,7 kg, com classificação de proteção IP64 e densidade de energia de 107 Wh/kg e 141 Wh/l, carrega e descarrega a 0,4 C, o que corresponde a cerca de 2,5 horas, e a configuração de 10 kWh entrega uma potência máxima de cerca de 4 kW; a propriedade também abriga cerca de 20 kW de energia solar fotovoltaica e uma pequena central hidrelétrica convertida de um antigo moinho. A empresa enquadra a instalação como o início de seu lançamento comercial, permanecendo ainda em estágio piloto, com mais sistemas piloto em locais selecionados de clientes na Alemanha planejados para as próximas semanas e medidores gratuitos fornecidos para coletar dados operacionais; os módulos são listados a EUR 599 cada e o conjunto de cinco módulos de 10 kWh a EUR 2.995, com a alocação de 2026 esgotada e reservas abertas para 2027. Potência nominal, vida útil de ciclo e números de eficiência não foram divulgados, e os primeiros dados operacionais reais de armazenamento doméstico de íons de sódio na Alemanha fornecerão amostras de validação para desempenho em baixas temperaturas e segurança.

artigo.texto: After pushback, Ottawa voters approve 10-year moratorium on data centers Ottawa residents voted overwhelmingly to impose a 10-year moratorium on data centers, joining a national trend of communities restricting data centers on the November Ballot. After pushback, Ottawa voters approve 10-year moratorium on data centers Ottawa residents voted overwhelmingly to impose a 10-year moratorium on data centers, joining a national trend of communities restricting data centers on the November Ballot. Ottawa, Kansas, residents voted by over 70% to approve a 10-year moratorium on data centers following a lengthy back-and-forth between county residents, city officials, and third party spending. It started when a proposal for a data center popped up just on the outside of Ottawa. Franklin County resident, Jessica Christopher, brought her concerns to the city. "When they had discussed putting up this 450 megawatt or whatever data center, it was going to be about a mile from my house," Christopher said. Christopher and other residents began to feel their concerns about the project were not being met. So they started petitioning to let voters weigh in on the issue, under Kansas law. "We rallied the troops. We went and did a few drive-thru events. And when I was sitting there counting the last ones, we had 1031 (signatures)," Christopher said. Despite gathering significant support, Christopher said the group faced obstacles. City officials argued the petition could not make it onto the ballot, as it was an administrative issue and not a legislative. That's when Ottawa residents, including Michael Lewis, sued the city. "We filed for a writ of mandamus, which what that says is that's compelling your elected officials to do their job since their job was to put it on the ballot or accept it. They didn't do their job. The district clerk or district court judge ruled that, yes, the citizens do deserve to be heard," Lewis said. The efforts surrounding the issue led to the formation of Ottawa United, a group of residents focused on the issue of data centers. "It was a mix between Republicans and Democrats and a bunch of unaffiliated voters. And we all just came together for a common good, which is why we named it Ottawa United," Chirstopher said. The campaign also faced challenges from outside influences. KMBC 9 uncovered tens of thousands of dollars in campaign filings from a Virginia-based political action committee, called the Defend US PAC. The PAC spending focused on urging residents to vote no on data center issues in Kansas communities, including in Ottawa and Emporia. "There was at least five or six different mailers that showed up at the doors. We had text messages come in every week," Lewis said. On election day, voters approved the moratorium in Ottawa by just over 70%. "I broke down, it was amazing. It was the thing that I have made that I am the proudest of, other than my children," Christopher said. Ottawa joins other Kansas communities, and communities across the U.S., in addressing the controversial issue of data center development. "It was kind of nice not only winning for our community, but also pushing back to the big money interests, saying that we're not for sale," Lewis said.

artigo.texto: O governo federal espera anunciar a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata) na semana de 16 de novembro, após uma nova discussão com o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. A previsão foi apresentada pela ministra da Casa Civil, Miriam Belchior, nesta sexta-feira, 6 de novembro, durante entrevista coletiva após a reunião do Conselho Nacional de Política Energética (CNPE). Segundo a ministra, a elaboração das regras está praticamente concluída, mas a discussão com Lula precisou ser adiada porque outros assuntos foram priorizados na agenda presidencial, incluindo os preparativos para a 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31), na Turquia. “Provavelmente, essa discussão deverá se dar com ele na outra semana, não na próxima, porque ele estará fora, mas na outra semana, quando a gente espera, então, anunciar a regulamentação”, afirmou Miriam. As expectativas em relação ao decreto com a regulamentação são grandes por conta da incerteza sobre o enquadramento do gás natural e da fonte nuclear no suprimento dos empreendimentos beneficiados. Autoprodução Mais cedo, em discurso na reunião do CNPE, o presidente Lula voltou a defender que os data centers invistam na energia elétrica necessária para atendimento da própria demanda. “Qual é o país que tem condições de investimento em data center, que consome energia pra caramba, mais que o Brasil? Exigindo que quem vier investir construa a sua própria energia, porque não vai ser a energia do povo que vai ser utilizada para data center. E nós queremos que venha muita gente para cá, para fazer os investimentos”, afirmou o presidente. A fala foi interpretada no mercado como uma sinalização em favor da autoprodução e do conceito de adicionalidade, criticado pelo segmento de gás, que alega que a construção de nova geração renovável para os data centers vai exigir mais contratação de termelétricas a gás para equilibrar a oferta de fontes flexíveis de geração. O Redata O Redata foi instituído pela Lei 15.504, sancionada em 15 de setembro de 2026, para conceder incentivos tributários à instalação, ampliação e modernização de centros de processamento de dados no Brasil. O regime contempla empreendimentos voltados a serviços como armazenamento de dados, computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial. A legislação prevê a suspensão de tributos federais incidentes sobre a aquisição de equipamentos e componentes destinados aos empreendimentos habilitados, incluindo PIS/Cofins, Imposto sobre Produtos Industrializados (IPI) e Imposto de Importação. No caso das importações, o benefício relativo ao Imposto de Importação é restrito a produtos sem produção nacional equivalente, conforme relação a ser estabelecida pelo governo. Em contrapartida, as empresas deverão cumprir requisitos relacionados ao atendimento do mercado interno, à sustentabilidade e ao desenvolvimento tecnológico nacional. Entre as exigências previstas na lei está a destinação de pelo menos 10% do fornecimento efetivo de serviços de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados instalado com os incentivos ao mercado brasileiro. A obrigação poderá ser substituída por investimentos adicionais em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação, nas condições estabelecidas pela legislação. As empresas também deverão investir em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação no país o equivalente a 2% do valor dos produtos adquiridos com os benefícios fiscais. Na área ambiental, o Redata exige que a totalidade da demanda de energia elétrica dos empreendimentos seja atendida por contratos de suprimento ou autoprodução a partir de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. A lei também estabelece um limite de eficiência hídrica de 0,05 litro por kWh, com aferição anual. A regulamentação deverá estabelecer as condições para habilitação das empresas, os critérios de sustentabilidade e os procedimentos e prazos para comprovação das contrapartidas. A habilitação e a coabilitação ao regime serão concedidas pela Receita Federal.

artigo.texto: Reedâs view The marketâs freakout, driven by AI-related stocks, suggests a US midterm election that spells disaster for the tech industry. Thatâs not the full story. For one, many of the 40 local and state anti-data center measures that passed this week wonât halt construction altogether and certainly wonât affect compute coming online until 2029, at the earliest. What they mainly do is require tech companies to offer concessions and guarantees that a lot of the hyperscalers and data-center builders were already moving toward anyway, such as by offering cheap power, school funding, or distributing stock to help spread the wealth. Despite the fair amount of mudslinging at data centers and Big Tech from a number of victorious Democratic candidates, many of the tech executives Iâve spoken to this week see the vote as a rejection of the fringes on both the right and the left â and theyâre relieved about that. A move to the center may mean more productive relations between government officials and the tech industry, they say, and neither side wants to screw it up. Democrats also donât want to cause a recession, and they know tech is the economyâs bright spot. Sure, a lot of tech leaders made tactical blunders over the last couple of years when it comes to politics. Supporting a single candidate or a single party is always a bad move in the long term. Companies that took money from the presidentâs family or got sweetheart government contracts are going to face real scrutiny. We all can agree that Metaâs Mark Zuckerberg went further than he needed to in bending the knee to President Donald Trump, and got little for it. But companies like Microsoft, Apple, and Alphabet, which have mostly played the long game politically, wonât have to change much â they stayed close to both parties. They get that the political landscape is always changing, sometimes very quickly and drastically. And when that happens, you want as many friends as you can get. Notable - The data center buildout will continue, National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said Friday, even after voters made clear they favor limits on AI infrastructure construction.
